title: A Year Without the Car
body:
Twelve months ago, my husband Tom and I sold our ten-year-old estate car to a young couple from Bath. Our friends thought we had lost our minds. We have two children, Maya, who is nine, and Leo, who is six, and we live on the edge of Bristol, not in the centre. “How will you do the weekly shop?” my mother asked. It was a fair question.

The decision didn't come out of nowhere. The car had been sitting outside the house for most of the week, and it was costing us a fortune: insurance, road tax, repairs and petrol added up to almost three thousand pounds a year. When the garage told us the clutch needed replacing, we finally sat down and did the maths.

The first month was hard. It rained almost every day, and I quickly found out that a good waterproof jacket is worth every penny. Tom bought a second-hand cargo bike, which can carry both children and four bags of shopping. The kids loved it from day one. Leo calls it “the bus”.

We have joined a car club, so when we really need a car, for a trip to the coast or a visit to Tom's parents in Devon, we book one on an app and pay by the hour. We have used it eleven times this year. For longer journeys we take the train, and we have got used to planning ahead to get cheaper tickets.

Has it been perfect? No. A few times we have missed a party because the buses stopped running too early. If we lived in a village, I don't think we could manage without a car at all.

But we have saved more than two thousand pounds, and we are all fitter. Maya has started cycling to school with her friends. Would we buy a car again? Maybe one day. For now, we don't miss it.

title: The Interview on King Street
body:
Ana Ferreira had been living in Toronto for exactly six weeks when she got the email. A small design studio on King Street had seen her portfolio online and wanted to meet her. She read the message three times before she believed it.

In Lisbon, Ana had worked as a graphic designer for eight years. She had designed book covers, posters and logos for restaurants and theatres. But in Canada nobody knew her name, and she had sent out more than forty applications without a single reply. A friend had told her that Canadian employers often looked for “Canadian experience”, and she had started to worry that she would never get her foot in the door.

The night before the interview, she couldn't sleep. She went over her answers in front of the mirror and printed her best work, even though everything was on her laptop as well.

The interview was nothing like the ones she remembered from home. The studio was open-plan, with plants everywhere and a dog asleep under a desk. The creative director, a friendly man called Marcus Chen, wore jeans and running shoes. He offered her a coffee and asked her to call him Marcus.

Instead of asking about her weaknesses, he asked her to walk him through one of her projects. Ana chose a poster campaign for a jazz festival. As she talked, she forgot to be nervous. Then Marcus asked a question she hadn't expected: how would she organize a project if the client kept changing their mind? Ana smiled. In Lisbon, that had happened all the time.

At the end, Marcus told her that they had seen twelve candidates and that they would let her know by Friday. He also said her colour choices were “brave”. Ana wasn't sure whether that was a compliment.

On Thursday afternoon her phone rang. They were offering her a three-month contract, with the possibility of a permanent position. She would start on Monday.

That evening she called her mother in Portugal. “They didn't care about my Canadian experience,” she said. “They cared about my work.”

title: Saturdays at the Shelter
body:
For the past two years, I've been spending every Saturday morning at an animal shelter in northeast Portland. My alarm goes off at seven, which my college friends think is crazy for a weekend. But by eight o'clock I'm standing in a room full of barking dogs, and I wouldn't change it for anything.

I signed up after my own dog, Biscuit, died. My apartment felt empty, but I wasn't ready to adopt another pet. A coworker suggested volunteering instead. “You get all the love and none of the vet bills,” she joked.

The first few weeks weren't exactly glamorous. New volunteers have to complete a training course, and then they're usually given the jobs nobody else wants: washing bowls, cleaning cages and doing laundry. The shelter goes through an incredible number of towels. I've lost count of how many I've folded.

These days I'm allowed to walk the dogs, which is the best part of my week. Some of them are shy and need time to trust people. Others pull so hard on the leash that I come home with sore arms. There was a big gray pit bull named Tank who was terrified of everyone when he arrived. It took him a month to take a treat from my hand. Last spring a retired teacher adopted him, and she still sends the shelter photos of him asleep on her couch.

Not every story has a happy ending, and some days are tough. Older animals and dogs with health problems can wait for months. If more people adopted instead of buying puppies, the shelter wouldn't be so crowded.

Volunteering has changed me, though. I'm more patient than I used to be, and I've made friends with people I would never have met otherwise: a retired firefighter, two high school students and a nurse who works night shifts and still comes in every Saturday.

If you've been thinking about volunteering, just give it a try. The animals don't care what you do for a living. They just want someone to show up.

title: From the Paper to the Phone
body:
When I was growing up in Cork in the 1990s, the news came into our house at fixed times. Every morning my father bought the Irish Examiner at the newsagent's on the corner, and he read it at the kitchen table while his tea went cold. At six o'clock and again at nine, the whole family sat down in front of the RTÉ news. Nobody was allowed to talk during the headlines. If you had something to say, you had to wait for the weather forecast.

My grandmother, who lived with us, used to listen to the radio all day. She knew the name of every newsreader and had strong opinions about all of them.

Today things look very different. My father, who is now seventy-two, gave up his newspaper subscription three years ago. He reads the news on a tablet and complains that the print is too small, even though he knows how to make it bigger. My mother gets most of her news from a family WhatsApp group, which is not always a reliable source. Last month she was convinced that a famous singer had died. He hadn't.

As for my own children, they hardly ever watch the news on television. My daughter, who is sixteen, follows journalists on social media and watches short videos explaining world events. She is often better informed than I am, but she admits that it's hard to tell what is true and what is fake. Her school has started teaching media literacy, and I think that's a good thing.

I'm somewhere in the middle. I listen to podcasts on my commute and check the headlines on my phone far too often. I sometimes miss the old days, when the news ended and you could switch it off.

Last Christmas, as a joke, I gave my father a paper copy of the Examiner. He read every page, including the death notices. Then he looked up and said, “This is much better than the tablet.” I'm still not sure he was joking.

title: The Rota on the Fridge
body:
There are five of us in the flat in Fallowfield, and until last Tuesday there was one frying pan. It had been sitting in the sink for four days, covered in something orange.

I'm Priya, and I'd love to say I wasn't the one who started the argument. I was.

“Whose is this?” I asked, holding up the pan when everyone was in the kitchen.

Josh didn't look up from his phone. “Not mine. I haven't cooked since Sunday.”

“It's Callum's,” said Ellie. “He made that curry at two in the morning.”

Callum, who was eating cereal straight out of the box, looked hurt. “I was going to wash it. I've had three essays due this week.”

“We've all got essays,” I said. “But the bins haven't been taken out, the bathroom smells, and there isn't a clean mug in the whole flat.”

Then everyone started talking at once. Ellie said she always cleaned the bathroom and nobody ever noticed. Josh said he paid the same rent as everyone else and shouldn't have to clean up after other people. Our fifth flatmate, Tomasz, who rarely says much, quietly pointed out that he had bought the last three packs of toilet roll and nobody had paid him back.

It got quite heated. At one point Callum said I was acting like his mum, which I didn't take kindly to.

In the end it was Tomasz who calmed us down. He suggested a cleaning rota: each person takes one job a week, and the jobs move round, so nobody gets stuck with the bathroom forever. Anyone who leaves dishes in the sink overnight has to buy biscuits for the flat. We also agreed to put a fiver each into a jar for things like washing-up liquid and bin bags.

The rota has been on the fridge for a week now. So far it's working, although Josh has already bought biscuits twice. Callum washed the frying pan. It's still slightly orange, but we've decided to let that go.

title: A Morning at Service NSW
body:
When Kiri and I moved from Melbourne to Sydney in March, I thought the hardest part would be the packing. I was wrong. The hardest part was the paperwork.

In Australia, if you move to a different state, you have three months to swap your driver licence for a local one. You also need to update your address on the electoral roll and with your bank and Medicare. Most of this can be done online, but the licence transfer has to be done in person at a Service NSW centre.

I tried to book an appointment on the website on a Sunday evening. The first available slot at our local centre in Parramatta was in three weeks' time, so I chose a centre in Chatswood instead, which had one on Thursday at 8.45 am. I took the morning off work.

The night before, I checked the list of documents twice. I needed my Victorian licence, my passport and proof of my new address, such as a lease or a utility bill. Luckily, our first electricity bill had just arrived.

At the centre, a friendly woman in a green shirt checked my booking on a tablet and told me to take a seat. I'd expected to queue for hours, but I was called after ten minutes. The man at the counter looked at my documents, then frowned. The electricity bill was in Kiri's name, not mine.

“I'm afraid we can't accept this,” he said. “It has to be in your own name.”

My heart sank. Then I remembered that my bank sends statements with my address on them. I opened the banking app, downloaded last month's statement, and he was happy to accept that.

After that, everything went smoothly. He took my photo, I passed a quick eye test, and I paid the fee by card. He kept my old licence and said the new one would arrive by post within ten days.

Kiri laughed when I told her the story. “Next time,” she said, “put the bills in your name.”

title: Numbers on a Screen
body:
Darnell Brooks had never paid much attention to his health. At fifty-two, he drove a city bus across Chicago's South Side five days a week, and he figured that if he felt fine, he was fine. So when his doctor's office called and asked him to come in to discuss his blood test results, he assumed it was a mistake.

It wasn't. Dr. Patel turned her computer screen toward him and pointed at two numbers. His cholesterol was high, and his blood sugar was in the range doctors call prediabetes. “This doesn't mean you have diabetes,” she explained. “But if nothing changes, there's a good chance you'll develop it within a few years.”

Darnell's father had had diabetes and had lost part of his foot to the disease. That memory scared him more than the numbers did.

Dr. Patel didn't give him any medication. Instead, she referred him to a nutritionist and suggested he cut down on sugary drinks, fried food and white bread. Darnell admitted that he drank at least three cans of soda a day and often grabbed fast food between shifts.

The first two weeks were miserable. He missed his soda so much that he got headaches. His wife, Renee, decided to change her diet with him, which helped. They started cooking at home on Sundays and packing lunches for the week: brown rice, beans, grilled chicken and lots of vegetables. Darnell discovered that he actually liked roasted sweet potatoes, which surprised everyone, including himself.

He also started walking. At first it was only around the block after dinner, but after a few months he and Renee were walking along the lakefront every Saturday morning.

Six months later, he had another blood test. His cholesterol had come down, and his blood sugar was back in the normal range. He had lost twenty-two pounds without really trying.

“I still have a slice of pizza now and then,” he told his coworkers. “I'm no saint. But I want to be around to see my grandkids grow up.”

title: The Village That Refused to Die
body:
Twenty years ago, the village of Glenbrae, on the west coast of the Scottish Highlands, seemed to have no future. The school had closed because only four children were left. The post office had shut down, and the last shop, run by the same family for three generations, was about to follow. Young people moved away to Glasgow or Inverness as soon as they finished school, and many of the stone cottages stood empty for most of the year, used only as holiday homes.

“People used to say the last one out should turn off the lights,” remembers Morag Mackenzie, who has lived in Glenbrae all her life. “We laughed, but it wasn't really a joke.”

The turning point came in 2009, when the estate that owned most of the land around the village was put up for sale. Instead of waiting for another wealthy buyer, the residents decided to buy it themselves. Under Scottish law, local communities have the right to buy land in some situations, and with the help of government grants and money raised by the villagers, the sale was completed two years later.

What happened next surprised even the most optimistic residents. The community used the land to build twelve affordable houses, which were offered first to young families with local connections. A small wind turbine was put up on the hill, and the money from the electricity it sells pays for community projects. The old shop was taken over by volunteers and now sells local cheese, fish and bread as well as basic groceries.

In 2018 the primary school reopened with eleven pupils. Today it has twenty-six.

Not everything has been easy. There have been long arguments at community meetings, and some residents worried that the village would lose its quiet character. Finding staff for the shop in winter is still a challenge.

But Morag is proud. “My granddaughter goes to the same school I went to,” she says. “If you'd told me that twenty years ago, I wouldn't have believed you.”

title: The Safe Account
body:
Patricia Hughes had been retired for nine years, and she was proud of how well she had learned to use technology. She did her banking on a tablet and had even ordered her weekly shop online. So when she nearly lost twelve thousand pounds, nobody was more embarrassed than she was.

It started with a text message on a Tuesday morning in Leeds. It looked exactly like the messages her bank usually sent, and it said that someone had tried to pay £850 to an online shop with her card. If this wasn't her, she should expect a call from the fraud team.

Ten minutes later, the phone rang. The man on the line was polite and calm, and he knew her name, her address and the last four digits of her card. He explained that criminals had got into her account and that her savings were at risk. To protect her money, he said, she would have to move it to a new “safe account” that the bank had set up for her. He would stay on the line and talk her through it.

Patricia was frightened, and the man kept telling her that time was running out. She had already opened her banking app and typed in the first payment when he made a mistake. He told her not to mention any of this to anyone at her local branch, because some staff there might be “involved”.

Something about that didn't feel right. Her late husband used to say that if someone was rushing you, you should slow down. Patricia told the man she needed to make a cup of tea, hung up and called the number on the back of her card.

The real bank confirmed her fears within minutes. It had been a scam. No genuine bank would ever ask a customer to move money to a safe account.

Now Patricia gives talks about fraud at her local community centre. Her advice is simple: “Hang up and call your bank yourself. A real bank will never mind waiting.”

title: Back to School at Forty-Five
body:
Lisa Moreno worked in retail for twenty-three years, most of them at a home goods store in Columbus, Ohio. At forty-five, she went back to school. Last May, two years later, she graduated as a registered nurse. We asked her about the journey.

What made you decide to go back to school?
The store was cutting hours, and I was tired of being on my feet all day for very little money. But the real reason was my mom. She was in the hospital for three weeks, and I watched the nurses take care of her. I remember thinking, I could do that. I'd like to do that.

Were you worried about your age?
Terrified. On the first day of class I was sure everyone would think I was somebody's mother who had come to the wrong room. Most of my classmates were nineteen or twenty. But one of them, a guy named Andre, sat down next to me and asked if I wanted to start a study group.

How did you pay for it?
That was the hardest part. I got a grant for part of the tuition, and the rest came from our savings and a small loan. I kept working at the store on weekends for the first year, which meant I was exhausted most of the time. My husband took over most of the cooking.

What was the most difficult subject?
Chemistry. I hadn't studied it since high school, and I had forgotten everything. I failed my first test. My instructor told me that if I came to her office hours every week, I would pass, and she was right.

Did your years in retail help?
More than I expected. In retail, you learn to stay calm when people are angry or upset, and you learn to listen. Patients aren't so different from customers.

What would you say to someone who is thinking about changing careers?
Don't wait for the perfect moment, because it won't come. It's never too late to start something new.

title: Three Months Old and Already Dead
body:
Owain Price had saved for almost a year to buy his laptop. He was studying architecture at Cardiff University, and he needed something powerful enough to run design software. In September he finally paid £1,100 for it at a big electronics shop in the city centre.

Three months later, just before his end-of-term deadline, the screen went black and never came back on. Owain tried everything he could find online: holding down the power button for thirty seconds, unplugging the charger, even connecting it to his television. Nothing worked.

The next day he took it back to the shop with the receipt. The young man at the customer service desk had a look and shook his head. “It's outside our thirty-day returns period,” he said. “You'll have to contact the manufacturer. They'll probably send it away for repair, which takes four to six weeks.”

Owain didn't have six weeks. That evening his sister, who works for a solicitor, told him he had more rights than he thought. Under the Consumer Rights Act, if a product develops a fault within six months, it is assumed that the fault was there when you bought it, unless the shop can prove otherwise. And it is the shop, not the manufacturer, that is responsible.

So Owain wrote an email. He kept it polite but firm. He explained what had happened, attached a photo of the receipt and said that he expected a repair or a replacement within a reasonable time, as the law requires. He also mentioned that he needed the laptop urgently for his studies.

Two days later he received a reply from the store manager. She apologised for the confusion at the desk and offered him a brand-new replacement, which he could collect the same afternoon.

Owain backed up all his files that night, both to the cloud and to a memory stick. “I've learned two things,” he told his flatmates. “Know your rights, and never trust a laptop with your deadline.”

title: My First Set of Wheels
body:
I passed my driving test on a Tuesday in June, three days after my seventeenth birthday. The examiner in Austin told me I'd done a great job, although I'd nearly forgotten to signal at the last turn. I drove home with my dad in the passenger seat, grinning the whole way.

The next problem was obvious: I didn't have a car. For two years I'd been working weekends at a taco truck near Zilker Park, and I'd saved $6,200. My dad offered to add another thousand, as long as I paid for my own gas and insurance.

We spent three weekends looking. A new car was out of the question, so we checked used-car websites every evening. My dad had one rule: “If a deal looks too good to be true, it probably is.” He was right. One seller had a beautiful red convertible for $4,000, but he wouldn't let us look under the hood, and he wanted cash only.

Finally we found a silver 2014 Honda Civic with 98,000 miles on it. It belonged to a nurse who was moving to Denver and didn't want to drive it all that way. She let me take it for a test drive, and it felt smooth and quiet. Before we agreed to anything, my dad insisted on taking it to a mechanic he trusted. The mechanic said the brakes would need replacing soon, but otherwise it was in good shape.

The nurse was asking $7,500. My dad told me to mention the brakes and offer $6,800. I was so nervous that my voice shook, but she agreed to $7,000. We shook hands, signed the title and drove away.

That was four months ago. I've already spent a fortune on gas, and I've had to give my little brother a ride to soccer practice more times than I can count. But every morning when I see my car in the driveway, I still smile.

title: The Long Way to the Museum
body:
Hana had been in Galway for two hours, and she was already lost. Her phone battery had died, and the paper map from the hostel had got wet in the rain. She stopped outside a pub on Shop Street, where an older man in a flat cap was sitting on a bench with a newspaper.

“Excuse me,” she said. “Could you tell me how to get to the city museum?”

The man folded his newspaper. “The museum? Ah, you're not far at all. Where are you from, if you don't mind me asking?”

“From Korea. Seoul.”

“Seoul! My nephew taught English there for two years. He came home better with chopsticks than with a fork.” He laughed and pointed down the street. “Right. Keep going down here until you come to a big stone church on your left. That's not the cathedral, mind you, that's St Nicholas'. People mix them up all the time.”

“A stone church on the left,” Hana repeated.

“That's it. Now, don't turn there. Carry on past it until the street turns into Quay Street. You'll know it because it's full of buskers and people eating ice cream, even in the rain.”

“And then?”

“Then you'll see the river in front of you. You can't miss it. When you get to the water, turn left and you'll see an old stone arch. That's the Spanish Arch. It's been standing there since the 1500s, which is more than you can say for my knees. The museum is the modern building right beside it.”

“How long will it take to walk?”

“Ten minutes, if you don't stop. But you will stop, because there's a lovely little café on the corner, and you'd be mad not to try the scones.”

Hana smiled. “Thank you so much. You've been very kind.”

“Not at all. And if you get lost again, just ask anyone. Galway people love giving directions. We're terrible at short ones, though.”

He was right on both counts. The walk took twenty-five minutes, and the scones were excellent.

title: A Night in the Gods
body:
Saturday, 12 October

I'm writing this on the last train back to Reading, still buzzing. Dev surprised me with tickets for my thirtieth birthday, and tonight I went to a proper West End theatre for the first time in my life.

Our seats were right at the top, in what Dev says people call “the gods”. You have to climb about a hundred stairs to get there, and when I sat down I could hardly see the stage without leaning forward. The seats were so close together that my knees touched the back of the woman in front. But they only cost twenty-eight pounds each, so I wasn't complaining.

Before the show began, a voice announced that the lead actor was ill and that his part would be played by his understudy. A few people groaned. I felt sorry for the understudy before he'd even said a word.

I needn't have worried. The play was about two brothers who haven't spoken for twenty years and meet again at their father's funeral. It was funny at first, then very sad. The understudy, a young actor with a Scottish accent, was brilliant. In the second half there was a scene where he simply stood still and cried, and the whole theatre went completely silent. I could hear the man next to me sniffing.

In the interval we queued for ages for two tiny tubs of ice cream, which cost almost as much as our tickets. Worth it, though.

At the end, everyone stood up and clapped for a long time. When the understudy came forward to take his bow, the applause got even louder. He looked as if he couldn't believe it.

On the train, Dev asked me whether I'd go again. I said yes, but next time I'm bringing binoculars. And maybe a cushion.

title: Soaked but Happy on Waiheke
body:
Subject: You should have been there!

Hi Ellie,

How's London? I hope the weather's better there than it was here on Saturday, because I've never been so wet in my life. And I've never had a better night.

You remember I told you that Mere and I had tickets for the concert at that vineyard on Waiheke Island? We'd bought them back in May, and we'd been looking forward to it for months. The forecast had said “light showers”, so we took the ferry from Auckland with nothing but thin jackets and a picnic blanket.

By the time we got to the vineyard, the light showers had turned into proper rain. The field in front of the stage was already muddy, and people were wearing bin bags. Mere looked at me and said, “Should we just go home?” I almost agreed. If the next ferry hadn't been two hours away, we probably would have.

I'm so glad we didn't. The support act was a young singer from Rotorua who played guitar and sang half her songs in te reo Māori. Then the main band came on and, honestly, they were incredible. The lead singer took off his shoes and danced in the mud, and after that nobody cared about the rain any more. Strangers were sharing umbrellas and hugging. A man next to us lent Mere his spare raincoat, which was about three sizes too big for her.

For the last song, the rain actually stopped for five minutes, and everyone switched on their phone torches. It looked like a sky full of stars. I got goosebumps.

We caught the last ferry back at eleven, soaking wet and freezing, and still singing. My trainers are ruined, and I think I'm getting a cold. Totally worth it.

When you come home at Christmas, we'll find another concert. Hopefully a dry one.

Lots of love,
Aroha

title: Just a Trim, Please
body:
I should have known something was wrong when the stylist said, “Trust me.”

I'd been growing my hair for almost two years. It finally reached the middle of my back, and I wanted it to look perfect for my sister's wedding. All I needed was a trim, an inch at most, to get rid of the split ends. My usual stylist, Rosa, was on vacation, so I booked an appointment at a new salon in my neighborhood in Brooklyn. It had great reviews online and a free coffee machine. What could go wrong?

The stylist, a cheerful guy named Kyle, washed my hair and asked me what I wanted. I showed him with my fingers: one inch. He nodded, and then he started talking. He told me about his roommate, his cat, his plans to move to Los Angeles and a TV show he was watching. I was enjoying the conversation so much that I didn't look in the mirror.

That was a mistake. When he finally turned the chair around, I couldn't believe my eyes. My hair stopped just below my chin.

“Isn't it amazing?” Kyle said. “All that length was dragging your face down. This is so much fresher.”

I wanted to scream. Instead, I heard myself say, “Wow. It's very different.” I paid, I even left a tip, and I cried all the way home on the subway.

My roommate, Jess, was honest with me. “It actually looks good,” she said. “But I get why you're upset. He should have asked you first.” She was right. I called the salon the next day, and the manager apologized and refunded my money. She also offered me a free styling session before the wedding, which I accepted.

The strange thing is that at the wedding, at least five people told me my hair looked great. My sister said I looked ten years younger. I still haven't decided whether I've forgiven Kyle. But I've learned my lesson: next time, I'm watching the mirror the whole time.

title: Tips for Your USCIS Interview
body:
Posted by maria_in_denver

Hi everyone. I've been reading this forum for almost two years, ever since I started my green card application, and your posts helped me so much that I wanted to give something back. Last Thursday I had my interview at the USCIS field office near Denver, and I was approved! Here are my tips. Some of them might seem obvious, but I wish someone had told me.

1. Get there early, but not too early. My appointment was at 9:30, and the security guard wouldn't let us into the building until thirty minutes before. We had to wait outside in the cold, so bring a jacket.

2. Leave your phone in the car if you can. You go through security like at the airport, and some offices are strict about electronic devices.

3. Bring the originals of everything, not just copies. The officer asked to see my birth certificate, our marriage certificate and our joint lease. Put everything in a folder in the same order as your application, so you're not digging through a pile of papers while the officer waits.

4. If you applied through marriage, your spouse must come with you. The officer asked us questions separately for a few minutes: how we met, where we went on our first date, which side of the bed I sleep on. Don't try to memorize answers. Just be honest.

5. Photos help. We brought a small album with pictures from our wedding and trips with family. The officer only looked at a few, but it made the conversation easier.

6. Stay calm. My hands were shaking when we walked in, but the officer was friendly and professional. The whole interview took about twenty-five minutes.

7. Don't panic if you don't get a decision on the day. Ours came through on the online system two days later.

Good luck to everyone who's still waiting. It's a long process, but it does end!

title: My First Tax Return
body:
Until this year, I thought tax returns were something only adults with proper jobs had to worry about. Then I turned nineteen, and my dad sat me down at the kitchen table in Brisbane and said, “Right. Have you done your tax yet?”

I hadn't. I'd been working part-time at a café since July last year, making coffees on weekday afternoons around my uni classes. In Australia the financial year runs from 1 July to 30 June, and if you do your own tax return, it has to be lodged by 31 October. It was already the middle of October.

My first problem was that I didn't have a myGov account, which you need to connect to the Australian Taxation Office online. Setting it up took longer than I expected, mainly because I'd forgotten which email address I'd used for my Medicare card years ago.

Once I'd logged in, though, it was much easier than I'd feared. Most of the information was already there. My employer had sent my income statement to the tax office, so I could see exactly how much I'd earned and how much tax had already been taken out of my pay. I just had to check it was right.

Then Dad asked whether I had any deductions. I didn't even know what the word meant. He explained that some work-related costs can be taken off your income, so you pay less tax. I'd bought two pairs of black shoes for work, and I'd paid for a food safety course. Dad said I could probably claim the course, but not the shoes, because normal shoes don't count. I checked the rules on the website, and he was right.

When I pressed submit, the screen showed an estimate: I was getting a refund of $640. I honestly screamed.

The money arrived in my bank account about two weeks later. Dad suggested putting all of it into savings. I put half into savings and spent the other half on concert tickets. I think that's a fair compromise.

title: Two Problems, Ten Minutes
body:
At five past eight on Monday morning, Kwame Asante was number fourteen in the phone queue for his GP surgery in Sheffield. He had a streaming cold, a sore throat and, more worryingly, a knee that had been swelling up since his five-a-side football match on Thursday.

After twenty minutes of music, a receptionist answered. She asked a few questions about his symptoms and offered him an appointment at 11.40 with Dr Okonkwo. “Just so you know,” she added, “appointments are ten minutes, and the doctor may only be able to deal with one problem.”

Kwame decided the knee was more important. Colds go away on their own, he told himself. Knees don't always.

In the waiting room, he sneezed four times and got a disapproving look from an elderly man reading a magazine. He felt so guilty that he put on one of the masks from the box near the door.

Dr Okonkwo turned out to be young, quick and very friendly. She asked how he had hurt his knee. Kwame explained that he had twisted it while turning too fast, and that it had been getting stiffer every day. She bent and straightened his leg, pressed gently around the kneecap and asked him to walk across the room.

“The good news is that I don't think you've torn anything,” she said. “It looks like a sprain. I'd like you to rest it, put ice on it for twenty minutes a few times a day and keep it raised when you're sitting down.” She told him he could take ibuprofen for the pain, and that if it wasn't better in two weeks, he could refer himself to NHS physiotherapy online.

Then she looked at him over her glasses. “And for that cold, drink plenty of water and stay at home for a few days. You don't need antibiotics. They don't work on viruses.”

“So no football this week?” Kwame asked.

She laughed. “No football for at least a month.”

title: Behind the Pharmacy Counter
body:
My name is Farah Haddad, and I've been a pharmacist in Halifax for eleven years. People often think my job is just counting pills. Let me tell you about last Wednesday morning.

We open at nine, but I'm usually in by half past eight to check the prescriptions that have come in overnight from doctors' offices. By the time I unlock the door, there's already a line. First is Mr. MacLeod, a retired fisherman who comes in every month for his heart medication. He always tells me about his grandchildren, and I always remind him to take his pills with food.

At 9:15 a young mother arrives with a baby who has a rash. She's worried it might be something serious. I take a look and ask a few questions. It looks like a mild reaction, probably to a new laundry soap, so I recommend a gentle cream. I tell her that if the baby gets a fever or the rash spreads, she must see a doctor straight away.

Then a university student comes in with the symptoms of a bladder infection. In Nova Scotia, pharmacists are allowed to assess and prescribe for some minor conditions, so she doesn't have to wait days for a doctor's appointment. We go into the small consultation room, I ask her some questions, and twenty minutes later she leaves with antibiotics.

Between customers, I give three flu shots, answer the phone about a dozen times and call a doctor's office because one prescription doesn't look right. The dose is ten times higher than it should be. The doctor's assistant checks and confirms it was a typing mistake. Catching errors like that is one of the most important parts of my job, even though nobody ever sees it.

At noon I finally get a cup of coffee, which has gone cold by the time I drink it. My feet hurt, and I've barely sat down. But I've helped about forty people, and that's a good morning.

title: Number Thirty on the Stairs
body:
The advert went up on a Tuesday at lunchtime: a one-bedroom flat in Rathmines, Dublin, €1,950 a month, viewing on Thursday at six. By the time Niamh Byrne finished her shift at the hospital and emailed the agent, more than two hundred people had already asked about it.

When she arrived on Thursday, the queue went out of the front door, down the steps and along the street. Niamh counted. She was number thirty. In front of her were a young couple from Brazil holding a folder of documents, and two students who were whispering about whether their parents would act as guarantors.

The agent, a tired-looking woman with a clipboard, let people in five at a time. Each group had about four minutes. The flat was small but bright, with a new kitchen and a window that looked over the back gardens. The bathroom was so narrow that you had to step sideways to close the door. A woman behind Niamh said quietly that it was the nicest place she had seen in three months of searching.

On the way out, the agent handed everyone a form. She told them that the landlord wanted references from a previous landlord and an employer, three months of bank statements and proof of income. Anyone who was interested should send everything by nine the next morning.

Niamh stayed up until midnight getting it all together. She also wrote a short letter about herself: a nurse, a non-smoker, no pets, quiet, and someone who had been renting for eight years without a single late payment. She had heard that a personal letter could help you stand out from the crowd.

She never heard back. A week later the advert disappeared.

In the end, she found a flat the old-fashioned way. A colleague's aunt was moving to Galway and was looking for someone reliable to take over her lease. Niamh moved in a month later. It's further from work, and the shower is cold in the mornings. She doesn't mind at all.

title: Cold Radiators and a Surprise Bill
body:
Subject: Flat 4, 27 Elmwood Road: heating problems and service charge statement

Dear Mr Hartley,

I am writing about two issues at Flat 4, which I have been renting from you since March last year.

Firstly, the radiators. Since the beginning of November, the radiators in the bedroom and living room have only been getting warm for an hour or two each evening, and the one in the bathroom has not worked at all. I reported this by phone on 6 November and again by email on 15 November, but nobody has come to look at it yet. The temperature in the flat has dropped to 14 degrees on several mornings, and I have had to buy an electric heater, which is expensive to run. As the heating in the building is communal, I am unable to fix this myself.

Secondly, the service charge statement. Under my tenancy agreement, I pay £85 a month towards the building's heating and maintenance. On Monday I received a statement asking me to pay an extra £420 for last year, mostly for “heating costs”. I find this difficult to accept, given that the heating has not been working properly for weeks. The statement also includes £160 for gardening, although the building has no garden, only a small paved area by the bins.

I would be grateful if you could:
1. arrange for an engineer to inspect the heating system within the next seven days;
2. send me a detailed breakdown of the service charge, including copies of the invoices;
3. confirm that I do not need to pay the extra £420 until these questions have been answered.

I have always paid my rent on time, and I would like to sort this out in a friendly way. However, if the heating is not repaired soon, I may need to contact the council's private housing team for advice.

I look forward to hearing from you.

title: The Film Inside the Camera
body:
Theo Nakamura goes to the Rose Bowl Flea Market in Pasadena on the second Sunday of every month. He's a photography student, and he likes old cameras the way some people like old records. Most of the time he just looks. But in March, at a stall full of lamps and old vases, he saw a silver film camera from the 1970s with a broken strap and a price tag that said $40.

The seller, an older man in a Dodgers cap, told him it had come from a house clearance in Long Beach. “I've got no idea if it works,” he said. “Thirty-five, and it's yours.”

When Theo got home, he noticed that the film counter showed the number 24. There was still a roll of film inside. Someone had used it and never taken it out.

He knew that film this old might be completely ruined, but he took it to a small lab in Burbank that specializes in developing expired film. A week later, the owner called him. “You're lucky,” she said. “About half of them came out.”

The photos were faded and slightly orange, but you could clearly see a family at a beach: a mother with big sunglasses, a father lighting a barbecue, and a little girl of about six holding up a crab and laughing. In the corner of each picture, the camera had printed the date: August 1987.

Theo posted three of the pictures online and asked if anyone recognized the family. For two weeks, nothing happened. Then a Long Beach community page shared the post, and within a day he got a message. “That's me with the crab,” a woman wrote. “Those are my parents. My dad passed away last year, and we cleared out his house in January.”

Her name was Denise. She was forty-five now and had two kids of her own. Theo mailed her the prints and the negatives, and she sent back a photo of them framed on her wall.

He kept the camera. It works perfectly.

title: The Noise
body:
Monday 3 June
There's a noise coming from somewhere under my car. It's a sort of low humming that gets louder when I go faster, and it's worse when I turn left. I turned the radio up on the way home from work. Problem solved, for now.

Wednesday 5 June
The radio isn't loud enough any more. On the motorway this morning, a truck driver looked at me as if I was driving a tractor. Hemi from work says it's probably a wheel bearing and that I shouldn't put it off, because if it gets bad enough, the wheel can actually lock up. I've booked the car into the garage near my flat in Christchurch for Friday. My Warrant of Fitness runs out at the end of the month anyway, so they can check that at the same time.

Friday 7 June
Dropped the car off at eight and caught the bus to work. At eleven the mechanic, Leanne, rang. Good news and bad news. The good news: Hemi was right, it's the front left wheel bearing. The bad news: while the car was up on the hoist, she noticed that the rubber cover on one of the CV joints is split, and both rear tyres are close to the legal limit. Without new tyres, the car won't pass its WOF.

The total quote was $890. I nearly dropped my phone.

I asked whether everything had to be done straight away. Leanne was honest. The bearing and the tyres couldn't wait, she said, but the CV joint would probably last another couple of months if I kept an eye on it. That brought it down to $610. Still painful, but better.

Saturday 8 June
Picked the car up this morning. It's so quiet that I keep thinking the engine has stopped. Leanne gave me the old bearing to look at, which was a nice touch, although I'm not sure what I'm supposed to do with it.

Note to self: start putting $50 a week into a car savings account. And next time there's a strange noise, don't just turn the radio up.

title: Medium Rare, Please
body:
It was Isla and Ravi's fifth anniversary, and they had booked a table at a small bistro in Edinburgh's New Town. The starters were delicious. Then the main courses arrived.

Ravi cut into his steak and frowned. It was grey all the way through. Isla's risotto looked fine, but when she tasted it, it was barely warm.

“Should we say something?” Ravi whispered. “I hate making a fuss.”

“We're paying sixty pounds for this,” Isla whispered back. “We're saying something. Politely.”

She caught the waiter's eye, and he came over with a smile.

“Is everything all right with your meals?”

“I'm sorry to bother you,” Isla said, “but I'm afraid there are a couple of problems. My partner asked for his steak medium rare, and this one is well done. And my risotto is lukewarm. It tastes lovely, but it's not hot.”

The waiter looked at the steak and winced. “You're absolutely right. That's not medium rare at all. I do apologise. Would you like me to ask the kitchen to cook you a new one?”

“Yes, please, if it's not too much trouble,” said Ravi.

“No trouble at all. And I'll get the risotto heated up straight away. Or would you prefer something else from the menu?”

Isla thought for a moment. “Actually, could I have the sea bass instead?”

“Of course. It'll be about fifteen minutes.”

A few minutes later, a woman in a black jacket came to their table and introduced herself as the manager. “I've heard what happened,” she said. “We've got a new chef on the grill tonight, but that's no excuse. Your main courses will be on the house this evening.”

“Oh, there's really no need,” Ravi said.

“I insist. And I hear it's a special occasion?”

When dessert came, there was a candle on top of the chocolate tart and a small card that said Happy Anniversary.

On the way home, Ravi admitted that complaining hadn't been so bad. “You did it so nicely,” he said. “I'd have just eaten the steak and been grumpy all night.”

title: Delivered, Apparently
body:
Gurpreet Sandhu spent most of November knitting a scarf and hat for her niece's first winter in Winnipeg. On the first of December, she wrapped them in tissue paper, added a card and a bag of homemade cookies, and sent the parcel from the Canada Post counter in her local pharmacy in Calgary. She paid a little extra for tracking. The clerk told her it should arrive within four business days.

On day three, the tracking page said “Delivered”. Gurpreet waited for her sister to call and say thank you. She didn't. When Gurpreet finally phoned her, her sister said that nothing had arrived. There was nothing in the mailbox, nothing at the door and no card saying the parcel was waiting at the post office.

Gurpreet's first thought was that someone had stolen it from the front step. Parcel theft had become a real problem in her sister's neighbourhood. But her sister had a doorbell camera, and the video from that afternoon showed no delivery at all.

The next morning, Gurpreet went online to report the problem. The website explained that she had to wait at least five business days after the expected delivery date before she could open an investigation. In the meantime, it suggested checking with neighbours, in case the parcel had been left at the wrong address. She also kept her receipt, which she would need if she made a claim. Her tracking included cover of up to $100.

Five days later, she filled in the claim form. She described the contents, attached a photo of the receipt and explained that the video showed no delivery. A week went by with no reply.

Then, on the nineteenth, her sister called, laughing. An elderly man had knocked on her door holding the parcel. He lived on a street with the same name, but “Crescent” instead of “Drive”, about three streets away. It had been sitting on his porch while he was visiting his son in Edmonton.

Gurpreet cancelled the claim. The cookies were a bit stale, but the hat fitted perfectly.

title: No Address, No Account
body:
When I arrived in Birmingham from Bogotá last September to start a job as a lab technician at a hospital, I had two suitcases, a contract and a list of things to do. Opening a bank account was near the top. I thought it would take an afternoon. It took nearly three weeks.

The problem is something every newcomer here seems to know about. To open an account, most banks want proof of your address, like a utility bill or a tenancy agreement. But to rent a flat, landlords usually want you to have a UK bank account. And to pay you, your employer needs your account details. I was staying in a short-let flat that I'd booked online, so I had nothing with my name and address on it.

At the first bank I tried, the adviser was very kind but couldn't help. “I'm afraid the system won't let me go any further without proof of address,” she said. At the second, I waited forty minutes only to be told that I needed an appointment.

A colleague from the Philippines, who had been through exactly the same thing two years earlier, gave me some advice. First, she said, ask HR for a letter confirming your job, your salary and your address in the UK. Second, if that doesn't work, try one of the app-based banks, which often let you open an account with just your passport and visa details.

The HR department wrote the letter the same day. I took it to a third bank, together with my passport and visa, and this time it worked. The adviser filled in the forms with me, explained the difference between a current account and a savings account, and told me my debit card would arrive by post within a week. It came in five days.

Looking back, it was frustrating, but I learned something useful: in a new country, the best information often comes from people who have just done it themselves. Now, whenever someone new joins our team, I'm the one who tells them to ask HR for that letter.

title: No, Thank You, Really
body:
Carlos Mendoza had been with the same phone company in Phoenix for six years, and his contract had finally ended. His bill had gone up three times in a year, and a rival company was offering the same plan for half the price. All he had to do was cancel. How hard could it be?

He called on a Saturday morning. After pressing four different numbers and listening to the same song for twenty-five minutes, he heard a voice.

“Thanks for calling. My name's Brandon. How can I make your day amazing?”

“Hi, Brandon. I'd like to cancel my account, please.”

There was a short pause. “Oh no! Can I ask why you're leaving us?”

“It's too expensive.”

“I totally understand. But you've been a loyal customer for six years, so I can offer you twenty percent off for the next twelve months.”

“That's kind, but I've already made up my mind.”

“What if I add unlimited data and a free streaming subscription?”

“No, thanks. I'd just like to cancel.”

“Okay. I have to let you know that if you leave today, you'll lose your loyalty points, and you might have to pay a fee for the router.”

Carlos took a deep breath. He had read his contract the night before. “My contract ended on the fourteenth, so there shouldn't be any cancellation fee. And I'll mail the router back this week.”

“You know your stuff,” Brandon said. “One last thing. If I could get your bill down to thirty-five dollars a month, would you stay?”

For a second, Carlos was tempted. Then he remembered that his bill had once been thirty-five dollars before it crept up. “No, thank you. Really. Please cancel the account.”

“All right. It's done. Your account will close at the end of the billing period.”

“Could I have a confirmation number, please?”

Brandon read out a long code, and Carlos wrote it down. Then he hung up. He felt as if he'd run a marathon.

That afternoon, he got a text from the company. It offered him forty percent off if he came back.

title: The Climbing Taster Session
body:
For three years, my commute has been the twelve steps from my bed to the desk in my spare room. I work from home as a software tester for a company in Leeds, and although I love not having to catch the tram every morning, I had noticed that some days I didn't leave the flat at all. My back hurt, my shoulders were stiff, and my step counter had become embarrassing.

So when my neighbour Femi mentioned that the new bouldering centre in Ancoats was offering free taster sessions, I ran out of excuses. Bouldering, if you haven't tried it, is climbing on low walls without ropes, with thick mats underneath to catch you when you fall. And you do fall.

The instructor, a cheerful woman called Jess, showed us how to warm up properly and how to land safely. Then she pointed at the easiest route, marked with little yellow holds. “Use your legs, not your arms,” she kept saying. I ignored her completely. By the end of the hour I had pulled myself up the yellow route four times, and I felt like a superhero.

The next morning I couldn't lift my coffee mug. My forearms were so sore that typing was a slow, painful business, and I had to turn my camera off during the team meeting because I was pulling faces every time I moved the mouse. My manager asked if I was all right. I told him I had been climbing. He laughed so much he had to mute himself.

That was six months ago. Since then I have been going three times a week, and I've worked my way up to the green routes. My back pain has almost disappeared, and I've made a group of friends who meet for pizza after the Thursday sessions. If someone had told me last year that I'd be spending my evenings hanging off a wall, I wouldn't have believed them. I still don't always use my legs, though. Jess says I'm a lost cause.

title: The Washington Trip Debate
body:
The meeting in the Lincoln Middle School cafeteria was supposed to last forty-five minutes. It lasted almost two hours.

Ms. Alvarez, the eighth-grade social studies teacher, began by presenting the plan for the spring trip: four days in Washington, D.C., with visits to the Capitol, the Smithsonian museums and the Lincoln Memorial. The students would fly from Chicago and stay in a hotel near the National Mall. Then she put the price on the screen: $1,450 per student.

There was a long silence. Then several hands went up at once.

Marcus Reed, whose twins are both in eighth grade, spoke first. “I'm sure it's a great trip,” he said, “but that's almost three thousand dollars for my family. We'd have to cancel our own vacation.” A few parents nodded. Another mother pointed out that some families at the school can barely pay their rent, and that a trip only wealthy kids could afford would divide the class.

Others disagreed. Dr. Karen Liu argued that the trip was a once-in-a-lifetime experience and that the school had been saving for it through bake sales for two years. “If we make it cheaper, it won't be the same trip,” she insisted.

Ms. Alvarez explained that a fund already existed for families who needed help, but that it only had about $6,000 in it. She admitted that wasn't enough.

In the end, a compromise was suggested by a father who hadn't said a word all evening. Why not take a bus instead of a plane and stay in a cheaper hotel outside the city? It would add travel time, but it could bring the price down to around $850. The parents also agreed to organize a car wash and a raffle to grow the fund.

A vote was held, and the bus plan passed by a large majority. Not everyone was happy. Dr. Liu said the kids would spend half the trip on the highway. But Marcus Reed shook hands with Ms. Alvarez on his way out. “Now my kids can both go,” he said. “That's what matters.”

title: Two Days Without My Rucksack
body:
Aisha Rahman realised her mistake about ten seconds after the doors closed. She was standing on the platform at London Paddington, watching the train slide away towards the depot, and her rucksack was still on the luggage rack above seat 42.

It wasn't the laptop inside that worried her most, although that was bad enough. It was her sketchbook. Aisha is an illustration student, and the book contained three months of drawings for her final project, which was due in two weeks.

She ran to the information desk, where a calm member of staff called Graham listened to her story. “Don't panic,” he said. “Things are found on trains all the time. The cleaners check every carriage at the end of the line, and anything they find is handed in.” He told her to fill in a lost property report online and gave her a reference number.

The next day was the longest of her life. She refreshed her emails every few minutes. She rang the lost property office twice and was told both times that nothing matching her description had been logged yet. Her flatmate tried to cheer her up by pointing out that nobody would steal a book of drawings of pigeons. It didn't help.

On the second morning, a message finally arrived: a navy rucksack containing a laptop and a sketchbook had been handed in at the depot and sent to the lost property office. To collect it, she would need to bring photo ID and describe the contents. There was also a small handling fee, which she would happily have paid ten times over.

At the office, a woman checked her passport, asked her what was drawn on the first page of the sketchbook and then brought out the bag. Everything was there. Aisha almost hugged her.

She has since written her name, phone number and university email on a label inside the bag. “I used to think labels were for children's lunch boxes,” she says. “Now I've learned my lesson.”

title: A Report at Pearse Street
body:
When Ciarán Doyle came out of the library on Pearse Street, his lock was still on the railing, cut neatly in two. His bike, a green second-hand road bike he had been riding to college for three years, was gone.

His first reaction was to walk up and down the street, as if the thief might have left it round the corner. Then he did what his flatmate had always told him to do: he went to report it. The Garda station was only five minutes away.

The guard at the front desk, Garda Siobhán Kelly, took out a form and asked him a list of questions.
“When did you last see the bike?”
“About half two. I locked it up and went into the library.”
“And when did you find it missing?”
“Just after six.”
“Can you describe it?”
Ciarán told her the make, the colour, and about the sticker of a sheep on the frame. Then she asked the question he had been dreading. “Do you have the frame number?”
He didn't. He had never even looked for it.

Garda Kelly was sympathetic but honest. Hundreds of bikes are stolen in Dublin every year, she explained, and only a small number are ever returned to their owners, mainly because nobody can prove which bike is theirs. She suggested he check online marketplaces over the next few weeks, since stolen bikes often turn up for sale. If he spotted his, he should contact the station rather than meet the seller himself.

She gave him a PULSE number, the reference the guards use for every incident, which he would need if he wanted to claim on his insurance. Unfortunately, his insurance didn't cover bikes.

Ten days later, Ciarán found a green road bike with a sheep sticker on a buy-and-sell website. He rang the station, and two guards went to meet the “seller”. The bike came back with a new saddle, which the thief had kindly fitted.

Ciarán has now written down his frame number, registered the bike on a national database and bought a much heavier lock. “It cost me sixty euro,” he says. “Best money I've ever spent.”

title: End of the Line in Sacramento
body:
The announcement came just after breakfast, somewhere north of Sacramento. “Ladies and gentlemen, this is your conductor speaking. Due to a mudslide on the tracks south of here, this train will be terminating in Sacramento. We apologize for the inconvenience.”

For a moment the dining car went quiet. The Coast Starlight was supposed to carry us all the way from Seattle to Los Angeles, a journey of thirty-five hours past mountains, forests and the Pacific coast. Now, eleven hours before the end, it was simply going to stop.

The woman across the table from me, a retired teacher named Gloria, put down her coffee. “Well,” she said, “I've always wanted to see Sacramento.” I couldn't tell if she was joking.

When we pulled into the station, Amtrak staff were waiting on the platform with clipboards. They explained that buses had been arranged to take passengers to Los Angeles, but the first one wouldn't leave for three hours and the trip would take about seven. Anyone who preferred could get a partial refund instead.

People reacted in very different ways. A young couple with a baby headed straight for the car rental counter, saying they would rather drive themselves. Two college students decided to spend a night in Sacramento and look around the old town. A businessman in a gray suit spent forty minutes on the phone, arguing loudly with somebody about a missed meeting, and then booked a flight from the local airport.

I had a cousin in San Francisco, which is only a couple of hours away, so I called her. She told me to take the regional train down to the Bay Area and stay with her for the weekend. I'd been meaning to visit her for years.

Gloria, meanwhile, took the bus. She texted me late that night: “Arrived in LA at 11 pm. Sat next to a man who told me his whole life story. Best part of the trip.”

I still haven't seen the whole route of the Coast Starlight. But if the train hadn't stopped in Sacramento, I wouldn't have spent the best weekend of the year with my cousin.

title: A Letter from Cairns
body:
Dear Nan,

Greetings from tropical Queensland! I'm writing this on the balcony of our apartment in Cairns, wearing a T-shirt with a cartoon crocodile on it and a pair of shorts that are two sizes too big. Let me explain.

You'll remember that Josh and I flew out of Melbourne last Saturday, with a stop in Sydney. Our connection there was very tight, and while we managed to run across the airport and catch the second flight, my suitcase obviously didn't. When we landed in Cairns, Josh's bag came round on the belt, and then we stood there for twenty minutes watching other people's luggage until the belt stopped.

The woman at the baggage desk was lovely. She took my details, gave me a reference number and told me that most delayed bags arrive within a day or two. The airline would also pay back reasonable costs for essentials while I waited. So that evening we went to the shops and I bought a toothbrush, sunscreen, some underwear and, yes, the crocodile T-shirt, which was the only one left in my size.

Day two: no suitcase. Day three: no suitcase, but an email saying it had been located in Brisbane, of all places. How it got there, nobody knows.

The funny thing is, I've hardly missed it. You always said I pack far too much, and you were right. I've snorkelled on the Great Barrier Reef in a borrowed wetsuit, walked through the rainforest at Kuranda in my sandals, and nobody has looked twice at my baggy shorts. It's been one of the best holidays I've ever had.

The suitcase finally turned up yesterday, delivered to our door by a courier. I opened it, looked at the five dresses, three pairs of shoes and a hairdryer inside, and laughed. Next time I'm taking hand luggage only.

I've kept every receipt for the airline, as Dad told me to. I'll show you the photos when we're back.

Lots of love,
Mia xx

title: Castle View, Allegedly
body:
When Ben booked a weekend in Edinburgh for his mum's sixtieth birthday, he paid an extra forty pounds a night for a “superior double with castle view”. The photos on the hotel's website showed a wide window and, behind it, Edinburgh Castle lit up in gold against the evening sky.

They arrived on Friday afternoon after the train from Newcastle. The receptionist handed over a key card for room 214, wished them a pleasant stay, and they took the lift to the second floor. Ben opened the door, walked straight to the window and pulled back the curtains.

He saw a brick wall. It was about two metres away, and it belonged to the building next door. If he pressed his face against the glass and looked up and to the left, he could see a small grey triangle of sky. There was no castle.

His mum, Linda, started laughing. “Maybe it's behind the wall,” she said. “You have to use your imagination.”

Ben didn't find it funny. He went back down to reception with his booking confirmation on his phone. The receptionist, a young man called Ravi, looked at the screen, looked at his computer, and went slightly pink. He explained that the castle-view rooms were on the other side of the building and that there had been a mix-up with the system. Unfortunately, the hotel was fully booked for the weekend because of a rugby match.

Ben was ready to make a fuss, but Ravi was clearly embarrassed and doing his best. He offered to refund the extra charge, and he promised to move them the next morning if anyone checked out early. Then he disappeared into the back office and came back with a bottle of prosecco “for the birthday girl”.

On Saturday, a couple from the fourth floor left a day early, and Ben and Linda were moved to room 408. The view was exactly as advertised: the castle on its rock, the rooftops of the Old Town, the hills beyond. Linda took about two hundred photos of it.

But when she tells the story now, she always talks about the brick wall. “Best laugh I've had in years,” she says.

title: Diary of a Nervous Patient
body:
Monday, March 3
I've finally done it. I phoned the dental clinic on Commercial Drive and booked an appointment for Thursday. It's been seven years since I last saw a dentist. One of my upper back teeth has been aching for weeks, and last night I couldn't sleep. My hands were shaking when the receptionist asked for my BC Services Card number. She must have heard it in my voice, because she said, “Lots of our patients are nervous. Just tell the dentist, and she'll take it slowly.”

Wednesday, March 5
Couldn't stop thinking about it. I used to be fine with dentists until I was twelve, when a dentist in Surrey filled a tooth without waiting for the freezing to work. I've never forgotten the pain. My sister Anjali says modern dentistry is completely different. She also says I'm a baby. Thanks, Anjali.

Thursday, March 6
I nearly cancelled three times this morning. I arrived twenty minutes early and sat in the car doing breathing exercises from an app. Inside, Dr. Okafor shook my hand and asked me what I was afraid of before she even looked in my mouth. I told her about Surrey. She nodded and suggested a signal: if I raised my left hand, she would stop immediately, no questions asked.

The X-ray showed a cavity, and an old filling had cracked. She numbed the area and waited, testing it twice before she started. I raised my hand once, just to check the deal was real. She stopped straight away. After that, I relaxed a bit. The drilling was noisy, but it didn't hurt. The whole thing took forty minutes.

Thursday, March 6, evening
Half my face is still numb, and I dribbled soup down my chin at dinner. But I feel ridiculously proud. Dr. Okafor wants to see me again in six months for a cleaning, and I've already booked it. Anjali sent me a gold medal emoji. I'm keeping it.

title: Kūmara at the Vet
body:
Kūmara has not eaten for two days. For most cats that might not be a disaster, but Kūmara is a large orange tabby who usually wakes me at five in the morning to demand breakfast. So when she ignored her food bowl two mornings in a row and spent the day hiding under my bed, I rang the vet clinic in Riccarton, and they fitted us in at four o'clock.

Getting her into the cat carrier took twenty minutes and cost me a scratch on the wrist. Now we're sitting in the waiting room, and she's pressed against the back of the carrier, making a low, unhappy noise.

The waiting room is full. Opposite me, an elderly man is holding a tiny dog wrapped in a blanket. He tells me she's called Princess, she's fifteen, and she's here for her heart medication. “She's outlived two of my mates,” he says proudly. Next to him, a boy of about eight is holding a shoebox with holes in the lid. His mum explains that it contains a hedgehog they found in the garden with a hurt leg. The boy has already named it Spike.

Then the door opens and a huge golden retriever bounds in, wearing one of those plastic cones around its neck. It knocks over a stand of leaflets and tries to say hello to everyone at once. Kūmara hisses so loudly that the whole room laughs.

At last the nurse calls our name. The vet, Dr. Hēmi Walker, is gentle and patient. He feels Kūmara's stomach, checks her teeth and takes her temperature, which she clearly considers an insult. It turns out she has a bad infection in one tooth, which must be why she wouldn't eat. She'll need antibiotics and probably a small operation next week to remove the tooth.

The bill is more than I'd hoped, but on the way out the boy with the hedgehog gives me a thumbs up. “Spike's going to be all right,” he says. “Is your cat?”
I tell him I think so. In the carrier, Kūmara is giving me a look that says I will pay for this.

title: Our Class Trip to the MFA
body:
Last Friday, our ESL class at the community center in Dorchester went on a field trip to the Museum of Fine Arts. Our teacher, Mr. Patel, had arranged a guided tour especially for English learners. There are twelve of us in the class, from nine different countries, and for most of us it was our first visit to a big American museum.

I was a little nervous. I can understand my teacher because he speaks slowly and clearly, but I was worried that a museum guide would use lots of difficult words about art. I needn't have worried. Our guide, a retired history professor named Eleanor, spoke clearly and stopped often to check that we understood. When someone looked confused, she pointed at the painting or used her hands to explain.

We started in the American wing. Eleanor showed us a portrait of Paul Revere, a silversmith who became famous during the American Revolution. He is holding a silver teapot and looking straight at the viewer. Eleanor asked us what we thought he was thinking. Yusuf from Somalia said, “He is thinking about how much to charge for the teapot.” Everyone laughed, including Eleanor.

After that we went to see paintings by Monet. Eleanor explained that the artist painted the same haystacks many times, at different times of day, to show how the light changes. My classmate Lucía from Colombia said it reminded her of the mountains near her village, which look different every hour. I loved that idea.

The best part for me was the Japanese collection, because my grandfather used to have a print like one of them in his house in Hanoi. I told Eleanor about it in English, and she listened as if I were an expert. At that moment I didn't feel like a student. I felt like a person sharing something important.

At the end, Mr. Patel gave us a worksheet with the new words from the day. I have already learned them all. Next month I want to go back with my daughter and be her tour guide.

Nguyen Thi Mai

title: Lovely Sofa, Shame About the Door
body:
★★★☆☆ Three stars
Reviewed by Hannah K., Sheffield

Let me start with the positives. The Harlow three-seater is beautiful. The velvet is soft, the colour (they call it “forest green”) is exactly like the photos, and it's the comfiest sofa I've ever sat on. I know this because I sat on it for an hour in my front garden.

That's where it stayed for most of the afternoon, because it wouldn't go into my house.

I live in a Victorian terrace with a narrow hallway and a tight turn into the living room. Before ordering, I measured the doorway carefully and compared it with the sizes on the website. The sofa was 88 cm deep and my door is 90 cm wide, so I thought I was fine. What the website didn't mention was that the arms are fixed and the back can't be removed, which makes the sofa much harder to turn at an angle.

The two delivery drivers were brilliant. They tried every possible angle for forty-five minutes, took off the legs and even suggested taking the front door off its hinges. In the end, they had to give up and put it back in the van.

Customer services were polite and offered me a full refund, which arrived within five working days. However, they also charged me a £49 collection fee, because, as they pointed out, “the item was not faulty”. Technically that's true, but I'd argue that the product description was misleading. If they'd listed the diagonal depth, I would never have ordered it.

So, three stars: five for the sofa, one for the information. My advice to anyone with an older house: ask for the diagonal measurement before you buy, or choose a model with removable arms. I've now ordered a smaller sofa from a different company. It comes as a flat-pack next week, and I'm already dreading the instructions.

title: Saturdays at Salamanca
body:
When I moved to Hobart from Santiago in February, my colleague Kate gave me one piece of advice: “Go to Salamanca Market on a Saturday morning, and talk to people.” I've been going every week since, and I've learned more about Tasmania there than from any guidebook.

The market stretches along a row of old sandstone warehouses near the harbour. There are hundreds of stalls selling everything from handmade jewellery to wooden chopping boards, but I always head for the food first.

My first friend was Doug, who grows apples in the Huon Valley, south of the city. The first time I stopped at his stall, I asked which apples were best for a cake. He looked at me as if I had asked a very serious question, then made me taste four different kinds, cutting slices with his pocketknife. “Tasmania used to be called the Apple Isle, you know,” he said. I didn't know. Now I buy a bag from him every week, and he always asks how the cake turned out.

Then there's Mei, who sells cheese made on Bruny Island. She noticed my accent straight away and told me she had spent a year in Chile as a student. We now chat in a strange mix of Spanish and English while she wraps my order. Last week she gave me a sample of a new blue cheese and asked for my honest opinion. I told her it was too strong for me. She laughed and said her husband had said the same.

My favourite stall, though, belongs to an old beekeeper called Ray, who sells leatherwood honey. He explained that leatherwood trees only grow in the rainforests in the west of the island, which is why the honey tastes so unusual. He also gives me advice about everything else: where to swim, which roads to avoid in winter, and why I should never trust a weather forecast in Hobart.

Some Saturdays I don't buy much at all. But I never go home without at least three good conversations, and in a new city that is worth more than anything in my basket.

title: One or Two?
body:
For about a year, Gareth Evans had been telling himself that the world was getting blurrier because of bad lighting. Menus were printed too small. Street signs in Swansea seemed to be fading. When his twelve-year-old daughter read out a bus timetable from across the road and he couldn't even see the numbers, she said, “Dad, you need glasses.” He told her not to be silly.

What finally changed his mind was his car. One evening he realised he couldn't read the number plate of the car in front until he was quite close. In the UK, drivers must be able to read a number plate from twenty metres away. The next morning he booked an eye test at the optician's on the high street.

The test took about half an hour. First, a machine blew a little puff of air into each eye to check the pressure, which made him jump. Then the optometrist, a friendly woman called Nia, asked him to read letters from a chart on the wall. He managed the top three lines. After that, the letters looked like ants.

Next came the part everyone remembers. Nia put a heavy metal frame on his face and kept changing the lenses. “Which is clearer, one or two?” she asked. “Two. No, one. Can I see them again?” It felt like an exam he could fail.

The result: Gareth is short-sighted, and he has a slight astigmatism as well. It's very common, Nia said, and nothing to worry about, but he should wear glasses for driving and for watching TV.

He spent forty minutes choosing frames, while his daughter sent opinions on every photo he texted her. A week later, he picked up the glasses and walked out onto the high street. Then he stopped. He could see individual leaves on the trees, the prices in the bakery window and the clock on the church tower.

“Why didn't I do this years ago?” he asked his daughter that evening. She didn't say “I told you so.” She didn't need to.

title: Notice of Intention to Marry
body:
Civil Registration Office, Galway
14 March

Dear Ms Aoife Brennan and Mr Tomasz Nowak,

Thank you for contacting us about your civil marriage. I am pleased to confirm that an appointment has been made for you to give notice of your intention to marry.

Date: Tuesday, 8 April
Time: 10.30 am
Place: Civil Registration Office, Galway

Please note that, under Irish law, you must give at least three months' notice before the date of your ceremony. Since you have told us you would like to marry on Saturday, 26 July, this appointment leaves enough time, but it cannot be moved to a later date without affecting your plans.

You must both attend the appointment in person. Please bring the following:
• a valid passport for each of you
• your PPS numbers
• your birth certificates (Mr Nowak's must be accompanied by an official translation into English, as it is in Polish)
• the full names and dates of birth of the two witnesses who will be present at the ceremony. Witnesses must be at least eighteen years old.

If either of you has been married before, you will also need to provide your final divorce papers.

A fee of €200 is payable when you give notice. If all your documents are in order, the registrar will issue a Marriage Registration Form. This form must be given to the person who performs your ceremony. Without it, the marriage cannot go ahead.

If you are unable to attend, please let us know as soon as possible so that we can offer you another appointment. Unfortunately, we are very busy in the summer months, and late changes may not always be possible.

We look forward to meeting you.

Yours sincerely,
Gráinne Murphy
Registration Services

Aoife's message to Tomasz, later that day:
“The letter's arrived! 8 April. Have you sent your birth certificate for translation yet? Please say yes.”
