title: Starting Over at Fifty
body:
For twenty-eight years, Ray Hoskins started his day at 6 a.m. by switching on the presses at Miller & Sons Printing in Dayton, Ohio. He printed restaurant menus, wedding invitations, church newsletters and, in the good years, catalogs for half the businesses in the city. Then, two years ago, the company announced it was closing. Orders had been falling for a decade as customers moved online, and the owners, both in their seventies, could no longer keep it going.

“I was fifty years old, and printing was all I knew,” Ray says. “I remember sitting in my truck in the parking lot after the meeting, thinking, who's going to hire me now?”

The first months were hard. He applied for dozens of jobs at other printers, but most of them were cutting staff too. His wife, Theresa, a nurse, kept the family going while he collected unemployment benefits. He admits he spent too much time on the couch.

It was his son who suggested heating and air conditioning. Ray had always been good with machines; after all, he had repaired the old presses himself for years. Through a state program for laid-off workers, he enrolled in a nine-month HVAC course at Sinclair Community College, and most of his tuition was covered.

Going back to school at fifty wasn't easy. Most of his classmates were young enough to be his children, and the first exam, on electrical systems, nearly made him quit. “I hadn't taken a test since 1991,” he laughs. But the younger students soon started asking him for help with the practical work, and he finished near the top of his class.

Today Ray works for a heating company on the east side of town. He earns slightly more than he did at the print shop, and he enjoys meeting new people every day.

“If someone had told me I'd be crawling around people's attics at fifty-two, I'd have laughed,” he says. “But losing that job turned out to be the push I needed. I just wish it hadn't taken me so long to get off the couch.”

title: Notes in the Close
body:
In the old tenement buildings of Glasgow, the shared stairwell is called the close. For years, the close at 41 Hyndland Street was a quiet, polite place. Then, last month, notes started appearing on the wall by the front door.

Note 1
To whoever owns the pram, the bike and the bags of recycling on the ground floor: could you please move them? I nearly fell over the bike on Tuesday night when the light wasn't working.
Morag (Flat 2/1)

Note 2
Hi Morag, the pram's ours, sorry! Our hall is tiny and we can't get it through our door without taking it apart. We'll fold it up every night from now on. The bike's not ours, though.
Priya and Sam (0/2)

Note 3
The bike's mine. I didn't realise it was in anyone's way. Where am I supposed to keep it, in the bath? And the recycling isn't mine either, before anyone asks.
Jamie (3/2)

Note 4
Dear residents, it has been brought to our attention that items are being stored in the close. Under fire safety regulations, the close must be kept clear at all times. Any items left there after 14 days will be removed and disposed of.
Westpark Property Factors

Things went quiet after that. Jamie carried his bike up and down three flights of stairs every day for a week, looking furious. The recycling bags stayed where they were, and nobody admitted they were theirs.

Then a fifth note appeared, in Morag's handwriting.

Note 5
Jamie, I've been thinking. There's an old coal cellar under the stairs that goes with my flat, and I never use it. You're welcome to keep your bike in there. I'll put a key through your letterbox. And to whoever owns those recycling bags: the blue bins are in the back court. They don't bite.
Morag

The next morning, the bags had gone. On Morag's doormat there was a packet of chocolate biscuits and a short note: “Thanks. Sorry about the bath comment. J.”

The wall by the front door is empty again. Well, almost. Somebody has put up a poster for a summer barbecue in the back court.

title: Forty Years, No Roses
body:
Petal & Stem, a small flower shop on Alberta Street in Portland, Oregon, is usually quiet on Tuesday mornings. Jamal Wright, the owner, was trimming roses when an elderly woman came in and stood in front of the cooler for a long time.

“Can I help you find something?” he asked.
“I hope so,” she said. “My husband and I will have been married for forty years on Friday. I've never bought him flowers. Not once.”
“Forty years is the ruby anniversary,” Jamal said. “Red roses are the traditional choice.”
She shook her head. “Walt grows roses. Our backyard is full of them. If I give him roses, he'll just tell me what's wrong with them.”

Jamal laughed. So they needed something Walt didn't grow. She explained that he liked unusual things and hated anything that looked like it came from a supermarket.

Jamal walked her around the shop. He showed her protea from South Africa, big and spiky, with petals like a crown. He showed her deep red ranunculus, which would match the ruby theme without being too obvious. He also suggested some eucalyptus, which smells wonderful and lasts for weeks.

“How much would something like that cost?” she asked, a little nervously.
“A medium arrangement would be around seventy-five dollars. Delivery is an extra fifteen.”
“I'll pick it up myself,” she said. “I want to see his face.”

They agreed on one protea in the middle, surrounded by red ranunculus and eucalyptus, wrapped in brown paper and tied with string. No plastic, no glitter. Before she left, Jamal asked her name for the card.
“Dorothy,” she said. “And on the card, just write: Forty years, and you still can't grow one of these.”

On Saturday, she came back. Walt had loved the flowers so much, she said, that he had already looked up how to grow protea in Oregon. Jamal told her it was probably too cold.
“Don't tell him that,” Dorothy said. “It'll keep him busy for the next forty years.”

title: Me Versus the DMV
body:
Monday
Today I officially became a car owner! I bought Mrs. Kim's 2012 Honda Civic for $6,500, which is most of the money I saved from two summers working at the pool. She signed the back of the title, gave me a smog certificate from last week and wrote out a bill of sale on a piece of notebook paper. My dad says that's fine as long as it has the date, the price and both our signatures. Now I have ten days to transfer the car into my name at the DMV. How hard can it be?

Tuesday
Very hard, it turns out. I tried to make an appointment online, and the first one available at the Fresno office was in three weeks. Dad says I should go first thing in the morning and wait in line. He also said, “Bring a book. Bring two books.”

Thursday
Got to the DMV at 7:30. The line was already around the building. When I finally reached the counter at 9:45, the clerk looked at my papers and said I'd filled in the wrong form. Apparently there's a separate application for transferring a title. She gave me the right one and sent me to the back of the line. I wanted to cry.

Thursday, later
My second attempt went better. The clerk checked the title, the smog certificate and my driver's license, then calculated the fees: transfer fee, registration fee and use tax. Total: $612. Nobody had warned me about the use tax. She gave me a registration card and stickers for the license plate. The new title will be mailed to me in a few weeks.

Saturday
Put the stickers on the plate this morning. Then I drove to Mrs. Kim's house to show her, and she gave me a box of cookies and a list of things the car doesn't like, such as cold mornings and going over 70.

Total cost of my car so far: $6,500, plus $612, plus one entire Thursday. Worth it? Ask me after I've paid for gas.

title: Left Turn, Right Turn
body:
Sione had passed her learner licence theory test on the first try, and she knew the road code almost by heart. Knowing it and doing it, she discovered, were two very different things.

Her fourth lesson with her instructor, Barbara, started on a quiet street in Mount Roskill, Auckland. Sione checked her mirrors, indicated, and pulled out so slowly that a man walking his dog overtook her. “You're allowed to go faster than a pedestrian,” Barbara said kindly.

Then they came to a T-intersection. Sione wanted to turn left. At the same moment, a white van on the opposite side of the road was waiting to turn right into the same street. Sione started to go, then panicked and braked, and the car stalled.

“Who gives way here?” Barbara asked calmly, while the van driver waited.
“Me?” said Sione. “But that feels wrong. He's turning across the traffic.”

Barbara explained the rule. In New Zealand, if you are turning left and a vehicle coming towards you is turning right into the same road, you must give way to it. The rule changed in 2012, she said, and even some experienced drivers still get it wrong. “Left turn gives way to right turn. Think of it as the left being polite.”

Sione restarted the car, let the van go, and turned left with her hands shaking slightly on the wheel.

After that, they practised roundabouts, where you give way to all traffic coming from your right. By the third one, Sione had stopped holding her breath. By the sixth, she was even indicating at the right moment as she left.

At the end of the lesson, Barbara said Sione had done well, except for the stall and one moment when she had forgotten to check her blind spot. If she kept practising with her dad at weekends, she could probably sit her restricted licence test in a few months.

That evening, Sione made her dad drive her to the same intersection three times, just to watch the cars. She was delighted to explain the rule to him, because he had been getting it wrong for years.

title: Package or Pick-and-Mix?
body:
On a rainy Saturday in January, the Shah family squeezed onto the sofa at Horizon Travel, a small independent agency in Leeds. Nadia and Imran have two children, Zara, fourteen, and Adam, nine, and one week in August to spend somewhere sunny. They had been arguing about it since Christmas.

The agent, a cheerful man called Pete, listened to everyone before he said a word.

Imran wanted a package holiday. “Flights, hotel, transfers, meals, all booked in one go,” he said. “I don't want to think for a whole week.” Pete showed them an all-inclusive resort in Majorca with three pools, a kids' club and a buffet that was open almost all day. The price for four was £4,200.

Nadia was less keen. “It looks lovely, but we'd never leave the hotel,” she said. “We'd come home without having seen anything real.” She wanted to fly to Lisbon, hire a car and drive down to the Algarve, staying in small guesthouses along the way.

Pete priced that up too. Flights and car hire came to about £1,600, and he estimated the accommodation at another £1,500, plus food and petrol. It might work out a little cheaper, he said, but there were risks. If a flight was cancelled, they would have to rearrange everything themselves. With a package, the whole trip would be financially protected, and the tour operator would have to sort out any problems.

Then Pete asked the children. Adam wanted a pool with a slide. Zara, who had been looking at her phone the whole time, said she wanted to see Lisbon because of a series she'd watched.

In the end, Pete suggested a compromise: a package with flights, four nights in a city hotel in Lisbon and three nights at a resort with a pool on the Algarve coast, with a transfer in between. It was protected, it was organised, and it had a slide.

Imran sighed with relief. Nadia smiled. Adam asked how big the slide was. Zara put her phone down for the first time and asked if she could plan the Lisbon days herself.

They booked before the rain stopped.

title: No Receipt, No Problem?
body:
Keisha Thompson's aunt has many wonderful qualities, but guessing clothing sizes is not one of them. For Keisha's birthday, Aunt Lorraine sent a beautiful wool jacket in dark red from a department store at the Garden State Plaza in Paramus, New Jersey. It was a size small. Keisha wears a large.

There was no receipt in the box, of course. Keisha didn't want to hurt her aunt's feelings by asking for it, so on Saturday she drove to the mall with the jacket, the box and a lot of hope.

At the customer service desk, a young employee named Carlos listened to her story and nodded sympathetically. “No problem,” he said, “but without a receipt, there are a few rules.” He explained that the store could look up the purchase if it had been paid for with a store card or a credit card. Keisha called her aunt, pretending she just wanted to say thanks again, and casually asked how she had paid. Cash, it turned out.

So Carlos explained the second option. Without proof of purchase, he could offer her store credit instead of money back. The amount would be based on the lowest price the jacket had sold for in the last ninety days. He checked the system. The jacket had cost $180 when her aunt bought it, but it had been on sale for $129 the week before.

“So I'd only get a hundred and twenty-nine dollars?” Keisha asked.
“In store credit, yes. And I'll need to see a photo ID. We keep a record of returns without receipts, to prevent fraud.”

Keisha thought about it. Then she asked if she could simply exchange it for the same jacket in a large. Carlos smiled. That was much easier: an exchange for the same item in a different size didn't need a receipt at all, as long as the tags were still on. He checked the stockroom and came back with the last large in dark red.

Keisha walked out ten minutes later wearing it. That evening she sent Aunt Lorraine a selfie. “It fits perfectly,” she wrote. And now, that was completely true.

title: Bikes or Parking on Agricola Street?
body:
HALIFAX: More than two hundred people packed into a church hall in the North End on Tuesday evening for a public consultation on the city's plan to build a protected bike lane on Agricola Street. If the plan is approved, around sixty on-street parking spaces will be removed to make room for the lane, which would connect the neighbourhood with downtown.

Supporters say the change is long overdue. “Right now, cycling on Agricola is terrifying,” said Emma Boudreau, a nurse who rides to the hospital every day. “Cars park in the bike lane, delivery trucks stop wherever they like, and I've been knocked off my bike twice. A proper protected lane would make it safe for my kids to ride to school.” City staff presented figures showing that bike traffic on the street has doubled in five years.

Many business owners, however, are worried. Raj Mehta, who has run a bakery on Agricola for eleven years, said that most of his customers come by car. “If they can't park, they'll go somewhere else,” he warned. “We can't afford to lose customers.” Others pointed out that older residents and people with disabilities depend on being able to park close to their homes.

The project's planners tried to find middle ground. They proposed keeping loading zones for deliveries and adding several accessible parking spots on side streets. They also cited studies from other Canadian cities, such as Montreal and Toronto, suggesting that shops on streets with bike lanes often see sales rise, because cyclists tend to stop more often and spend more over time.

Not everyone was convinced. “Studies are one thing,” said one retired man, to loud applause. “My knees are another.”

Councillor Lisa Fraser, who represents the area, promised that no decision would be made before the end of the consultation period in March. Residents can still send in comments online. She admitted that it would be impossible to please everyone. “But doing nothing is also a decision,” she said, “and right now, it isn't working for anybody.”

title: Home or Office? Two Views
body:
This month, our staff newsletter asked two colleagues from the Birmingham office to share their views on hybrid working. Both work in the marketing team. Both are allowed to work from home three days a week. They could hardly feel more differently about it.

Ade Okafor, 47, Senior Account Manager
“For me, working from home has been a blessing. Before 2020, I spent nearly two hours a day commuting from Solihull, stuck in traffic. Now I use that time to take my daughters to school and go for a run. I get more done at home, too. In the office, someone is always stopping by my desk for a quick chat that turns into twenty minutes. At home I can switch off notifications and focus. I'll admit I miss the banter sometimes, but not enough to give up my mornings. If the company asked us to come back full-time, I'd seriously think about looking for another job.”

Megan Price, 24, Marketing Assistant
“Honestly? For me it's more of a curse. I joined the company eighteen months ago, straight out of university, and I live in a tiny flat in Digbeth with two flatmates. On home days I work from my bed because there's no room for a desk. It's hard to switch off when your office is also where you sleep. But the biggest problem is learning. When you're new, you learn so much just by listening to how experienced people handle phone calls or sort out problems. You can't overhear anything on a video call. I've asked to come in four days a week, but on Mondays and Fridays the office is almost empty, so even then I'm often on my own.”

So who is right? Perhaps both. When we asked them what would make hybrid working better, they came up with the same suggestion: fixed “team days”, when everyone comes in together. Ade said he'd happily give up one home day for that. Megan said it would be the best day of her week.

HR is now looking into the idea. Watch this space.

title: The Building That Started Talking
body:
For the first two years Lina Haddad lived at Riverside Apartments in Parramatta, she knew exactly one neighbour by name: Gavin, because his parcels kept being delivered to her door. The building has a hundred and forty units across twelve floors, almost all of them rented, and people came and went without saying much more than “morning” in the lift.

That changed last spring, when a pipe burst on the eighth floor and water came through the ceilings on three levels. The building manager was on holiday, the real estate agents weren't answering their phones, and nobody knew who to call. In a panic, Lina made a group chat on a neighbourhood app, printed a QR code for it and stuck it up in the lift. Within a day, sixty residents had joined.

The flood was sorted out within a week, but the group didn't go quiet. If anything, it got busier. People started lending each other ladders, drills and baby car seats. A retired engineer on level 3 offered to help anyone who was struggling with their tax return. A student on level 11 started a Sunday morning running group with a strict no-complaining rule. When a family from Afghanistan moved into level 5 with almost no furniture, the group had furnished their flat within forty-eight hours.

The app has also given tenants a stronger voice. When several people discovered they had all been waiting months for their air conditioning to be repaired, they wrote a single letter to the agency, signed by forty-two households. The repairs were done within a fortnight.

Of course, not everything is perfect. There have been heated discussions about noise and, memorably, about whether it's acceptable to cook fish on a balcony. Lina has become an unofficial moderator, reminding people to be kind.

But she wouldn't go back to the old silence. “I used to think it was normal not to know your neighbours in a city,” she says. “Now I can't walk to the letterboxes without stopping for a chat. It takes me twenty minutes to get my mail. I love it.”

And Gavin? His parcels still arrive at her door. But now she gets a coffee in return.

title: Two Hundred Square Feet
body:
A year ago, Jordan and Priya Banks were paying $3,400 a month for a one-bedroom apartment in Brooklyn. Today they live in a tiny house of just 220 square feet on a friend's farm in the Hudson Valley, two hours north of New York City. We asked them how it's going.

Why did you decide to leave the city?
Priya: Money, mostly. Rent was eating more than half of what we earned, and we were never going to save enough to buy a place in New York. Then Jordan's company let him work remotely. Suddenly we didn't have to live there anymore.
Jordan: I'd also been watching tiny-house videos for years. Priya used to tease me about it.

How much did the house cost?
Jordan: We bought it used for $52,000. It's built on a trailer, so technically it's a vehicle. That made things simpler, because we didn't need to buy land. We pay our friends $500 a month to park it on their farm, and that includes water and electricity.

What was the hardest part?
Priya: Getting rid of our stuff. We had to fit everything we owned into a space smaller than our old living room. I sold or gave away about eighty percent of my clothes. I cried over some of my books.
Jordan: And we had to get used to a composting toilet. I won't go into details.

Have there been any surprises?
Priya: How much time we spend outside. The house is small, so the world becomes your living room. We hike, we help on the farm, we sit by the fire in the evenings.
Jordan: The winter was a shock, though. When it's ten degrees outside and the wood stove goes out at 3 a.m., you find out how strong your relationship is.

Would you recommend it?
Priya: Only if you really like each other. There's no door to slam.
Jordan: We've saved more in one year than in the previous five. In two years, we hope to buy some land and build something a little bigger. Maybe 400 square feet. Pure luxury.

title: A Month Without Plastic (Almost)
body:
It all started with my bin. One Sunday in January I was taking out the recycling and noticed that the three of us had filled the whole bin with plastic in just two weeks: yoghurt pots, crisp packets, the trays that mushrooms come in, and the film wrapped around cucumbers. I felt slightly sick. So I made a decision: for the month of February, I would try to buy nothing wrapped in plastic.

The first trip to the supermarket was a disaster. Almost every fruit and vegetable was in a bag or on a tray. Pasta, rice, cheese, meat: all plastic. I came home with loose bananas, a glass bottle of milk and a sense of failure.

Things got better when I changed where I shopped. In Cork we are lucky to have the English Market, where I could buy fish and meat wrapped in paper, or put straight into the containers I'd brought from home. The butcher looked at my old lunch box with suspicion the first time, but by the third week he was weighing my sausages in it without a word. I also discovered a refill shop in Douglas, where you bring your own jars and fill them with rice, oats, lentils, washing-up liquid and even shampoo.

Some things were harder. My teenage son, Cian, refused to give up crisps, and there is no such thing as a plastic-free crisp packet. We agreed that he could buy them with his own money and put the packets in his own bin. Toothpaste was another problem. I tried tablets you chew, which my husband described as “like brushing your teeth with chalk”.

It also took more time and, I'll admit, more money. Loose vegetables are sometimes dearer than packaged ones, and driving to the refill shop isn't exactly green either.

But by the end of February, our recycling bin was less than a quarter full after two weeks. I haven't kept every new habit, but most of them have lasted. If everyone made a few small changes, it would make a real difference. And I'm still not buying wrapped cucumbers. They don't need a coat.

title: Two Languages at the Dinner Table
body:
When I was five, my kindergarten teacher in Brampton phoned my parents. She was worried, she said, because I hardly spoke in class. My mother, who had moved to Canada from Punjab only six years before, was horrified. That evening my parents made a decision they would regret for years: from now on, they would speak only English at home.

It didn't last. My father's English was good, but my mother's was still shaky, and she couldn't tell me stories, scold me or comfort me properly in a language that wasn't hers. After a few months, Punjabi quietly crept back in. By grade three, I was talking non-stop in both languages, often in the same sentence. My teacher later admitted that I had simply been shy.

Growing up between two languages wasn't always easy. At school I was embarrassed when my mother picked me up and called out to me in Punjabi in front of my friends. At my grandparents' house in India, my cousins laughed at my accent and my mistakes. For a while I felt as if I didn't fully belong anywhere: too Canadian for one side, not Canadian enough for the other.

As a teenager, I became my parents' unofficial interpreter. I translated letters from the bank, phone calls with the landlord and, once, a very awkward conversation with my mother's doctor. It made me grow up quickly, and it also made me realize how much my parents depended on me.

Now, at twenty-six, I see things differently. I work as a nurse in a hospital where many older patients speak only Punjabi or Hindi, and I'm often called to help when they are frightened and confused. Being able to explain a diagnosis to someone in their own language is one of the most valuable things I can do.

Last month my mother asked me, half joking, whether I'd forgiven them for the English-only experiment. I told her the truth: if they had kept it up, I would have lost something I could never replace. When I have children of my own, they'll hear both languages from day one. And if their teacher phones me, I'll tell her not to worry.

title: Not Going to Uni
body:
When the A-level results came out in August, most of Leah Carter's friends from sixth form were busy choosing student halls and buying duvet covers. Leah was checking the government's apprenticeship website for the twentieth time that day.

She had never really wanted to go to university. She liked maths and physics, but she liked them most when she could see them working: fixing her mum's car, building a go-kart with her granddad, taking apart old laptops to see what was inside. The idea of three more years in lecture halls, followed by a large student loan, didn't appeal to her. An engineering apprenticeship seemed like the perfect answer. She would earn a wage, study for a qualification at college one day a week, and finish without debt.

Finding one turned out to be harder than she had expected. The best schemes, at big companies in and around Derby, had opened their applications the previous autumn, and most were already closed. She applied for six that were still open. Two never replied. Three sent polite rejection emails. Her mum told her not to take it personally, but it was hard not to.

The sixth was a small company that makes parts for trains. Leah was invited to an assessment day, with a maths test, a group task in which candidates had to build a tower from paper and tape, and an interview. In the interview, they asked her to describe a time she had solved a problem. She told them about the go-kart, and about the brakes that hadn't worked the first time. The two managers laughed and asked lots of questions.

A week later, she got the call. The apprenticeship lasts four years. In the first year she'll earn just over £17,000, which will rise as she gains skills, and at the end she'll have a recognised qualification and, hopefully, a permanent job.

Some of her friends still don't quite understand her choice. But in October, while they were waiting for their first student loan payments, Leah was putting on her safety boots for her first day at work. “I'm getting paid to learn,” she says. “I'm not sure why more people don't do it.”

title: Black Spots on the Ceiling
body:
When Priya and her partner Joel moved into their flat in Levenshulme, Manchester, the bathroom looked fresh and clean. Six months later, black spots had appeared on the ceiling above the shower. At first Priya wiped them off with bleach every Sunday, but they always came back, and the window frame had started to smell of damp.

She rang the letting agent, who sent a man round to inspect the flat. He looked at the ceiling for about thirty seconds. “It's condensation,” he said. “You must be drying clothes inside. Mould like this is usually caused by the people who live here.”

Priya was furious. “We've been opening the window after every shower,” she told Joel that evening. “But the extractor fan hasn't worked since we moved in. If it worked, the steam would have somewhere to go.”

Joel thought they should simply put up with it until the tenancy ended, because he was worried about losing their deposit. Priya disagreed. She did some research and found out that landlords in England are responsible for repairs, including broken fans and leaking pipes. She also read that if a landlord ignores a serious problem, tenants can contact the council's environmental health team.

So she wrote a polite but firm email. She attached photos, explained that the fan had been broken for six months and asked for it to be repaired within fourteen days.

The reply came two days later. An electrician was sent the following week, and he discovered that the fan had never been connected properly. He also noticed that a pipe behind the wall had been leaking slowly.

Now the fan hums every time the light is switched on, the pipe has been fixed, and the ceiling has been painted with anti-mould paint. So whose fault was it? Partly the tenants', perhaps: Priya admits they used to dry towels on the radiator. But mostly it was a problem with the building. “The lesson,” she says, “is to write everything down and not to accept the first answer.”

title: Five Days in Our Own Backyard
body:
Monday
We were supposed to be driving to the Sunshine Coast this week, but in October the car's gearbox died and the repair ate our whole holiday budget. When we told the kids, Ava (11) cried and Noah (8) said it was the worst thing that had ever happened to him. So Dan and I made a deal with them: we would have a proper holiday, just without leaving Brisbane. We wrote three rules on the fridge. No chores, no work emails, and no screens before five o'clock.

Tuesday
We pitched the old tent in the backyard and slept outside. A possum ran across the roof at midnight and Noah screamed so loudly that the neighbours turned their lights on. Nobody got much sleep, but everyone was laughing at breakfast.

Wednesday
We caught the CityCat ferry all the way down the river, which the kids had never done. Then we spent the afternoon at Streets Beach, the free lagoon at South Bank. I had forgotten how good it feels to float in the water and do nothing at all. We had to put on sunscreen three times, though.

Thursday
Bushwalk up Mount Coot-tha. It was steep and hot, and Noah complained for the first half hour. When we got to the lookout, he went quiet. You could see the whole city and the hills beyond it. “It's like being on a plane,” he said.

Friday
Cooking night. The kids took turns choosing the menu, so dinner was sausages, then pancakes, then mangoes for dessert. Not very healthy, but it was a holiday.

Saturday
I asked them what the best part of the week had been. Ava said the possum. Noah said the lookout. Dan said not checking his phone. For me, it was having everyone together, with no rush. If we'd gone away, we'd have spent two days in the car. Maybe next year we'll travel again, but we've learnt that you don't need to go far to make the most of a holiday.

title: Back to Mam's House
body:
For thirty years, Ciarán Murphy saw his mother four times a year: at Easter, in the summer, at her birthday and at Christmas. He lived in Dublin, worked long hours in an insurance office, and rang her every Sunday evening. Bríd, who is now 84, lived alone in the same terraced house in Cork where Ciarán had grown up.

Then, two winters ago, she fell in the kitchen and broke her hip. A neighbour found her the next morning. In hospital, a doctor told Ciarán that his mother could go home, but only if someone was there to help her. “She can't manage on her own any more,” he said. “Has she got family nearby?”

Ciarán's sister lives in Boston, so the decision was really his. After a few sleepless nights, he asked his company if he could work from home, and he moved back into his old bedroom in Cork. “I thought it would be for a few months,” he says. “That was nearly two years ago.”

The first months were hard. He had to learn how to help his mother wash and dress, how to sort her tablets, and how to cook meals she would actually eat. A public health nurse visits once a week, and a home help comes for an hour every morning, but the rest is up to him. Some nights he was so worn out that he fell asleep on the sofa at nine.

There have been arguments too. Bríd used to be the one who looked after everybody, and she hates relying on her son. “Stop fussing,” she tells him when he follows her up the stairs.

But Ciarán says he wouldn't change his decision. Twice a month, his mother goes to a day centre, which gives him some time to himself. In the evenings they watch quiz shows together and she tells him stories about his father that he had never heard. “If I'd stayed in Dublin,” he says, “I would have missed all of this.”

title: Four Nights on The Canadian
body:
When I graduated from the University of Toronto in May, my friends flew off to Europe. I did something different: I took the train to Vancouver. The Canadian, run by VIA Rail, covers about 4,500 kilometres in four nights. A plane would have taken five hours, but I wanted to see the country I had grown up in.

Day 1
We set off from Union Station in the evening. My sleeper cabin is tiny, with a bunk that folds down from the wall, but it has a window, and that's all I need. I fell asleep somewhere north of the city, surrounded by forest.

Day 2
Northern Ontario is lakes, rocks and trees, for hours and hours. Hardly any roads, hardly any towns. We were delayed twice because freight trains have priority on the tracks, so we had to wait for them to pass. Nobody seemed to mind. I spent most of the day in the dome car, which has a glass roof, chatting to a retired couple from Halifax who have done this trip six times.

Day 3
The prairies! After Winnipeg, the land became completely flat and the sky looked enormous. At one stop we were allowed to get off for twenty minutes, so everyone rushed out to stretch their legs and take photos of the grain elevators.

Day 4
I woke up and the Rocky Mountains were outside my window. Honestly, I gasped. We stopped in Jasper for an hour, and I saw an elk standing calmly next to the station car park.

Day 5
We arrived in Vancouver eight hours late, which apparently is quite normal. My friends have been posting photos of Paris and Rome, and I'm sure their trips are amazing. But I've seen my own country from coast to almost-coast, I've met people from four provinces, and I've realized how little of Canada I actually knew. Would I recommend it? Absolutely. Just don't book anything important for the day you arrive.

title: The Day the Tube Stopped
body:
Millions of Londoners had to find another way to work yesterday after a 24-hour strike closed the entire Underground network. Not a single Tube train ran between Sunday evening and Tuesday morning, the first full shutdown in several years.

The strike was called by the RMT union after talks about pay and working conditions broke down last week. The union says its members have been offered a pay rise that is far below the rate of inflation. Transport for London says it simply cannot afford more. Both sides have blamed each other for the disruption.

By seven o'clock in the morning, the queues at bus stops in Brixton and Stratford were already stretching down the street. Many buses were so packed that they didn't stop at all. Taxi and ride-sharing prices doubled within an hour, and every hire bike at King's Cross had disappeared by eight.

Some commuters decided to walk. Hannah Okafor, a nurse, set off from Walthamstow at half past five to reach her hospital in central London. “It took me two and a half hours,” she said. “My feet are killing me, but patients still need us, strike or no strike.”

Others simply stayed at home. Many offices told staff to work from home, and the City was strangely quiet. Sandwich shops and cafés near the big stations reported a sharp drop in customers. “On a normal Monday we sell four hundred coffees before ten,” said one café manager in Moorgate. “Today it was about sixty.”

Not everyone was angry with the strikers, however. A young teacher waiting for a bus in Camden said she understood them. “Everything has got more expensive,” she said. “If my union went on strike, I'd probably join in too.”

Trains were running normally again this morning, but the problem has not been solved. The union has warned that further strikes could be announced next month if no agreement is reached.

title: A New Chair for the Bowls Club
body:
For twenty-five years, every meeting of the Roslyn Bowling Club in Dunedin has started the same way. Graham Pearce, now 79, stands up, taps his glass with a spoon and says, “Right, let's get on with it.” Last Thursday he did it for the last time.

Graham announced in March that he would be stepping down as chair at the annual general meeting. “I've loved every minute,” he told the members, “but the club needs fresh ideas, and I've run out of them.”

The club does need new ideas. When Graham took over, it had nearly two hundred members. Today it has sixty-three, and most of them are over seventy. The clubhouse roof leaks, and the green costs thousands of dollars a year to look after.

Two members stood for the position. Ross Whitaker, 72, a retired accountant, promised to fix the roof and keep things as they had always been. “Our traditions are what make this club special,” he said. Mere Tipene, 41, who joined only three years ago, had a different plan. She wanted to open the green on Friday evenings for barefoot bowls, with music and a barbecue, so that young people from the neighbourhood could try the game.

Some older members were worried. “It'll turn into a pub,” one man muttered. But others pointed out that without new members, there might not be a club in ten years' time.

The ballot papers were counted twice, because the result was so close. Mere won by four votes. She thanked Ross warmly and asked him to become the club's treasurer, which he accepted.

The first Friday barefoot night is planned for next month. Graham says he will definitely be there. “I've never bowled without shoes,” he laughed, “but if I'd been afraid of new things, I would never have been chair for twenty-five years.”

title: Yesterday's Bread
body:
Every evening at seven, when Rosa's Bakery in southeast Portland closes, there is a pile of bread left on the shelves: sourdough loaves, bagels, a few croissants, sometimes a whole tray of cinnamon rolls. For the first three years, owner Marco Ruiz threw most of it into the dumpster behind the shop.

“It used to make me feel sick,” he says. “My grandmother grew up in Mexico with very little. If she had seen me throwing away good food every night, she would have been ashamed of me.”

Marco had thought about donating the bread, but he was worried. What if someone got ill and sued him? Then a customer told him about a federal law that protects businesses which donate food in good faith. As long as the food is safe when it leaves the shop, the donor can't be held responsible.

That customer was Jasmine Lee, a student at Portland State University, who runs a volunteer group called Second Rise. Every evening, a volunteer cycles to the bakery with a trailer, picks up whatever is left, and delivers it to a homeless shelter and a family center a few blocks away.

But there was still too much bread. So last year Marco also signed up for a food waste app. Customers can buy a surprise bag of leftover baked goods for five dollars, about a third of the normal price. The bags usually sell out within an hour of being posted.

The results have surprised him. Almost nothing goes to waste now, and some of the app customers have become regulars who come back to pay full price. He has also started baking slightly less in the afternoon, because he now pays closer attention to what doesn't sell.

“Food that ends up in a landfill doesn't just waste money,” Jasmine says. “It produces methane, which heats the planet. Saving bread from one bakery is small. But imagine if every bakery in the city did it.”

title: My Year as an Au Pair in Boston
body:
Dear Jonas,

It's my last week in Brookline, and I've been thinking about everything that has happened since I arrived here last August. You asked me in your last message whether you should become an au pair after school, so here is my honest answer.

The first month was the hardest. My host family, the Coopers, are lovely, but I was looking after two four-year-old twins who had never been told “no” in English by someone with a German accent. They didn't understand me, and I didn't understand them. I was so homesick that I cried on the phone to Mama nearly every night.

Things got better slowly. I learned that American kids eat dinner at half past five, that a “snow day” means school is closed and the twins are home all day, and that people here drive everywhere, even to a shop three blocks away. I got used to the carpool, the peanut butter and the enormous fridge.

Au pairs in the US have to take classes, so I studied psychology at a community college two evenings a week. That's where I made friends: Valentina from Colombia, Aiko from Japan and Chloé from France. We spent our weekends exploring Boston together, and in the spring we took a bus to New York.

The work itself is real work. I was in charge of the twins for up to forty-five hours a week. The weekly pay is small, but you live for free, and the family paid for my classes. If you want a cheap holiday, this isn't it.

But would I do it again? Yes, without thinking twice. My English is completely different now. I can deal with a screaming child in a supermarket and stay calm. And last night, when Lily hugged me and asked, “Why can't you stay forever?”, I realized I had a second family.

See you at the airport on Saturday!

Love,
Marie

title: The Family Meeting
body:
It started, as these things often do, at the dinner table in the Moreno family's house in Austin. Luis asked his daughter how her day had been, and Maya, who is thirteen, didn't answer. She was scrolling through videos under the table.

“That's it,” said her mom, Dana. “Family meeting. Sunday, four o'clock. Everybody comes.”

On Sunday, Dana put a sheet of paper on the table. “Maya, you spent seven hours on your phone yesterday. Eli, you played video games until eleven on a school night.”

“Only because it was a really important level,” said Eli, who is nine.

“Nothing is that important at eleven o'clock,” Luis said.

Maya crossed her arms. “This isn't fair. Everyone in my class has a phone. If I don't see the group chat, I miss everything. And Dad, you check your email at dinner all the time.”

There was a silence. Luis went slightly red. “Okay,” he admitted. “That's a fair point.”

Dana had expected an argument, but she hadn't expected to be on the losing side so quickly. She looked at her own phone, lying next to her coffee. It showed four hours of screen time.

“Right,” she said. “Then the rules are for all of us, not just you two.”

It took an hour, but they came up with a deal. All phones, including the parents', go into a basket in the kitchen during dinner. On school nights, screens go off at nine, and every device is charged downstairs, not in the bedrooms. On weekends the kids can have more time, as long as homework is done first. And on Saturday mornings the whole family does something together without any screens: a bike ride, a trip to Barton Springs or just pancakes.

Three weeks later, the rules have mostly stuck. Eli still argues about video games, and Maya says the basket is “ridiculous.” But last night, nobody looked at a phone during dinner, and they talked for forty-five minutes.

title: Don't Bin It, Mend It
body:
On the first Saturday of every month, St Mark's community hall in Easton, Bristol, turns into something between a workshop and a tea party. By ten o'clock there is a queue outside the door: a man holding a toaster, a girl with a teddy bear that has lost an eye, a woman carrying a lamp that has stopped working.

This is the Easton Repair Café. It was set up four years ago by Femi Adeyemi, a retired electrician who was tired of seeing perfectly good things thrown out. “People think that if something breaks, they have to bin it and buy a new one,” he says. “Often all it needs is a new fuse or ten minutes with a screwdriver.”

The café is run entirely by volunteers. There is a table for electrical items, a table for bikes, and a sewing table where Agnieszka, a former dressmaker, repairs zips, tears and hems. Nobody pays for repairs, although most visitors drop a few pounds into the donation jar. The tea and cake are free too.

The most important rule is that you can't just leave your broken item and come back later. You have to sit with the volunteer while they work. “We want people to learn,” Femi explains. “Next time, maybe they can fix it themselves.”

Today, Jake, who is fourteen, is watching closely as a volunteer takes his headphones apart. A wire inside has come loose. Twenty minutes later, after a bit of soldering, they work perfectly. “I was going to ask for new ones for my birthday,” he says, grinning. “Now I can ask for something else.”

Not everything can be saved. Some modern products are glued together so tightly that they can't be opened without breaking them. But the volunteers manage to repair about two thirds of what comes through the door. Since the café opened, they have kept more than three tonnes of stuff out of landfill.

Femi hopes more halls will follow their example. “Repairing used to be normal,” he says. “Our grandparents mended things all the time. We've just forgotten how.”

title: Standing Room Only at Town Hall
body:
Brattleboro Town Hall has room for about two hundred people. On Tuesday night, more than four hundred tried to get in. It was standing room only: dozens stood along the walls, and others listened through the open windows in the cold. They had all come for one reason: the plan to build 140 apartments on the land next to Living Memorial Park.

The developer, a company from Burlington, says the project would help solve the town's housing crisis. Rents in Brattleboro have risen by almost forty percent in five years, and young families and nurses at the local hospital say they can't find anywhere affordable to live. Thirty of the new apartments would be offered at below-market rents.

But many residents are strongly against the plan. The land is currently a meadow where people walk their dogs and children go sledding in winter. Opponents say the extra traffic would be dangerous for kids walking to the park, and that the town's schools are already full.

The meeting quickly became heated. When the developer's spokesperson said the building would be “in keeping with the character of the neighborhood,” several people in the audience laughed loudly. One man shouted that the whole thing had been decided behind closed doors, and the chair of the select board had to ask him twice to sit down.

Not everyone in the room was against it, however. Kayla Brooks, a 29-year-old teacher, said she had been living in her parents' basement for two years. “I grew up here and I love this town,” she said, her voice shaking. “But if nothing is built, people like me will have to leave.” Her words were met with both applause and silence.

After three hours, the board agreed that the decision should be postponed. A smaller public hearing will be held next month, and residents can send written comments until then. Whatever is decided, it is clear that the town is deeply divided.

title: Amal Takes the Oath
body:
Last Thursday, in a small courtroom in Winnipeg, Amal Haddad stood up with sixty-two other people, raised her right hand and took the oath, promising to be loyal to Canada. When the judge said, “Congratulations, you are now Canadian citizens,” the room burst into applause. Amal's two daughters, who were waiting at the back, waved small red and white flags.

It had been a long journey. In 2013, Amal and her husband Khaled escaped from Aleppo with their daughters, who were then two and four years old. They spent three years in a refugee camp in Lebanon, living in a tent and hoping that one country would accept them. In 2016, they were told that they had been chosen for resettlement in Canada.

“We knew almost nothing about Winnipeg,” Amal remembers, laughing. “Someone told us it was cold. We had no idea what minus thirty really meant.”

Because they arrived as government-assisted refugees, the family became permanent residents as soon as they landed. They were given a small apartment, a monthly allowance for their first year, and free English classes. Khaled, who had been an engineer in Syria, worked in a warehouse at first while his qualifications were being checked. Amal volunteered at a community centre and later trained as a teaching assistant.

To apply for citizenship, a permanent resident must have lived in Canada for at least three of the last five years. They also have to prove that they can speak English or French and pass a citizenship test about Canadian history, geography and government. Amal studied the official guide every evening for two months. “My daughters asked me questions at breakfast,” she says. “Who is the head of state? What are the three founding peoples? They knew all the answers before I did.”

She needed fifteen out of twenty to pass. She got nineteen.

Now Amal is looking forward to voting for the first time. “In Syria, my vote did not count,” she says. “Here, it will. That is the part that makes me want to cry.”

title: No Certificate, No Job
body:
When Jess Nguyen was offered a job as an educator at a childcare centre in Fremantle, there was one condition. Before her first day, she had to complete a first-aid course. In Western Australia, as in the rest of the country, every childcare centre must have staff on site at all times who hold a current first aid, CPR, asthma and anaphylaxis certificate. Without one, Jess simply couldn't be put on the roster.

“To be honest, I thought it would be a boring day of slideshows,” she admits. “I was wrong.”

The course took place on a Saturday in a training room in Perth, with twelve other people: two more childcare workers, a swimming teacher, a sports coach and several parents. The trainer, a former paramedic called Wayne, started by asking how many of them had ever seen someone stop breathing. Three people put their hands up.

Most of the morning was spent practising CPR on dummies of different sizes: adults, children and tiny babies. Jess was surprised by how hard and fast you have to push. “If you're doing it right,” Wayne told them, “you'll be exhausted after two minutes.” They also practised using a defibrillator, which turned out to be much easier than she had expected, because the machine tells you exactly what to do.

After lunch, they learned what to do in situations that are common with small children: choking, burns, allergic reactions and asthma attacks. Each person had to show the trainer how to use an adrenaline pen and an asthma puffer with a spacer. At the end there was a written test and a practical assessment.

Jess passed, and three weeks later the training was needed. A three-year-old at the centre started coughing and couldn't breathe after eating a sandwich that had been brought from home. Jess recognised the signs straight away, gave the back blows she had practised and the piece of food came out.

“I'd never have known what to do before the course,” she says. “Now I understand why it's compulsory. I think everyone should do one, not just people who work with kids.”

title: Notes Through the Letterbox
body:
Note 1, pushed through the letterbox of No. 14, Monday
Hi, I'm Siobhán from No. 12, next door. Sorry to bother you, but I work from home and your dog barks almost all day while you're out. Yesterday it went on from nine until half four. I'm sure you don't realise, but it's making it very hard to concentrate. Could we have a chat? Siobhán

Note 2, Tuesday
Siobhán, thanks for letting me know, and sorry, I genuinely had no idea. I'm Declan. I'm a nurse at University Hospital Galway and I've just started twelve-hour shifts. Biscuit is a rescue dog and I've only had her a month. I thought she'd sleep while I was gone. I'll try to sort something out. Declan

Note 3, the following Monday
Declan, it's still happening, I'm afraid. I had to do a work call from my car today because nobody could hear me over the barking. I don't want to complain to the council, but I'm running out of patience. Siobhán

After the third note, Declan knocked on Siobhán's door with a box of chocolates and a very embarrassed face. They ended up talking on her doorstep for half an hour. He explained that he couldn't afford doggy daycare every day, and that he couldn't change his shifts. A trainer had told him Biscuit was probably anxious and lonely, not badly behaved.

That was when Siobhán had an idea. She had grown up with dogs and had been missing having one around. What if Biscuit spent the long shift days at her house? She would get company, Declan would save money, and the street would get some peace.

That was three months ago. Now Biscuit comes over at seven in the morning on Declan's work days and lies under Siobhán's desk while she works. At lunchtime they walk together along the Salthill prom. Declan pays for her food and has fixed Siobhán's broken gate as a thank-you.

“I was ready to report him,” Siobhán admits. “If I had, I'd have ended up with an enemy instead of a dog.”

title: The Pill Box That Talks Back
body:
Three years ago, Elena and Sofia Ramirez were worried about their grandmother. Abuela Carmen, who lives alone in Phoenix, had to take seven different pills a day, and she kept forgetting them. Sometimes she took the same pill twice. Once she ended up in the emergency room because she had missed her heart medication for three days.

“We tried everything,” says Elena, 29, who was working as a software developer at the time. “Alarms on her phone, a plastic pill organizer, sticky notes on the fridge. Nothing worked, because she would turn off the alarm and then forget why it had gone off.”

Sofia, an engineering student, had an idea. What if the pill box itself knew whether the pills had been taken? The sisters started working on it in their parents' garage in Mesa, mostly at night and on weekends. The first version was made from a shoebox, a cheap sensor and a speaker. When it was time for a pill, the right compartment lit up and a recorded voice said, in Spanish, “Abuela, it's time for your blue pill.” If the compartment wasn't opened within thirty minutes, a text message was sent to the sisters.

It worked. Their grandmother hasn't missed a dose since.

When friends saw it, they asked if they could have one for their own parents. That was when the sisters realized they might have a business. They entered a start-up competition at Arizona State University and won $25,000, which they used to build a hundred better-looking boxes. Elena gave up her job last year to work on the company full-time.

It hasn't been easy. They have made almost no money so far, and they've been turned down by more than thirty investors. Medical products also have to meet strict safety rules, which takes time. “Some days I wonder if I've made a huge mistake,” Elena admits.

But last month a chain of pharmacies agreed to test the box in ten of its stores. And every Sunday, the sisters still have lunch with Abuela Carmen, who likes to tell everyone that she is the company's first customer.

title: From Car Park to Cabbages
body:
Five years ago, the space behind the Lincoln Green flats in Leeds was a car park. It was full of potholes, broken glass and a few abandoned cars that nobody had moved for years. Most residents didn't even own a car. Children weren't allowed to play there because it wasn't safe.

Today the same space is full of raised beds, fruit trees and a wooden shelter where people drink tea when it rains. On a sunny Saturday in June, there are about thirty people working, chatting and picking strawberries.

The change began with one woman. Bernadette Osei, a retired dinner lady who has lived in the flats for over thirty years, was fed up with looking at the car park from her kitchen window. She knocked on every door in the block and asked people a simple question: would you rather have a car park or a garden? Out of 112 households, 97 chose the garden.

With the support of the residents' association, she took the idea to the council, which owns the land. At first the answer was no. Officials said it would cost too much and that the garden would be vandalised within weeks. Bernadette didn't give up. She found a local charity that agreed to pay for the first beds, and a building company donated soil and timber.

The tarmac was dug up in the spring of 2021. Volunteers of all ages built the beds, and the council finally agreed to lease the land to the residents for a small fee. Each family that wants one now has its own bed, and there are shared areas for herbs, flowers and a pond.

The garden has never been vandalised. “If people feel that something belongs to them, they look after it,” says Bernadette. Neighbours who had never spoken to each other now swap seeds and recipes. Last autumn, the garden held its first harvest festival, with a barbecue and a prize for the biggest pumpkin.

“I used to think nothing would ever change round here,” says Imran, sixteen, who helps with the bees. “Now I know it can, if enough people want it.”

title: The Trainers That Never Arrived
body:
Dear Kirsty,

I feel really stupid writing this. Three weeks ago I saw an advert on Instagram for a pair of designer trainers that normally cost £180. They were on sale for £55. The website looked completely professional, with photos, reviews and a countdown saying the offer would end in two hours. I paid by bank transfer because the card payment “wasn't working”. Since then: nothing. No trainers, no reply to my emails, and now the website has disappeared. Is my money gone for good?

Rory, Paisley

Dear Rory,

First of all, you are not stupid. Fake online shops are designed by professionals to fool people, and thousands of Scots are caught out every year. You have done the right thing by speaking up.

Unfortunately, I have to be honest with you. Paying by bank transfer is exactly what scammers want, because it's much harder to get the money back than with a credit card. If you had paid by card, your bank might have been able to reverse the payment. That said, you should still contact your bank immediately. Many UK banks now refund victims of this kind of scam, especially if you report it quickly.

You should also report it to Police Scotland by calling 101, and report the advert to Instagram so that it can be taken down. Keep screenshots of everything: the advert, the website and your emails.

For next time, here are some warning signs that I wish everyone knew:

The price is too good to be true. Designer goods are rarely sold at 70% off.
There is a countdown or pressure to buy now.
The site was set up recently. You can check this with free online tools.
The reviews all sound the same, or only appear on the shop's own website.
You are asked to pay by bank transfer instead of by card or PayPal.

The golden rule is simple: if something feels rushed, slow down. A genuine shop will still be there tomorrow.

I hope your bank can help. Let me know how you get on.

Kirsty

title: A Night at Mueller Hut
body:
My sister Aroha had been talking about Mueller Hut for years. It sits high on a ridge in Aoraki/Mount Cook National Park, at 1,800 metres, and there is no road, no electricity and no phone signal. “It's the most beautiful place in New Zealand,” she kept telling me. I wasn't convinced. I like hot showers and Wi-Fi.

But in February, she booked two bunks through the Department of Conservation website and gave me a list of things to pack: sleeping bag, head torch, gas cooker, warm layers, food for two days and a rubbish bag, because everything you carry in, you must carry out.

The walk up took us five hours. The first part is over a thousand steps, and my legs were shaking long before the top. The last section is loose rock and snow, and I had to stop every few minutes to catch my breath. Then the bright red hut appeared, and behind it, across the valley, the enormous white face of Aoraki itself. I forgot how tired I was.

Life in the hut is simple. There are mattresses in a shared room, a long table, a water tank and a toilet outside. Solar panels power a small radio for the warden, but that's all. When the sun went down, everyone lit candles or switched on their head torches. Twenty strangers from six countries cooked noodles on tiny stoves and shared chocolate, stories and tips about other walks.

At about ten, the warden told us to go outside. I have never seen so many stars. The Milky Way was so bright that it threw shadows on the snow. Every few minutes we heard a loud crack from the glacier opposite, as huge pieces of ice broke away and fell into the valley.

I barely slept, partly because of the cold, partly because a man from Germany snored all night. But when the sun rose over the mountains at six, turning the snow pink, I finally understood what Aroha had meant. I didn't miss my phone once. We're already planning to go back next summer.

title: Nine People, One Kitchen
body:
At half past six on a weekday morning, the kitchen of the Santos family's house in Chula Vista, near San Diego, is already busy. Lola Remy, 81, is frying garlic rice. Her son Ben, 54, is making coffee. His wife Grace is packing lunches. Upstairs, their three teenagers are fighting over the bathroom, and in the room above the garage, their eldest daughter Kat and her husband Jordan are getting their baby ready for daycare.

That's nine people, three generations and four cars under one roof.

It wasn't always like this. Ben and Grace bought the house fifteen years ago when there were only five of them. Lola moved in after her husband died in 2019, because she didn't want to live alone in Manila. Then, two years ago, Kat and Jordan were spending almost two thirds of their income on rent for a one-bedroom apartment. When their baby was on the way, Ben suggested they move into the room over the garage and save for a deposit.

“In the Philippines, this is completely normal,” Grace explains. “Grandparents, parents and children often live together. Here in the US, people sometimes look at us as if we're strange. But a lot of our friends are doing the same thing now, because housing is so expensive.”

There are clear advantages. Lola looks after the baby two afternoons a week, which saves Kat and Jordan hundreds of dollars. The teenagers have learned to cook Filipino dishes from their grandmother. And when Ben had surgery last year, there were always people around to help.

Of course, it isn't always easy. There's one washing machine and a long list of rules about who uses it when. Privacy is hard to find. Jordan, who grew up as an only child in Ohio, admits that the noise took some getting used to. “The first month, I used to sit in my car just to get some quiet,” he laughs.

The arrangement won't last forever. Kat and Jordan hope to buy their own place next year. But they've already decided that they want somewhere close by. “We've got used to having everyone around,” Kat says. “I think I'd miss the chaos.”

title: Back on Two Wheels
body:
When Tom Fairbairn arrived in Cambridge to start his master's degree, he had a secret. He hadn't ridden a bike since he was ten, when he crashed into a hedge in his grandparents' village and broke his wrist. He had grown up in central London, where he took the Tube everywhere, and he had never felt the need to try again.

In Cambridge, that wasn't really an option. The city is flat, the old streets in the centre are narrow, and almost everyone cycles: students, professors, mums with children in boxes on the front, even elderly men in suits. On his first morning, Tom walked to the department and arrived twenty minutes late, sweating, while his classmates locked up their bikes outside.

“Everyone assumed I could ride,” he says. “I was too embarrassed to tell them.”

He bought a second-hand bike for £60 from a shop on Mill Road and started practising on Midsummer Common early in the morning, when nobody was around. The first few days were a disaster. He kept wobbling and putting his feet down, and once he rode straight into a puddle in front of some cows. But slowly his balance came back. As people say, you never really forget how to ride a bike.

The traffic was a different matter. Tom had to learn how to signal with his arms, how to look over his shoulder before turning, and how to deal with buses and taxis on narrow roads. He signed up for a free cycle training session run by the council, where an instructor rode around the city with him and explained the rules. “Ride confidently,” she told him. “If you hug the kerb, drivers will try to squeeze past you.”

Three months later, Tom cycles everywhere. It takes him twelve minutes to get to the department, he saves money on buses, and he has never been fitter. He has had his bike stolen once, which apparently happens to most students in Cambridge sooner or later, but he now uses two locks.

“I wish I'd done it years ago,” he says. “The only thing I'm still scared of is the cows.”

title: Ten Months with Juniper
body:
When Marcus Bell told his colleagues at a Halifax engineering firm that he was going to take ten months of parental leave, one of them asked if he was joking. “Who's going to look after the baby, then?” another said. “I am,” Marcus replied. “That's the whole point.”

In Canada, parents can share up to eighteen months of parental benefits through Employment Insurance. Marcus and his wife, Priya, decided that she would stay at home for the first six months, and he would take over when she went back to her job as a lawyer. Their daughter, Juniper, was born last March.

We spoke to Marcus at the end of his leave.

Why did you decide to take such a long break?
Priya's career is just as important as mine. And honestly, I wanted to know my daughter, not just see her for an hour before bed. My own dad worked all the time. I love him, but I hardly knew him when I was small.

What was the hardest part?
The first month alone was terrifying. Juniper refused to take a bottle, and I phoned Priya at work in a panic at least twice a day. I also felt quite lonely. At the baby groups in the library, I was usually the only man, and some mums seemed surprised that I knew how to change a diaper.

And the money?
The benefits are much lower than my salary, so we had to cut back. No vacations, fewer meals out. But we'd been saving for a year, so we managed.

Has it changed you?
Completely. I'm much more patient now. I know what it means to spend a whole day with a small child, and I've realized how much work Priya was doing in those first months.

Are you worried about going back to work?
A bit. Some people think that men who take long leave aren't serious about their careers. But my manager has been supportive, and two younger colleagues have already asked me how to apply. If more fathers did this, nobody would think it was strange.

Marcus goes back to work on Monday. Juniper starts daycare the same week.

title: Three Days or Five?
body:
I've been an intensive-care nurse at St James's Hospital in Dublin for eleven years. Last month my manager told me that a part-time position had become available: three twelve-hour shifts a week instead of the four or five I do now. I have to give her my answer by Friday, and I've been going back and forth about it ever since. So I'm writing it down.

The reasons to go part-time are obvious. I'm tired. Not normal tired, but the kind of tired where you sit in the car outside your house for ten minutes because you can't face going in. In intensive care, every patient is seriously ill, and you are responsible for keeping them alive. After a run of night shifts, it takes me two days to feel like myself again. My son Oisín is seven, and I've missed more of his football matches than I want to admit. With one or two extra days off a week, I'd be a better mother and probably a better nurse.

But there are also good reasons to stay full-time. The first is money. Dublin rents are among the highest in Europe, and my partner works in a café. If I went part-time, we'd lose about a third of my salary, and we'd have to give up the idea of saving for a house for a few more years. My pension would also be smaller.

The second reason is harder to explain. The unit is short-staffed. If I reduce my hours, the hospital may not be able to replace me, and my colleagues will have to cover more shifts. I know exactly how exhausted they are. I feel guilty even thinking about it.

My friend Aoife, who went part-time last year, says I'm looking at it the wrong way. “If you burn out completely,” she told me, “they'll lose you for all five days, not just two.” I think she might be right.

I still haven't decided. But writing this, I've noticed something. Every reason to stay is about other people. Every reason to go is about me and Oisín. Maybe that's my answer.

title: Thursday Nights at the Pantry
body:
I started volunteering at the Logan Square Community Pantry in Chicago two years ago, mainly because I'd been laid off from my marketing job and I needed a reason to get out of bed. I thought I'd go for a month. I'm still going every Thursday.

The pantry is in the basement of a church on Kedzie Avenue. Every week, about three hundred families come to pick up groceries: canned beans, rice, pasta, fresh vegetables, milk and sometimes chicken. Most of the food is donated by supermarkets and a regional food bank, which collects surplus from farms and companies. The rest is bought with money from local donors.

Before I started, I had a picture in my head of who used food pantries. I was wrong. Of course some of our guests are homeless, but many have jobs. On my first night, I helped a woman in hospital scrubs. She was a nursing assistant who had just finished a twelve-hour shift. Her rent had gone up by $300, and she couldn't feed her kids and pay it at the same time. I've also met retired teachers, students, delivery drivers and a man who used to own a restaurant.

What surprised me most was how the pantry is organized. A few years ago, guests were handed a box of food that had been packed in advance. Now the basement is set up like a small supermarket. People walk around with a cart and choose what they want. That way, nobody gets a can of something they won't eat, and less food is wasted. It also feels more respectful. “People want to be treated like customers, not like charity cases,” our coordinator, Denise, always says.

My job changes every week. Sometimes I unload the truck, sometimes I stack shelves, and sometimes I sit at the front desk, checking people in and chatting in my rusty Spanish.

I found a new job last spring, but I've kept my Thursday nights free. I've made real friends there, and I've learned that almost anyone could need help one day. When I lost my job, I was lucky to have savings. Not everyone does.

title: Where Did £1,200 Go?
body:
Every April, Nadia Hussain gets a letter from the company that manages her block of flats in Croydon. She owns her one-bedroom flat on a long lease, which means she is technically a tenant of the freeholder, and once a year she has to pay a service charge for things like cleaning the stairs, insuring the building and looking after the lifts. Usually the bill is about £1,400. This year it was £2,600.

“I nearly dropped my tea,” she says. “Nobody had warned us. There was just one line: total costs for the year.”

Nadia's first reaction was to pay it and complain later, because she was afraid of getting into trouble. But her neighbour, Gary, who used to work in accounting, told her to wait. By law, he explained, leaseholders have the right to ask for a summary of the costs and to see the invoices and receipts behind them. The managing agent has to provide them.

So Nadia wrote to the agent and asked for a full breakdown. When it arrived three weeks later, she and Gary sat down with it at her kitchen table and went through it line by line.

Some of the increase was fair. The building insurance had gone up, and the roof had been repaired after a storm. But other things didn't make sense. The block had been charged for gardening every month, although there is no garden, only a small strip of gravel. The cleaners were said to come twice a week, but residents had only ever seen them once a fortnight. And there was a £400 fee for a lift inspection, even though the lift had been out of order for most of the year.

Together with eight other leaseholders, Nadia sent a polite but detailed letter listing the charges they disagreed with. They said that if the problem couldn't be solved, they would take the case to a tribunal.

It didn't come to that. Two months later, the agent admitted that some costs had been “wrongly allocated” and reduced everyone's bill by £1,200. Nadia now checks every service charge carefully. “It's boring,” she says, “but it's my money.”

title: Meat-Free Mondays at Level 3
body:
The staff canteen on the third floor of Harbour Insurance's Melbourne office feeds around six hundred people every lunchtime. In February, management announced a six-month trial: every Monday and Thursday, the canteen would serve only vegan food. No meat, no fish, no cheese, not even milk in the coffee, although oat and soy milk would be free.

The announcement went down badly with some staff. On the internal chat, a man from the IT department wrote that he would “bring a sausage roll from home and eat it in protest.” Others asked why the company was telling them what to eat. The head of the canteen, Chef Tran Minh, replied that nobody was being forced to do anything. “You can still bring your own lunch,” he wrote. “But I think you'll be surprised.”

The reasons for the trial were partly environmental and partly about health. The company had promised to cut its carbon emissions by half by 2030, and producing meat, especially beef, creates a lot of greenhouse gases. A staff survey had also shown that many employees wanted healthier options at work.

The first few weeks were a challenge. On the first Monday, the number of people who bought lunch dropped by almost a third. A tofu stir-fry was described by one employee as “edible but sad.” Chef Tran listened to the complaints and changed the menu. Instead of trying to copy meat dishes, he started cooking food that is naturally vegan: Indian dhal, Lebanese falafel with tabbouleh, Vietnamese rice paper rolls, and a spicy pumpkin curry that quickly became famous across the building.

By May, sales on vegan days were almost back to normal. A second survey found that 64% of staff wanted the vegan days to continue, 20% wanted them to stop, and the rest didn't mind either way.

Even the man from IT has changed his mind, sort of. “I still think it should be up to me,” he says. “But I'd be lying if I said that curry wasn't good. I've had it every Thursday for two months.”

The trial has now been extended until the end of the year.

title: Coffee, Cookies and Conversation
body:
Every Wednesday at six o'clock, a meeting room on the fourth floor of the Seattle Central Library fills with noise. Around thirty people sit at small tables with paper cups of coffee and a plate of cookies. Each table has a little flag on it: Spanish, Japanese, Korean, French, Vietnamese, Amharic. And every table, for half the evening, switches to English.

This is the library's free language café, and it has been running for six years. The idea is simple. People who are learning a language sit with people who speak it well. For the first forty-five minutes they talk in one language, and then they switch. Nobody is a teacher, and there are no textbooks or grammar exercises, just conversation.

“The rule is that mistakes are welcome,” says Hana Kim, the librarian who started the café. “In a classroom, people are often scared of getting things wrong. Here, everyone is a learner at something.”

At the Spanish table tonight, Derek, a retired firefighter, is practicing for a trip to Mexico with his grandchildren. Opposite him is Lucía, who moved from Guadalajara eight months ago and wants to improve her English for job interviews. They have been meeting every week since January. When Derek gets stuck, Lucía helps him find the word. Forty-five minutes later, it's his turn to correct her.

“My English teacher at college is great, but I only speak in class,” Lucía says. “Here I can talk about real things: my family, the news, the Seahawks. Derek has explained American football to me three times. I still don't understand it.”

For some people, the café has become more than language practice. Many regulars arrived in Seattle recently and didn't know anyone. Friendships have formed across tables. Last year, two members who met at the Japanese table got married, and half the café was invited to the wedding.

Hana says the café costs the library almost nothing, apart from the cookies. “We could have spent money on new computers,” she says. “But I think this room does more for the city than any computer would.”
