title: The Brown Envelope
body:
Rhys Morgan found the envelope on the doormat of his new flat in Cardiff on a Tuesday morning in April. It was brown, with “HM Revenue & Customs” printed in the corner, and the word REMINDER in large letters at the top. His stomach dropped.

The letter said that he hadn't sent his Self Assessment tax return for the previous year, which had been due by 31 January. Because of that, he had been given a £100 penalty. If he still didn't send it within three months, he would be charged £10 a day on top.

Rhys was confused. He had started working as a freelance photographer the year before, and he knew that self-employed people had to fill in a tax return. But he had been waiting for HMRC to write to him with instructions first. Now he realised what must have happened: the first letter had been sent to his old address in Swansea. He had moved out in November and, in all the chaos of packing, he had forgotten to tell HMRC.

He rang his old landlord, who checked the post that was still piling up in the hallway. There it was: an envelope from HMRC, dated October, which explained exactly what he needed to do and by when.

That evening, Rhys sat down with a pile of receipts and his laptop. He set up an online account, updated his address and filled in the return. It took him four hours, mainly because his receipts were in a shoebox and some of them had faded so much that he could hardly read them. He owed £1,340 in tax, which he paid the next day.

Then he appealed against the penalty. He explained that he had moved house and had never received the first letter. Unfortunately, HMRC replied that it was his responsibility to tell them about a change of address, so the £100 had to be paid.

“It was an expensive lesson,” Rhys says. “But I learnt two things. Always redirect your post when you move. And never keep your receipts in a shoebox again.” He now uses an app to photograph every receipt as soon as he gets it.

title: The Night the Eden Rose
body:
It had been raining for three days when the warning came. At nine o'clock on a Saturday night in December, Helen Atkinson's phone buzzed with an alert from the Environment Agency: severe flood warning, danger to life, for the River Eden at Appleby. She looked out of the window of her cottage on Bridge Street. The river, which is normally a gentle stream you can see the stones through, had turned brown and was moving terrifyingly fast.

Helen, 67, has lived in the Cumbrian town all her life. Her husband, Pete, began carrying things upstairs straight away: photo albums, the laptop, his mother's sewing machine. Helen put sandbags against the front door, though she suspected they wouldn't be enough. By eleven, water was coming up through the floorboards.

At midnight there was a knock at the door. Two volunteers from the mountain rescue team, in waterproofs and head torches, told them they had to leave. The water in the street was already up to their knees. Pete didn't want to go. “We'll be fine upstairs,” he said. But one of the volunteers was firm. “If the electricity goes and the water keeps rising, we might not be able to get back to you.” They were taken to the community centre on higher ground, where about forty neighbours were drinking tea and wrapped in blankets.

When they returned two days later, the house smelt of mud and oil. The water had reached a metre up the walls. The sofa, the kitchen units and the carpets were ruined. Helen sat on the stairs and cried.

But what happened next is what she remembers most. Within hours, people were arriving from all over the county with shovels, buckets and food. Strangers carried soaking carpets to skips.

It took eight months and a large insurance claim before the couple could move back. Today, the electric sockets in their house are a metre above the floor and the floors are tiled, so the next flood will cause less damage. Helen hopes there won't be one. “But the river was here first,” she says. “We're only borrowing the space.”

title: From Manchester to the Dales
body:
It's been six months since we swapped our flat in Manchester for a stone cottage near Hawes, in the Yorkshire Dales. Friends keep asking whether we regret it, so here is the honest answer.

For years we talked about moving out. Tom used to joke that our children thought cows only existed on television. When he was offered a job he could do mostly from home, we ran out of excuses. We sold the flat and bought a cottage with three bedrooms, a garden and a view of the hills. In the city, we could never have afforded a garden.

The first weeks were harder than I'd expected. The nearest supermarket is twenty minutes away by car, the bus comes twice a day, and the mobile signal disappears in the kitchen. In Manchester I used to pop out for milk at ten at night. Here, if you forget something, you go without.

The children, on the other hand, settled in almost immediately. The village school has only forty pupils, so Isla and Arjun were noticed straight away. Isla has joined a young farmers' club, and Arjun spends every free minute building dens in the woods. They sleep like logs.

The neighbours have been wonderful. On our first evening, an elderly farmer called Geoff turned up with a box of eggs and a list of useful numbers: the plumber, the vet, the man who clears snow from the lane. I must admit I miss the restaurants, and Tom misses his football mates. But if someone offered us our old flat back tomorrow, I'm fairly sure we'd say no.

My advice? If you're thinking of moving to the countryside, rent for a year first and spend a winter there. Summer is easy. February tells you the truth.

title: Twelve Hours on an Ambulance
body:
My name is Marcus Reed. My alarm goes off at 5:30 a.m., and by seven I'm at the firehouse on the South Side of Chicago, checking the ambulance with my partner, Elena Ruiz. We go through the same list every morning: oxygen, medicines, the defibrillator, the stretcher. If something is missing, we might not notice until we really need it.

I've been working as a paramedic for eight years. People imagine our job is all sirens and dramatic rescues, like on TV. Some days it is. But most calls are quieter: an elderly man who has fallen in his bathroom, a woman with chest pain who isn't sure she should bother anyone, a teenager who's had an allergic reaction at a party.

Last Tuesday was a typical shift. Our first call came in at 7:40: a construction worker had cut his hand badly. We stopped the bleeding and drove him to the hospital. Then came a diabetic patient whose blood sugar had dropped so low that she didn't know where she was. Ten minutes after we gave her glucose, she was sitting up and apologizing for the trouble.

The hardest call came in the afternoon. A man had collapsed in a grocery store, and a customer had already started CPR when we arrived. We worked on him for twenty minutes and managed to get his heart going again. I don't know yet whether he'll make a full recovery. In this job, you often never find out what happens next.

People ask me how I cope. Honestly, it's my coworkers. After a bad call, we talk it through over terrible coffee. We can also see a counselor for free, and I'm not ashamed to say I've used her.

Would I recommend the job? Only if you can stay calm when everyone around you is panicking. If you can, nothing is more rewarding than seeing a patient walk out of the hospital.

title: A Day in the Medieval City
body:
Last Thursday, the Transition Year students of Ardmore Community College in Dublin swapped the classroom for the streets of Kilkenny. Ms Byrne, our history teacher, had promised us the trip would be more interesting than any textbook. Most of us didn't believe her. By the end of the day, she had been proven right.

Our first stop was Kilkenny Castle. Our guide, Declan, told us that a stone castle was built on the site by the Normans over 800 years ago. For nearly six centuries it was owned by the Butler family, one of the most powerful families in Ireland. In 1967 they sold it to the people of Kilkenny for just fifty pounds. “Even back then, that was a bargain,” Declan said, and everyone laughed.

After lunch we walked along the Medieval Mile, a route through the old town that connects the castle with St Canice's Cathedral. On the way, we stopped outside Kyteler's Inn. Declan explained that its owner, Alice Kyteler, was accused of witchcraft in 1324. She managed to escape, but her servant was not so lucky. Several of us went quiet after that story.

The highlight for many of us was climbing the round tower next to the cathedral. It's about a thousand years old, and the steps inside are narrow and steep. Aoife, who is afraid of heights, almost turned back halfway, but we persuaded her to keep going. From the top you can see the whole city and the green fields around it.

On the bus home, Ms Byrne asked us what we would remember. Jamal said the castle, Aoife said the view, and I said the fifty pounds. What surprised me most was how much history is hidden in a town you could walk across in twenty minutes. If you get the chance, go to Kilkenny, and bring good shoes.

title: Goodbye, 3 a.m.
body:
For almost two years, I knew the ceiling of my bedroom better than any painting in the National Gallery of Victoria. I would fall asleep at midnight, wake up at three and lie there until the sun came up, worrying about work, money and the fact that I wasn't sleeping.

I tried everything my friends in Melbourne suggested: herbal tea, lavender oil, a new mattress, even counting sheep. Nothing worked. Eventually my GP referred me to a psychologist who specialises in sleep. Thanks to a mental health plan, part of the cost was covered by Medicare, which made it possible for me to go.

“Let's look at the facts, Mei,” Dr Okafor said at my first appointment, and she asked me to keep a sleep diary for two weeks. I wrote down when I went to bed, when I woke up and how long I lay awake. When she looked at it, she pointed out something I'd never noticed: I was spending nine hours in bed but only sleeping five.

Her solution sounded crazy. Instead of going to bed earlier, I had to go later. I was only allowed to be in bed for six hours, from 12:30 to 6:30, even at weekends. If I couldn't sleep after about twenty minutes, I had to get up, sit in the living room with a book and go back only when I felt sleepy. My phone had to stay in the kitchen.

The first fortnight was awful. I was so tired that I nearly fell asleep on the tram to work. But slowly my body got the message. The bed became a place for sleeping again, not for worrying. After six weeks, I was allowed to go to bed fifteen minutes earlier, and then fifteen more.

Today I sleep about seven hours most nights. I still have bad nights now and then, but they don't frighten me any more. If you're lying awake as you read this, my advice is simple: get out of bed, and then go and see your GP.

title: Zoe's Big Announcement
body:
Fifteen-year-old Zoe Martinez had been planning the conversation for weeks. One evening in Austin, while her parents were clearing the table, she finally said it.
“I want to be an influencer. A real one, with brand deals.”
Her dad, Luis, put down the plates. “What happened to wanting to be a vet?”
“I can do both,” Zoe said. “But I'm good at this. My makeup videos already have twelve thousand followers.”

Her mom, Rachel, had seen the videos. They were funny and well edited, and she was secretly proud. But she had also read the comments, and some of them were cruel.
“Here's my worry,” Rachel said. “When you post something online, it stays there forever. Strangers can find out which school you go to. And if your happiness depends on likes, one bad week could make you miserable.”
“So you're saying no?”
“I'm saying let's make some rules.”

They talked for over an hour and finally agreed on a deal. Zoe could keep posting, but she would never show the school, the house or the street. Her parents would be able to see her account, and any brand that contacted her would have to talk to them first. Homework had to be finished before filming, and her grades couldn't drop.

“What if a company wants to send me free stuff?” Zoe asked.
“Then we read the contract together,” said Luis. “Your aunt is a lawyer, remember?”

Three months later, Zoe has nineteen thousand followers and has turned down two offers that her mom described as “a bit shady.” She has also discovered that editing a two-minute video takes about four hours.
“It's actually a job,” she admitted last week. “A real one.”
Rachel smiled. “That's what we've been trying to tell you.”

title: Read Every Page
body:
When Kwame Mensah got his first job as a junior engineer in Bristol, he couldn't wait to stop sleeping on his cousin's sofa. After three weeks of viewings, he finally found a one-bedroom flat in Bedminster for £950 a month. The letting agent asked him to pay a holding deposit to take it off the market, and a week later he was invited to the office to sign the tenancy agreement.

“I thought I'd just sign and get the keys,” Kwame says. “But my dad had told me to read every page, so I did. It took me forty minutes.”

Some things were straightforward: the rent, the date it was due and the length of the contract, which was twelve months. Others were less clear. One clause said that the tenant was responsible for “all repairs.” Kwame asked about it, and the agent admitted it had been copied from an old contract. In England, the landlord has to repair things like the boiler, the heating and the plumbing. The clause was changed before he signed.

He also checked the deposit. By law, it can't be more than five weeks' rent, and it must be protected in a government-approved scheme. If the landlord keeps money unfairly at the end, the tenant can challenge it for free. Kwame received a certificate within thirty days, just as the law says.

The most useful advice came from his cousin: take photos of everything on the first day. The inventory said the carpet was in “good condition,” but there was a large stain under the bed. Kwame photographed it and emailed the pictures to the agent the same afternoon.

“If I hadn't done that, they could have taken the cost out of my deposit when I move out,” he says. “It's boring, but it's your money.”

title: The Door on Bloor Street
body:
I've been cycling to work in downtown Toronto for six years, and I always thought I was careful. I wore a helmet, used the bike lane on Bloor Street and never listened to music while riding. None of that helped on a grey Tuesday morning last October.

I was riding past a row of parked cars when a driver suddenly opened his door right in front of me. There was no time to brake. I hit the door, flew over the handlebars and landed on my left arm. For a few seconds I couldn't breathe. Then people were everywhere: a woman from a coffee shop, a courier who had seen it all, and the driver, who kept saying, “I didn't see you, I'm so sorry.”

Someone called 911, and an ambulance took me to St. Michael's Hospital. My helmet was cracked, which told me exactly what would have happened to my head without it. The X-ray showed a broken wrist, and I left that evening with a cast and some painkillers.

The courier had given his number to the police officer at the scene, and that turned out to be important. In Ontario, opening a car door into a cyclist's path is an offence, and his statement made the case clear. The driver was fined, and his insurance paid for my bike.

The cast came off after six weeks, but getting my confidence back took longer. For the first few rides I was terrified every time I passed a parked car. “Start on quiet streets at weekends, Nadia,” my physiotherapist told me, and she was right. Slowly it worked.

I'm back on my bike now, though I ride a metre further from parked cars. And when I drive, I always open my door with my right hand. It forces you to turn and look behind you. It's called the Dutch reach, and it might save someone's wrist, or more.

title: Dear Money Desk: Our Basement Flooded
body:
Dear Money Desk,
Last month, a huge storm hit our town in New Jersey. Within two hours, the water in our street was a foot deep, and it poured into our basement through the windows. We lost a washer, a freezer, my husband's tools and boxes of family photos. The walls will have to be replaced.

We've had homeowners insurance with the same company for eleven years and have never made a claim. So we were shocked when they wrote to say they wouldn't pay a cent. The adjuster said the damage was caused by “surface water,” which our policy doesn't cover. How can this be legal? Should we hire a lawyer?
Frustrated in Edison

Dear Frustrated,
I'm very sorry. Unfortunately, your insurer is probably right. Almost all standard homeowners policies in the US exclude flood damage, meaning water that comes into the house from outside. Many people only find this out after a disaster. To be protected, you would have needed a separate flood policy, which is usually bought through the National Flood Insurance Program.

That said, don't give up yet. First, ask the company to explain the decision in writing and to show you the exact words in your policy. Second, check whether any water came up through the floor drain. Some policies cover sewer backup, either as standard or as an extra you might have added years ago and forgotten about. Third, contact FEMA and your town hall. After major storms, federal assistance is sometimes made available to homeowners, even if their insurance pays nothing.

A lawyer is only worth it if you think the company has misread your policy. If you do decide to appeal, keep every receipt and take photos before anything is thrown away.

Finally, when this is over, buy flood insurance. New policies usually take thirty days to start, so don't wait until the next storm is on the news.
Money Desk

title: The Morning After in London Fields
body:
Every sunny Monday morning, before most people have had breakfast, Rosa Adeyemi is already in London Fields with a grabber and a roll of bin bags. By nine o'clock she and a dozen other volunteers have usually filled forty of them.

“On a hot weekend, thousands of people come here, and that's wonderful,” says Rosa, a retired nurse who has lived next to the park in Hackney for thirty years. “But a lot of them leave everything behind: cans, bottles, pizza boxes, even tents. The foxes and seagulls rip the bags open, and by Sunday night the place looks like the morning after a festival.”

The problem has got worse since the pandemic, when parks became the main place for young Londoners to meet. Disposable barbecues are a particular worry. They leave black patches on the grass and have caused small fires in dry summers. Broken glass is another. Last August a child cut her foot badly near the paddling pool.

Hackney Council says it has already added more bins and empties them more often at weekends. A spokesperson admitted, however, that in a heatwave the bins are “still overflowing by Saturday evening.” From next summer, disposable barbecues will be banned in the park, and people caught dropping litter could be fined £150.

Not everyone thinks fines are the answer. Tom Clarke, 24, who was having a picnic with friends on Sunday, believes most people aren't lazy, just badly organised. “If the bins are full, people put their rubbish next to them and hope someone will deal with it. If there were more bins near the exits, I think most people would use them.”

Rosa agrees, but she has a simpler suggestion. “Bring a bag and take it home with you. If you could carry it here when it was full, you can carry it home when it's empty.”

title: Three Days on the Routeburn
body:
Day 1, Routeburn Falls Hut
We booked our beds in the Department of Conservation huts back in June, on the day bookings opened. Three hours later, every bed for the summer had gone. So here we are, Tama and I, finally on the Routeburn Track, one of New Zealand's Great Walks. Today was gentle: four hours through beech forest beside a river so clear you could count the stones. My pack weighs fourteen kilos, and I'm already wondering which of my three books I should have left at home.

Day 2, Lake Mackenzie Hut
The big day. We climbed above the bushline to Harris Saddle, the highest point of the track. The weather up there can change in minutes, and the hut warden had warned us to turn back if the cloud came down. We were lucky. The sky stayed blue, and the view across the Hollyford Valley took my breath away. At lunch a kea, a big green mountain parrot, tried to steal Tama's sandwich and then started pulling at his bootlaces. Keas are clever, cheeky birds, and they're endangered, so you're not allowed to feed them.

The descent to Lake Mackenzie was steep, and by the time we arrived my knees were complaining. But the lake was so still that the mountains were reflected perfectly in it. Tama swam. I watched. It was freezing.

Day 3, The Divide
Rain at last, as if the track wanted to show us its other side. Earland Falls was so full that the path below it was soaked. At The Divide we waited for the bus to Te Anau, wet, tired and very happy.

I've done plenty of day walks, but this was different. After three days, you stop thinking about emails and start thinking about water, food and the next hill. I already know what I'm doing next winter: setting an alarm for the day bookings open.

title: Minus Forty and the Northern Lights
body:
Hannah Price, a third-year geography student at the University of Birmingham, has just come back from a semester at the University of Alaska Fairbanks. We asked her about life near the Arctic Circle.

Why Alaska?
I study climate change, and Fairbanks is one of the best places in the world to see it happening. The permafrost, ground that has been frozen for thousands of years, is starting to melt there. Some of the roads near the town have become so uneven that they look like a roller coaster.

What was the hardest part?
The dark. I arrived in January, when the sun rises at about eleven and sets before three. For the first few weeks I felt tired all the time. A friend from Anchorage told me to buy a light therapy lamp and to go outside at lunchtime, even for ten minutes. It made a huge difference.

And the cold?
Once it reached minus forty. That's the temperature where Celsius and Fahrenheit are the same, which was the only fun fact about it. Your eyelashes freeze, and if you throw boiling water into the air, it turns into snow. People plug their cars in at night so that the engine doesn't freeze. I'd never have believed it if I hadn't seen the cables outside the supermarket.

Was studying there different from Birmingham?
Very. Classes were smaller, and we were expected to speak in every seminar. I also did fieldwork with a research team, measuring how quickly the ground was sinking. At home I'd only read about that in articles.

Any highlights?
The northern lights, obviously. The first time I saw them, green and purple across the whole sky, I actually cried. And a moose walked past the library one morning as if it owned the place.

Would you recommend it?
Absolutely, but pack properly. If you're cold, you can't think about anything else.

title: Second Tenor, Next to Dai
body:
For twenty-three years, Gareth Lloyd had been the quietest person at Morgan & Price, a firm of accountants in Cardiff. He arrived at 8:30, checked tax returns all day and rarely said more than a few words at lunch. Nobody knew that in the car, on the way home, he sang at the top of his voice.

It was his colleague Siân who found out. One evening she pulled up next to him at a red light and saw him singing along to the radio, eyes closed, completely lost in the music. The next morning she left a leaflet on his desk: the Pontcanna Male Voice Choir was looking for new members. Rehearsals were on Tuesday nights at the rugby club. No experience needed.

Gareth put the leaflet in a drawer. Then he took it out again. It took him three weeks to work up the courage to go.

The first rehearsal was terrifying. Sixty men in a hall, most of them twice his size, and a conductor called Bethan who could hear a wrong note from across the room. She asked him to sing a few lines on his own so that she could decide where to put him. His voice shook, but she nodded and said, “Second tenor. Sit next to Dai.”

Dai, a retired miner of eighty-one, turned out to be the best thing about the choir. He showed Gareth how to breathe properly, explained the Welsh words he didn't understand and always bought the first round after rehearsal.

Eight months later, the choir gave its Christmas concert in a packed chapel. In the middle of “Calon Lân,” Gareth stepped forward for a short solo. He had been practising it in the car for weeks.

On Monday, there was a card on his desk from Siân. It said: “I told you so.”

title: Nine Minutes on Screen
body:
Laura Bennett had never had a video appointment before. When she booked through the NHS App, she chose it only because the next face-to-face slot at her GP surgery in Leicester was in three weeks. At 10:40 she propped her phone against the fruit bowl, and Dr Shah appeared on the screen.

“Morning, Laura. Can you hear me all right?”
“Yes. Oh, you've frozen. No, you're back.”
“Good. You wrote that you've got a rash on your arm. When did it start?”
“On Saturday. I'd spent the whole day clearing the garden. By Sunday it was red and itchy, and now there are little blisters.”
“Could you move closer to the window and hold the camera near it? That's it. Turn your arm a little. Thank you.”

Dr Shah asked whether Laura had a temperature, whether the rash was spreading and whether she had touched any unusual plants. Laura remembered a huge plant with white flowers growing by the fence.
“That sounds like giant hogweed,” said Dr Shah. “Its sap makes your skin very sensitive to sunlight. It looks nasty, but in most cases it heals on its own within a few weeks.”

She told Laura to keep the arm covered when she went out and sent a prescription for a cream straight to the pharmacy round the corner.
“If it gets much worse, or if you get a fever, ring 111 or book another appointment. And please wear gloves next time you're in the garden. Hogweed can be dangerous.”
“Will I need to come in?”
“Not unless it gets worse. Send me a photo through the app in a week if you're not sure.”

The whole appointment took nine minutes. Laura picked up her cream on the way to work. Afterwards she rang the council about the hogweed, and two men in protective suits came to remove it.

title: Emails from Seattle
body:
From: Jordan Kim
To: Tasha Green
Subject: Month one

Hi Tash,
Greetings from Seattle! Yes, it rains a lot, but it's mostly a light drizzle, and nobody here uses an umbrella. The job is great so far. The hospital's data team is small, my manager, Ruth, is patient with my questions, and I've already been given my first real project: figuring out why so many patients miss their appointments. The bad news is the rent. My studio costs nearly twice what I paid in Columbus, and it's the size of your kitchen.

Subject: Month two

Tash, I'm going to be honest: this month was hard. Everyone at work is friendly, but at five o'clock they all disappear. A coworker told me about the “Seattle Freeze,” the idea that people here are polite but hard to get close to. I've spent most weekends alone, eating takeout and watching the shows we used to watch together. I nearly called Mom and told her I was coming home.

Subject: Month three

Good news! I took your advice and signed up for a beginners' climbing class at a gym near my place. On the first night, I was paired with a nurse called Miguel, who had moved here from Texas last year and felt exactly the same way. Now there's a group of six of us, all newcomers, and we go climbing on Tuesdays and out for pho afterward. Last Saturday we took the ferry to Bainbridge Island, and on the way back Mount Rainier came out from behind the clouds. I've never seen anything like it.

At work, I presented my project to the hospital managers. They've decided to send text reminders two days before every appointment. Ruth says if it works, my name will be on the report.

I still miss you, and I still miss Columbus in the fall. But I think I'm staying.
J.

title: Three Seconds to Write
body:
It started with a text that took Orla three seconds to write. Her best friend Grace was moving flat in Galway on Saturday and had asked if Orla could help carry boxes. Orla had had an exhausting week, and the thought of four flights of stairs made her want to cry. So she wrote back: “So sorry, I've been asked to work Saturday. Good luck!”

It wasn't a big lie, she told herself. Grace had her brother and two cousins. One person more or less wouldn't make a difference.

On Saturday afternoon, Orla's sister rang and persuaded her to come out for a quick drink on Quay Street. One drink became three, and somebody's friend took a group photo outside the pub and posted it online. Orla was right in the middle, holding a pint and laughing. She didn't even notice she'd been tagged.

Grace noticed. That evening, sitting on a box in a half-empty flat with a sore back, she saw the photo. She didn't send an angry message. She didn't send any message at all, which was worse.

For almost three weeks, Grace ignored Orla's texts. When they finally met for coffee, Grace explained that the lie hurt far more than the missing help. “If you'd just said you were wrecked, I'd have understood,” she said. “Now I keep wondering what else you haven't told me.”

Orla apologised properly, without excuses. She admitted that she found it hard to say no to people, and that lying had seemed easier than disappointing anyone. Grace listened, and by the end of the second coffee they were almost laughing about it.

They're still best friends, but something has changed. Orla has realised that a small lie is never really small if someone finds out. These days, when she's too tired, she just says so. It's surprisingly easy.

title: A Year Without New Clothes
body:
A year ago, I watched a documentary that ruined online shopping for me. It followed a bundle of old clothes from a charity bin in Britain to a market in Accra, Ghana. Most of what arrived there was too damaged to sell, and much of it ended up on a beach, tangled in the sand. In one scene, a woman held up a T-shirt with the label still on. It was from a shop I had bought from the week before.

That night I counted the clothes in my wardrobe. There were 143 items, and I had worn at least forty of them fewer than three times. So I made a decision: for one year, I would buy nothing new.

The first month was the hardest. I'd got used to treating myself to something whenever I'd had a bad day. Instead, I started exploring the charity shops in Headingley, in Leeds, where students leave amazing things behind at the end of every summer term. I found a wool coat for £12 that has had more compliments than anything I've ever bought at full price.

I also discovered apps for buying and selling used clothes. Selling turned out to be as satisfying as buying. I've made over £300 from things that were just taking up space. My friend Aisha and I now host a clothes swap every few months, and last time thirty people came.

It hasn't all been easy. Second-hand shopping takes time, and if you need something specific, like black trousers for a job interview, you can spend whole Saturdays looking. I also had to learn to sew on buttons, which my gran found hilarious. “Chloe, love, I taught your mother that when she was seven,” she said.

The year finished last week. Have I gone back to new clothes? Not really. I've realised that I didn't need more things. I needed to stop buying things I didn't need.

title: The Corner at Hogan's
body:
When Ciarán and Lena moved from a flat in Dublin to a cottage outside Kilfenora in County Clare, everyone warned them about the same thing. “Country people are lovely,” said Ciarán's mother, “but it'll take you ten years to be accepted.”

For the first few weeks, it looked as if she was right. In Hogan's, the only pub in the village, there was a corner of the bar where the same four regulars sat every evening: Mickey, a retired farmer; his brother Joe; Tom the postman; and a sheep farmer called Pat who rarely spoke. People greeted the newcomers politely, but the corner stayed closed.

Things changed on a wet Thursday in November. The pub held a quiz every week, and the corner always entered as a team called the Old Reliables. That night, Tom was in bed with the flu, and the team was one person short.
“You,” said Mickey, pointing at Lena. “Do you know anything about music?”
“A bit,” said Lena, who had worked at a radio station for six years.

The Old Reliables had never won the quiz. They knew everything about hurling, local history and cattle prices, and almost nothing about anything that had happened after 1990. Lena answered every question in the pop music round, and Ciarán, who had been sent to the bar for drinks, came back just in time to name the film in the final question. They won by two points. The prize was a bottle of whiskey and a ham, and Mickey insisted on sharing both.

Since then, there have always been two extra stools in the corner. Lena has been taught how to judge a good pint, and Ciarán has learned more about sheep than he ever wanted to know. Last month, Pat invited them to his daughter's wedding.

Ciarán's mother was wrong. It didn't take ten years. It took one quiz.

title: Dear Jenna, at Twenty
body:
Dear Jenna,

Today I turn forty. I'm sitting on the steps of our house in Halifax, the one you'll buy in about fifteen years, with a cup of tea and the harbour in the distance. My kids made me a cake this morning that looked like a crime scene. It was delicious. I wanted to write to you, because there are a few things I wish someone had told me at twenty.

First, stop apologizing for taking up space. You say “sorry” when people bump into you. You'll keep doing that for years, and it will cost you a promotion you deserved. Speak up in meetings. Your ideas are better than you think.

Second, you're going to move to Vancouver for a man called Ryan. I won't tell you not to, because you wouldn't listen. Just know that it won't work out, and that's fine. You'll learn to cook, to climb mountains and to live on your own, and you'll come home stronger than you left.

Third, call Grandma MacLeod more often. I know she repeats the same stories about the fishing boats. Write them down. One day you'll want to tell them to your own children, and you'll only remember half.

Fourth, look after your knees. Seriously.

If I could change one thing, though, it would be how much time you spend worrying about what other people think of you. Almost nobody is thinking about you. They're too busy worrying about themselves. Once you realize that, life gets much lighter.

I won't tell you everything. Some of the best things that have happened to me were complete surprises, and I wouldn't want to ruin them. But I can tell you this: forty is not old, the best friends you'll have aren't the ones you have now, and it all turns out better than you fear.

With love and a slightly sore back,
Jenna (40)

title: The Kitchen Closes at Eight
body:
Every January, Kevin Larson steps on the bathroom scale and groans. This year, after a Thanksgiving that lasted until Christmas and a Christmas that lasted until New Year's, the number was eleven pounds higher than in October. A high school teacher in Minneapolis, Kevin had tried diets before. This time his brother-in-law suggested something different: intermittent fasting.

The idea is simple. Instead of changing what you eat, you change when you eat. Kevin chose the popular 16:8 method, which means eating only during an eight-hour window, in his case from noon to 8 p.m. For the other sixteen hours, he was allowed water, black coffee and tea, but nothing else.

“The first week was rough,” Kevin admits. “By ten in the morning I was so hungry that I was grumpy with my students. I had headaches, too.” But by the third week, his body had adjusted. He stopped snacking in the evening, and he noticed he had more energy in the afternoon.

After two months, he had lost nine pounds. Is fasting the reason? Not necessarily, says Dr. Angela Reyes, a dietitian at a clinic in St. Paul. “Several studies suggest that intermittent fasting works about as well as ordinary calorie counting. For many people, the real benefit is that it gives them a clear rule. If the kitchen is closed after eight, you can't eat chips in front of the TV.”

She also warns that fasting isn't for everyone. People with diabetes who take medication, pregnant women and anyone with a history of eating disorders should talk to their doctor first. “And if you fast all morning and then eat a whole pizza at noon, it won't help,” she adds.

Kevin plans to keep going, though maybe not forever. “I don't really think of it as a diet anymore,” he says. “It's more like a habit. And honestly, breakfast was never my favorite meal.”

title: Nine Waiting Lists
body:
When Lucy Nguyen was five months pregnant, a friend gave her some advice that sounded like a joke. “Put your baby's name down for childcare now,” she said. “Before it's even born.”

Lucy laughed. A year later, she isn't laughing. Her daughter Ava is eleven months old, Lucy is due back at her job as a pharmacist in three weeks, and not a single childcare centre in Marrickville, in Sydney's inner west, has offered them a place.

“We're on nine waiting lists,” says her husband, Sam. “Three of them charged us a fee just to put her name down. One centre told us the wait for babies under two was eighteen months. By then she'll be nearly three.”

The Nguyens are far from alone. In many parts of Sydney, demand for places, especially for babies, is much higher than supply. Centres need more staff to look after very young children, and there aren't enough trained educators. Many have left the industry because of low pay.

The family has looked at every option. A nanny would cost more than Lucy earns. Sam's mother can help, but only on Mondays and Tuesdays, because she still works part-time herself. Lucy has asked her manager if she could work fewer days, but the pharmacy is short of staff too.

In the end, they found a family day care educator, a woman called Fatima who looks after four children in her own home ten minutes away. She had one place left for three days a week. With help from the government's Child Care Subsidy, they can just about afford it.

“It's not what we planned, but Ava loves her already,” says Lucy. “What makes me angry is that we're the lucky ones. If we hadn't found Fatima, I'd have had to give up my job.”

title: A Concert Hall with a Cat
body:
Tonight's venue holds forty people, has a cat called Biscuit and smells of chili. It's the living room of Dana and Mark Hoffman in Milwaukee, and for the next two hours it will be a concert hall.

I've been playing house concerts for five years now, ever since a promoter canceled my tour three days before it began. A fan in Ohio emailed to ask if I'd play in her basement instead. I nearly said no. I'm glad I didn't.

The idea is simple. Someone who likes your music offers their home. They invite friends, neighbors and coworkers, and everyone pays a suggested donation, usually twenty dollars, which goes straight to the musician. People bring food to share. There's no stage, no bar and, in Dana's case, no microphone. I sit on a kitchen chair in front of the fireplace with my guitar, about six feet from the front row.

That closeness terrified me at first. In a club, the lights are in your eyes and you can't see anyone's face. In a living room, you can see everything: the man who checks his phone, the teenager who is clearly there only because his mom made him come, the woman who starts crying during a song about my father. There's nowhere to hide. But there's also nothing between you and the audience, and that's exactly why it works.

Tonight, halfway through the second set, Biscuit jumps onto the piano and sits there for three songs as if he'd bought a ticket. Everyone laughs, including me. Afterward, people stay for an hour, asking about the songs and buying records. The teenager buys one too.

I earn more from a good house concert than from most club shows, and I've slept in more guest rooms than hotels. Some hosts have become close friends. When people ask me what the future of live music looks like, I tell them it might look like a living room in Milwaukee.

title: In Praise of the 7:42
body:
Every weekday for the past seven years, I've caught the 7:42 from Hebden Bridge to Manchester Victoria. It takes about forty minutes, if it's on time, and I've come to think of it as the most important part of my day.

I know how that sounds. Commuting is supposed to be miserable, and sometimes it is. Last winter, my train was cancelled eleven times in one month. During the strikes, I worked from my kitchen table for weeks. My annual season ticket costs more than my first car did, and on Friday mornings, when the carriages are packed, I've stood with my face pressed against a stranger's rucksack all the way to Manchester.

But there are things I'd miss if I gave it up. The train gives me forty minutes that belong to nobody. I can't do the washing up, nobody can ring me, and the signal in the tunnels near Todmorden is so bad that my emails have to wait. I've read more books on that train than in the rest of my adult life. On the way home I watch the Calder Valley go past, green in summer, grey and mysterious in November.

Then there are the regulars. Nobody introduced us, but after seven years I know them all: the nurse who does crosswords in pen, the two lads who argue about football every single day, and Margaret, who knits on the 17:58 and has made jumpers for half the carriage. When I had an operation on my knee last year, three of them carried my bags for a month.

My advice to new commuters? Claim Delay Repay every time your train is late. It's your money. Get a seat facing forward, put your phone away and look out of the window. And learn the names of the people around you. You might be seeing them every day for years.

title: Notes on the Notice Board
body:
NOTICE TO ALL RESIDENTS
From the Strata Council, 1450 Commercial Drive, Vancouver

It has come to our attention that bicycles are being left in the hallways and in the lobby. Under Bylaw 12, hallways must be kept clear at all times. This is not just a matter of appearance: in a fire, blocked hallways can cost lives. Any bicycle found in a hallway after March 1 will be removed. Bicycles must be stored in the bike room in the parkade.

A handwritten note appeared under the notice the next morning:

Dear Council,
We'd love to use the bike room. Unfortunately, it has space for twelve bikes, and there are at least thirty in this building. The lock has been broken since October, and two bikes were stolen in January, including mine. Nobody is leaving a $1,500 e-bike down there. Fix the room, and the hallways will be clear.
Priya, Unit 304

Below that, in green pen:

Agree with Priya. Also, I'm 74 and can't carry my bike down two flights of stairs. The elevator doesn't go to the parkade.
Walter, Unit 108

And below that, in pencil:

Could we please stop blocking the hallway with bikes AND the notice board with notes? This board is for building news.
Unit 210

The argument continued for two weeks, until Priya organized a residents' meeting in the lobby. Twenty-two people came, along with two council members. By the end of the evening, they had agreed on a plan. The council would replace the broken lock with a key-card system and install racks on the walls, which would double the number of spaces. Residents who couldn't manage the stairs would be allowed to keep their bikes in a small storage room by the front door.

Six weeks later, a new notice went up:

The new bike room is now open. Thank you for your patience and cooperation.

Underneath, in green pen, someone had added: “Much better. Thanks, Priya. W.”

title: Terrible at Bowling, Great at Pancakes
body:
How We Met: Andre and Leila

Leila: I'd been on the app for about a year, and I was ready to delete it. I'd been on maybe fifteen first dates, and most of them were fine but forgettable. One man spent the whole dinner talking about his ex. Another turned out to be ten years older than his photos.

Andre: My sister set up my profile, actually. I'm a chemistry teacher, and she said my photos looked like a school ID card. She made me upload a picture of me hiking at Stone Mountain and write something honest. So I wrote: “Terrible at bowling. Great at pancakes. Looking for someone to laugh with.”

Leila: The pancakes got my attention. I swiped right, we matched, and his first message was a question about my favorite building in Atlanta, because my profile said I'm an architect. Nobody had ever asked me that. We messaged for about two weeks. He never sent anything weird, which on a dating app is rarer than you'd think.

Andre: Our first date was supposed to be at Ponce City Market, but a thunderstorm shut down half the city that evening. So we had a video call instead and talked for three hours. When we finally met in person the following Saturday, it didn't feel like a first date at all.

Leila: He was exactly like his profile. That sounds like a low bar, but trust me, it isn't. And he really is terrible at bowling.

Andre: I've been practicing.

Leila: He hasn't. Anyway, that was two years ago. We moved in together last spring, and in June he proposed, over pancakes, of course.

Andre: My advice for anyone on the apps? Be honest, ask real questions, and don't give up too quickly. If Leila had deleted her account that week, I'd still be eating pancakes on my own.

title: Question Time from the Gallery
body:
At eight o'clock on Wednesday morning, twenty-six Year 10 students from Levin East College climbed onto a bus to Wellington. Their social studies teacher, Mr Tipene, had one rule for the day: “Ask at least one question you actually want the answer to.”

Their guide at Parliament, a former teacher called Ruth, started with a surprising fact. New Zealand's Parliament has only one house. It used to have two, but the upper house was abolished in 1951. “So when a bill passes here, that's it,” she explained. “There's no second chamber to stop it.”

She led them through Parliament House, past portraits of former prime ministers, and pointed out the Beehive next door, the round building where the ministers have their offices. Then she showed them the debating chamber, where about 120 MPs sit facing each other. Members can speak in English, te reo Māori or New Zealand Sign Language.

At two o'clock, the class sat in the public gallery to watch Question Time. Ana, who had expected something serious and dignified, was shocked. MPs shouted across the room, laughed at each other's answers and were told off several times by the Speaker. “It's like our classroom on a Friday afternoon,” whispered her friend Liam.

Afterwards, their local MP came out to meet them. She had been told the students had questions, and she wasn't disappointed. Ana asked why sixteen-year-olds couldn't vote when they could work and pay tax. The MP said it was a serious debate that had even reached the Supreme Court. She didn't promise anything, but she said the question deserved a proper answer, not a joke.

On the bus home, Mr Tipene asked who would like to be an MP one day. Three hands went up. Ana's wasn't one of them. “I'd rather be the Speaker,” she said. “The Speaker's the only one who gets to tell them all to be quiet.”

title: Sneezing Since Year Seven
body:
Every year, around the middle of May, Becky Hall knows that summer has arrived before she even opens the curtains. Her eyes are itchy, her nose is running and she's sneezed six times before breakfast.

“I've had hay fever since I was eleven,” says Becky, 34, who teaches PE at a secondary school in Nottingham. “For someone who spends half the day on a playing field, it's the worst allergy you could possibly have.”

Hay fever is an allergic reaction to pollen, the fine powder that plants release to reproduce. Around one in five people in the UK suffer from it. Most, like Becky, react to grass pollen, which is at its worst from late May to July. Others are allergic to tree pollen, which comes earlier in spring.

For years, Becky simply suffered. “I used to think it was just something you had to put up with, like rain.” Then a pharmacist gave her advice that changed everything: start the treatment before the symptoms begin. Now she starts using a steroid nasal spray in early May, two weeks before the grass season, and takes an antihistamine every morning.

She has also collected a list of small tricks. She checks the pollen forecast on the Met Office website and plans outdoor lessons for the morning when the count is high. She wears wraparound sunglasses, puts a little Vaseline around her nostrils to trap pollen, and showers and changes her clothes as soon as she gets home. On high-pollen days, her washing is dried inside, never on the line.

“It's not cured,” she says. “I still have bad days, especially after a thunderstorm. But it used to ruin three months of my year, and now it's more like a nuisance.”

If your symptoms don't improve with treatment from the pharmacy, see your GP. For some people with severe hay fever, a long course of immunotherapy may be an option.

title: The Last Morning at Russo's
body:
For forty years, the lights at Russo's Bakery on the corner of Ninth and Morris Street in South Philadelphia came on at four o'clock every morning. Last Sunday, they came on for the last time. On Monday, a handwritten letter was taped to the window:

Dear neighbors,
After forty years, Teresa and I have decided to close the bakery. It wasn't an easy decision. We're both over seventy now, and my knees have started to complain about standing for twelve hours a day. Our children have good jobs of their own, and we didn't want to push them into a life of 4 a.m. alarms. We tried to sell the business, but nobody wanted to take it on.
We have watched your kids grow up. We made their birthday cakes, then their wedding cakes, and lately their kids' birthday cakes. Thank you for every cannoli, every loaf and every conversation at the counter.
With love,
Frank and Teresa Russo

By lunchtime, the window was covered in sticky notes. “You made my mom's 90th birthday perfect,” said one. “Who's going to make the Easter bread now?” asked another.

On the sidewalk, Denise Carter, who has lived on the block since 1989, was taking a photo of the letter. “It's not just a bakery,” she said. “Frank knows everybody's name. When my husband was in the hospital, he sent bread to my house every day for a week and refused to take any money.”

Small, family-owned bakeries have been disappearing across the country for years. Rents have gone up, supermarkets sell cheap bread, and fewer young people want to do such hard physical work for small profits.

There may be a happy ending, however. Since the letter appeared, a young baker named Marisol Vega, who trained in New York, has contacted the Russos about renting the space. Frank has promised that, if she takes it, he'll teach her his grandmother's recipe for Easter bread. “Somebody has to,” he said.

title: Sixty Fridays Around the Table
body:
Five years ago this month, I sent a message to four friends: “Board games at my place, first Friday of the month? I'll make chili.” I expected it to last until summer. Last Friday, we played our sixtieth game night.

In that time, twenty-three different people have sat around my kitchen table in Winnipeg. Some came once and never returned. Others have hardly missed an evening, even in January, when it's minus thirty outside and the car takes ten minutes to warm up. My friend Kofi once walked twenty minutes through a snowstorm because the buses had stopped. He arrived with frozen eyebrows and a new game under his arm.

Over the years we've developed a few rules. The host chooses the first game, and everyone else brings snacks. Phones go in a basket by the door. Whoever comes last in the final game does the dishes. And arguments about the rules have to be settled by reading the instructions out loud, which usually takes longer than the argument.

Our favourite games have changed. In the first year, we played Catan almost every month, until Marc built so many roads that nobody else could win and we banned it for a while. Then we discovered cooperative games, where everyone plays together against the game. Those have saved several friendships.

Game night has also been there for the big moments. Jess and Daniel met at my table in year two and got married last fall. When Priyanka lost her job, we spent the evening playing a silly drawing game instead of strategy, because she needed to laugh, not think. And for the last few months, Kofi's nine-year-old daughter has joined us. She's already beaten all of us at chess.

People sometimes ask why we don't just meet at a bar. The answer is simple. At a bar, you talk. Around a game, you play, and somehow you talk more.

title: Two Buckets and a Lot of Sand
body:
Before we had children, Tom and I used to travel light. One backpack each, a cheap flight to Lisbon, and no plans beyond dinner. Last August we went on our first holiday as a family of four, and I can tell you: those days are over.

We had booked a cottage near St Ives in Cornwall, about five hours' drive from our home in Reading. A friend had warned me, “With small children, it isn't a holiday, it's a trip.” I laughed at the time. I'm not laughing now.

The packing alone took two evenings. Isla, who is four, insisted on bringing eleven soft toys, and Noah, who is eighteen months old, needed a travel cot, a buggy, nappies, snacks and his favourite blue blanket. By the time we had loaded the car, there was hardly any room left for us.

The journey should have taken five hours. It took eight. We stopped at three service stations, Noah was sick just outside Exeter, and we got stuck in a traffic jam on the A30 because a caravan had broken down. When we finally arrived, both children fell asleep instantly, and so did Tom.

The week itself was a mix of chaos and magic. It rained for two days, so we spent hours at the aquarium in Newquay and in a café that, luckily, had a play corner. But when the sun came out, we built sandcastles on Porthminster Beach and ate pasties on the harbour wall while seagulls tried to steal them.

Some things didn't go to plan. We never managed a proper restaurant meal, and I read exactly four pages of my novel. If I did it again, I would book somewhere with a garden and pack half as much.

Still, on the last evening Isla looked at the sea and said, “Can we live here forever?” Tom and I looked at each other. We were exhausted, but we had already started planning next summer.

title: Notes from a Math Tutor
body:
September 12
Today I met Sofia for the first time. I signed up for the university's tutoring program because I wanted to give something back, and because, honestly, it looks good on a résumé. Sofia is in eighth grade at a middle school in Pilsen, Chicago, and she is failing algebra. Her mom told me Sofia has been struggling since sixth grade. Sofia herself didn't say much. She just stared at the worksheet and said, “I'm bad at math. Everybody knows that.”

September 26
Two sessions in, and I've realized something: Sofia isn't bad at math. She's scared of it. When I ask her a question, she guesses quickly so that the moment is over. I've started telling her it's fine to be wrong, and that mistakes are how we figure things out. Today she solved an equation on her own and then checked it twice, as if she couldn't believe it.

October 17
I tried something new. Sofia loves basketball, so we worked out the shooting percentages of her favorite Chicago Sky players. Suddenly fractions and decimals made sense. She even corrected one of my calculations, which she found hilarious.

November 7
Bad week. She got a C minus on a test and almost gave up. She said, “What's the point? I'll never be like you.” I told her that I used to fail tests too, which is true. In high school my teacher had to stay after class with me twice a week. If he hadn't believed in me, I wouldn't be studying engineering now.

December 12
Last session before winter break. Sofia brought her report card to show me: a B in algebra. Her mom hugged me and gave me a box of homemade tamales. I've been tutoring her for three months now, and I'm honestly not sure who has learned more, Sofia or me.

title: Nana's Soda Bread
body:
For years, Aoife Brennan had bought her bread in a supermarket in Galway: sliced, wrapped in plastic and stale within three days. So when her grandmother, Bríd, offered to teach her how to make soda bread the way it was made in her own childhood, Aoife drove out to Connemara the very next Saturday.

Bríd's kitchen hadn't changed much in fifty years. There was a turf fire, a heavy black pot beside the hearth, and a wooden table covered in flour. “Your great-grandmother taught me at this table,” Bríd said. “I was seven, and I made a terrible mess.”

The recipe turned out to be shockingly simple: flour, salt, bread soda and buttermilk. No yeast, no machines, no waiting for hours. The difficult part, Bríd explained, was the feel of it. “You mustn't knead it like a city loaf. Handle it gently, or it'll be as hard as a rock.”

Aoife's first attempt was a disaster. She poured in too much buttermilk, and the dough stuck to everything, including her hair. Bríd just laughed and added another handful of flour. Then she showed Aoife how to shape the dough into a round and cut a deep cross on top. “That's to let the fairies out,” she said with a wink. “Or to help it cook evenly, if you don't believe in fairies.”

In the old days, the bread was baked in that black pot, which is called a bastible, with hot turf placed on the lid. Bríd still bakes this way at Christmas, but on ordinary days she uses the oven like everybody else.

Forty minutes later, the kitchen smelled wonderful. Bríd tapped the bottom of the loaf, and it sounded hollow, which meant it was ready. They ate it warm with salted butter and strong tea.

Since that day, Aoife has baked soda bread every Sunday. It's never quite as good as Nana's, but she's getting closer.

title: Who Gets the Credit?
body:
When Grace Chen became head of marketing at Maple Fizz, a small sparkling-drinks company in Toronto, she was told the team was “a bit tense.” Within a week, she realized that was an understatement.

The problem had started in the spring. Two of her team members, Omar Haddad and Jessica Tremblay, had worked together on a summer campaign called Taste the Lake. It was a huge success: sales went up by twenty per cent, and the campaign was mentioned in a national business magazine. But at the company party, the CEO thanked only Jessica, because she had presented the results. Omar, who had come up with the original idea, felt completely ignored.

Since then, the two of them had barely spoken. They sent each other cold emails and copied in half the office. In meetings, Omar criticized every suggestion Jessica made, and Jessica rolled her eyes whenever Omar talked. The rest of the team had begun to take sides, and two deadlines had already been missed.

Grace decided she couldn't let it go on. She met each of them separately first. Omar admitted he was hurt rather than angry. Jessica said she had tried to mention Omar's role, but the CEO had interrupted her. “I should have corrected him afterwards,” she told Grace. “I didn't, and that was wrong.”

Then Grace brought them together. It was an uncomfortable hour, but by the end they had agreed on a few simple rules: every project would list everyone who had contributed, and results would be presented as a team.

Grace also changed something herself. She now starts each Monday meeting by asking, “Who has done something great this week that nobody noticed?” At first people found it awkward. Now it's the team's favourite part of the week.

The atmosphere isn't perfect yet. But last month Omar and Jessica went out for lunch together, and nobody in the office could stop talking about it.

title: Kieran Does the Maths
body:
Kieran Walsh finished his plumbing apprenticeship in June, and two weeks later he was offered a full-time job with the same company in Salford. His pay went up to a salary of about £2,100 a month after tax. For the first time, moving out of his mum's house in Stockport seemed possible.

“Before you sign anything,” his mum said, “sit down and write a budget.” Kieran sighed, but he did it anyway. He has been glad ever since.

He found a one-bedroom flat in Eccles for £850 a month. Then he wrote down everything else he would have to pay:
Rent: £850
Council tax: £110
Gas and electricity: £120
Internet and phone: £45
Food: £250
Van insurance and fuel: £180
Gym: £25

That came to £1,580, which left him about £500. It looked like a lot until his older sister, Chloe, pointed out what he had forgotten: a TV licence, contents insurance, haircuts, presents, nights out and, most importantly, savings for emergencies. “If your boiler breaks or you need new tools, where does the money come from?” she asked. As a plumber, he couldn't really argue about boilers.

The upfront costs were another shock. The landlord asked for a deposit of five weeks' rent plus the first month in advance, which came to nearly £1,850. Luckily, Kieran had been putting money aside since he was seventeen, so he could just about afford it. He also bought a second-hand sofa and borrowed a bed frame from his uncle.

Kieran now follows a simple rule. Every payday, £200 goes straight into a savings account before he spends anything. He checks his banking app every Sunday and limits nights out to twice a month.

Three months in, he hasn't gone overdrawn once. “It's not glamorous,” he admits. “But nothing beats opening your own front door, even if the fridge is half empty.”

title: Mr Nguyen's New Routine
body:
Year 5 teacher Daniel Nguyen has taught at our school in Brisbane for nine years. Last year, at the age of 36, he was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes. He spoke to the school newsletter about how his life has changed.

How did you find out?
For months I was always thirsty and tired, and I'd lost eight kilos without trying. I thought it was just stress at the end of term. Then my wife made me see a GP. The blood test showed very high sugar levels, and I was sent straight to hospital. To be honest, I was terrified.

What does type 1 diabetes mean in everyday life?
My body no longer produces insulin, so I have to replace it. I wear a small sensor on my arm that measures my glucose all day, and I inject insulin before every meal. I also have to count the carbohydrates in everything I eat. At first I had to look up every sandwich and banana. Now I can estimate most meals in my head.

Has it affected your teaching?
A little. If my sugar drops too low, I can feel shaky and confused, so I always keep jelly beans in my desk drawer. The students know what they're for, and they're under strict instructions not to eat them! I've also explained my sensor to the class. They had loads of questions, and one boy asked if I was a robot.

What has been the hardest part?
Probably accepting that it won't go away. There's no day off from diabetes. On sports carnival day, for example, I have to plan my food and insulin very carefully, because exercise lowers my sugar.

Any advice for others?
Don't ignore the warning signs. If I had gone to the doctor sooner, I wouldn't have ended up in hospital. And don't be embarrassed to ask for help. My colleagues have been brilliant. One of them even started a staff walking group at lunchtime, which has done all of us good.

title: The Code That Wasn't for Me
body:
It was a Tuesday evening in Phoenix when Linda Morales got a message from her friend Teresa. “Hi! I accidentally sent you a six-digit code. Could you send it back to me? It's urgent!” Linda was cooking dinner, so she didn't think twice. She found the code in her texts, sent it, and went back to her enchiladas.

Ten minutes later, she was locked out of her own account.

The message hadn't really come from Teresa. Teresa's account had been hacked the day before, and the code Linda sent was the verification code for her own account. With it, the criminals could log in on their phone and take over her account. By nine o'clock, they had messaged dozens of her contacts: “I'm in trouble and need $400 for a car repair. Can you send it today? I'll pay you back tomorrow.”

Linda's phone started ringing nonstop. Her brother called, then a woman from her church. Most people were suspicious, because Linda never asks anyone for money. But one former colleague had already sent $250 through a payment app. That money was never recovered.

Linda's daughter, Camila, who works in IT, came over and helped her get the account back. It took two days and a lot of patience. Afterward, Camila gave her mother a short list of rules, which Linda has stuck on her fridge:
1. Never share a verification code with anyone, not even a friend.
2. Turn on two-step verification and choose a PIN.
3. If a friend asks for money by message, call them first.
4. Use a different password for every account.

Linda still feels embarrassed. “I've always thought of myself as careful,” she says. “But they caught me at a busy moment, and they used a friend's name. That's how they get you.”

Now, whenever she gets a strange message, she puts her phone down, takes a breath, and calls the person. “If it's really urgent,” she says, “they'll pick up.”

title: Six Months for One Day
body:
Every year on the last Saturday of February, the main street of Greytown in the Wairarapa is closed to traffic, and around eight thousand people arrive for the Greytown Summer Fair. Most visitors think it simply happens. Mere Tipene knows better. For the past three years, she has been the volunteer who organises it.

“People see the stalls, the music and the kids' rides,” she says, sitting in her kitchen surrounded by folders. “They don't see the six months of emails behind it.”

Planning begins in August. First, the committee of eight volunteers sets a budget and applies to the district council for permission to close the road. Then come the bookings: over a hundred stallholders, from beekeepers and potters to a family who sells the best whitebait fritters in the region. Mere has to make sure each stall has the right space and power, and that every food seller has a food safety certificate.

Health and safety takes up a surprising amount of time. There have to be first-aid volunteers, portable toilets, rubbish bins, a plan for lost children and a plan for bad weather. “Two years ago we had a storm warning the night before,” Mere remembers. “I didn't sleep at all. In the end the rain stopped at seven in the morning. I nearly cried.”

The fair is also where the community shows off. The local kapa haka group opens the day with a performance, the primary school runs a cake stall to raise money for new sports equipment, and the fire brigade lets children climb onto the fire engine.

Mere admits there are moments when she wonders why she does it. But every year, something reminds her. Last February, an elderly man came up to her and told her he had been to every fair since 1978. “He shook my hand and thanked me for keeping it going,” she says. “That's worth all the emails.”

title: Our Bin-Free February
body:
In January, I noticed something depressing. Our family of four was filling our black wheelie bin every single fortnight, and most of it was packaging. So my husband Chris and I made a decision: for the whole of February, we would try to send nothing to landfill. Our children, Tolu, 12, and Ada, 9, were less enthusiastic. Tolu asked if he would still be allowed crisps. The answer, sadly, was no.

Week one was a shock. I hadn't realised how much of our food came wrapped in plastic: cucumbers, cheese, bread, even bananas. We started shopping at a refill shop on Gloucester Road here in Bristol, where you bring your own jars and fill them with pasta, rice, oats and washing-up liquid. It took twice as long as the supermarket, and I felt slightly ridiculous carrying a bag of empty jam jars across the city.

By week two, we had got into a routine. Chris bakes bread on Sundays, we buy milk in glass bottles from a local dairy, and the butcher happily puts meat into our own containers. Ada became the family's waste inspector and checked the recycling every evening with great seriousness.

Not everything worked. Chris's homemade toothpaste tasted like chalk and was quietly abandoned after four days. Birthday parties were difficult too: Ada came home from one with a plastic party bag, and we decided not to make a fuss. Some rules are made to be broken.

At the end of the month, everything we couldn't recycle or compost fitted into one large jam jar. Compared with a full bin, that's a huge difference.

Will we carry on? Not completely. Living totally waste-free takes time that we don't always have. But we've kept the habits that were easy: the refill shop, the milk bottles, the cloth bags. And Tolu has negotiated one packet of crisps a week. I think that's a fair compromise.

title: A Year on My Own
body:
Hi Jordan,

You asked me what my first year as a freelance translator has really been like, so here's the honest version, not the one I post online.

When I left the translation agency in Montreal last October, I thought the hardest part would be finding clients. It wasn't. Through old colleagues, I had three regular clients within a month: a law firm, a tourism board and a company that makes snowmobiles. I translate their documents from French into English, and I've learned more about snowmobile engines than I ever wanted to know.

The hardest part has been the money. Clients often take sixty days to pay, and one small company still hasn't paid an invoice from March. In January I earned almost nothing, and in May I earned more than I used to make in three months. If I hadn't saved six months of expenses before I quit, I would have panicked. Also, nobody warned me about taxes. Because I'm self-employed, I have to put money aside for income tax and pay it in instalments. I now keep thirty per cent of every payment in a separate account and never touch it.

Then there's the loneliness. At the agency I used to complain about my noisy colleagues. Now I miss them. Some days the only person I speak to is the barista at the café downstairs. I've started working from a co-working space twice a week, which has helped a lot.

But the freedom is wonderful. I choose my projects, I go cross-country skiing on Mount Royal on quiet weekday mornings, and I can say no to work I don't like. Last month I turned down a huge project because the deadline was impossible, and the sky didn't fall.

My advice? Save before you start, charge what you're worth, and get a good accountant. Oh, and buy a proper chair. My back has never forgiven me for the kitchen stool.

Call me if you want to talk it through.

Nadia

title: Cars Out, Scooters In
body:
Parents and pupils at Elmwood Primary School in Lewisham, south-east London, are celebrating after the council agreed to make the school's “School Street” permanent.

Since a trial began last September, Hollydale Road has been closed to cars for forty-five minutes at the start and end of every school day. Only residents, delivery vans and emergency vehicles are allowed through. Anyone else who drives into the zone during those times is caught on camera and fined £130.

The idea was first suggested by a group of parents who were worried about safety and air pollution. “Before, the road was chaos every morning,” says Harriet Osei, whose two children attend the school. “Cars were double-parked, engines were running, and the kids had to squeeze between them. Someone was going to get hurt.”

Now the street looks very different. Children arrive on scooters and bikes, and a teacher plays music at the gate. According to the council, the share of pupils who walk, cycle or scoot to school has risen from 58 to 74 per cent. Air quality monitors outside the school have also recorded lower levels of nitrogen dioxide.

However, not everyone is happy. Some residents say the traffic has simply moved to neighbouring streets. Dev Patel, who owns a corner shop nearby, claims he has lost customers. “People used to stop for a newspaper on the way to drop-off,” he says. “Now they don't come this way.” A few parents who work far from home also complain that they have to park further away and are often late for work.

The council says it has listened to these concerns. It will introduce a new pedestrian crossing on the main road and review traffic in the surrounding area after six months.

For the children, though, the decision is simple. “It's quieter, and I can ride my scooter right up to the gate,” says Maya, aged eight. “I wish every road was like this.”

title: Opening Night at the Parish Hall
body:
When Siobhán O'Leary put a notice in the window of the Ballincollig library last January, she wasn't sure anyone would answer it. “New drama group. No experience needed. Tea and biscuits provided.” Eleven people turned up to the first meeting, including a retired postman, two teenage sisters, a nurse who worked night shifts and a man who admitted he had only come for the biscuits.

None of them had acted before, apart from Siobhán, who had been in school plays forty years earlier. They chose a comedy written by one of the members, a retired English teacher called Dermot. It was a murder mystery set in a crumbling hotel on the west coast, and it had far too many characters, so some people had to play two parts.

Rehearsals took place every Tuesday and Thursday in the parish hall. At first, it was hard work. People forgot their lines, laughed at the wrong moments and walked into the furniture. The postman, Gerry, had terrible stage fright and could only rehearse with his back to the empty seats. But slowly, things came together. The nurse turned out to be a brilliant comic actor, and the sisters painted the scenery, which looked surprisingly professional.

The play was put on for three nights in May. On opening night, the hall was packed with friends, family and neighbours. Not everything went smoothly. The lights went out during the second act, the “dead” body sneezed loudly, and a door fell off the set. But the audience assumed it was all part of the comedy and laughed even harder.

The biggest cheer of the night was for Gerry. He delivered every line facing the audience, without a single mistake. Afterwards, his wife said she hadn't seen him so happy in years.

The group raised €2,400 for the local hospice in Cork. They have already started rehearsing their next play, and this time they have twenty-three members. The man who came for the biscuits is now in charge of the lighting.

title: My New Colleague Never Sleeps
body:
Three months ago, an email arrived from our CEO with a cheerful subject line: “Meet your new teammate!” The teammate, it turned out, was an AI assistant. From that Monday, every employee at our Denver accounting firm could use it to write emails, summarize reports and search through thousands of client documents in seconds.

The reaction in the office was mixed, to put it mildly. Some colleagues were excited. Others were openly worried. “If it can do half my job,” my coworker Luis said at lunch, “why would they keep paying me?” Nobody had a good answer.

I'll admit that I was a skeptic. I have worked here for eleven years, and I've seen plenty of new systems come and go. But after a few weeks, I had to change my mind about some things. The assistant is extremely good at boring tasks. It can turn a messy two-hour meeting into a one-page summary. It drafts polite replies to angry clients faster than I can make coffee. I now leave work on time far more often than I used to.

However, it has some serious weaknesses. Last month it confidently gave me a tax rule that simply doesn't exist. If I hadn't checked, a client could have paid the wrong amount. That's the danger: it never sounds unsure, even when it's wrong.

There's also a human cost that is harder to measure. Junior staff used to learn the job by doing the dull work, the summaries and first drafts. If the machine does all of that, how will they learn?

So, is it help or a threat? For now, I'd say it's a bit of both. It hasn't replaced anyone in our office, and I don't think it should. But it has changed what a good employee looks like. The people who do best are not the ones who know the most facts, but the ones who ask the right questions and notice when an answer looks wrong.

Luis, by the way, is still here. He now uses the assistant more than anyone.

title: Forty Years in Boxes
body:
The house in Glenelg had belonged to the Kowalski family for forty-two years. When their mother, Barbara, moved into an aged care home in March, her three children agreed it was time to sell. Before the house could be put on the market, though, someone had to clear it out. So on a hot Saturday in April, Megan, Josh and Anna met on the front verandah with a car full of empty boxes and very different ideas.

Megan, the eldest, had brought a strict plan: keep, donate, throw away. “If nobody has used it in five years, it goes,” she announced. Josh, who lives in Darwin and hadn't been home in two years, wanted to keep almost everything. Anna, the youngest, mostly wanted to avoid an argument.

The kitchen was easy. Their mother had kept every ice-cream container she had ever bought, and nobody fought over those. The garage was harder. Their late father had been a carpenter, and his tools were still hanging exactly where he had left them. Josh picked up a worn wooden plane and turned it over in his hands. “He taught me to use this when I was ten,” he said quietly. Megan put down her clipboard. The plane went into the keep pile.

By the second day, the tension was building. Megan accused Josh of turning the house into a museum, and Josh said Megan was treating their childhood like rubbish. Anna finally lost her patience and made them sit down with a cup of tea. They agreed on a new rule: each of them could choose ten special things, no questions asked. Everything else would be shared out or given to charity.

In the end, the hardest room was the spare bedroom. Inside the wardrobe they found a shoebox full of letters their parents had written to each other in 1979, when Dad was working in the mines up north. The three of them sat on the floor and read them aloud, laughing and crying.

They kept the letters, of course. Next Sunday, they're taking them to read to Mum.
