title: My Landlady Is Eighty-Four
body:
When I got my place at the University of Edinburgh to study veterinary medicine, I was thrilled. Then I looked at the rents. A room in a shared flat near the campus cost more than my whole student loan. That's when my mum found a homeshare scheme online.

The idea is simple. An older person with a spare room offers it to a young person for very little money. In exchange, the young person helps around the house for about ten hours a week and spends some evenings at home. It isn't care work: you don't give medicine or help anyone wash. You're more like a useful, slightly messy grandchild.

That's how I met Margaret. She's eighty-four, a former maths teacher, and has lived in the same stone house in Morningside since 1971. Her husband died three years ago, and her son lives in Singapore. He worried about her being alone, especially in winter.

Our first week was awkward. Margaret had very firm opinions about how to load a dishwasher, and I had very firm opinions about sleeping until ten. We had to set some ground rules. I do the big shop on Saturdays, take the bins out, and cook dinner on Tuesdays and Thursdays. I let her know if I'm staying out late. She doesn't comment on my music. Mostly.

What surprised me was how much I'd get out of it. Margaret is brilliant company. She helped me with the statistics in my first-year course, and she beats me at Scrabble every single time. In return, I've taught her to video call her grandchildren, which she now does every Sunday morning.

Of course, it isn't for everyone. My friends sometimes tease me that I live with my gran, and I can't exactly throw parties. But I pay £150 a month instead of £750, and I've got a friend I didn't expect to have.

Last week Margaret was in hospital for two nights after a fall. I visited every day. When she came home, she squeezed my hand and said, “I'm glad it was you who answered that advert.” So am I.

title: Cash in Envelopes
body:
Two years ago, Brianna and Tyler Jackson sat at their kitchen table in Columbus, Ohio, and finally added up what they owed. The number shocked them both: $18,400 on three credit cards, plus a car loan. “We both had good jobs,” says Brianna, a dental hygienist. “We just had no idea where the money was going.”

A friend at church suggested the envelope method, an old-fashioned way of budgeting that their grandparents might have used. At the start of each month, you take out your spending money in cash and divide it into envelopes, one for each category: groceries, gas, eating out, clothes, entertainment. When an envelope is empty, you stop spending in that category until next month. No exceptions, and no borrowing from the other envelopes.

The first month was painful. The eating-out envelope, which held $120, was empty by the tenth. “We'd been spending about $600 a month on takeout and restaurants without noticing,” Tyler admits. “Swiping a card doesn't feel like real money. Handing over actual twenty-dollar bills does.”

They also cut up two of the credit cards and canceled several streaming subscriptions they rarely watched. Every dollar they saved went toward the debt, starting with the card that had the highest interest rate. Tyler started driving for a delivery app on weekends, and Brianna sold furniture they no longer needed.

It wasn't always easy. There were arguments, especially about birthdays and Christmas presents, and once Tyler “borrowed” from the grocery envelope to buy concert tickets. He hasn't been allowed to forget it.

Last month, after twenty-two months, they made their final credit card payment. They celebrated with a dinner out, paid for, of course, from the eating-out envelope.

These days they use a budgeting app instead of paper envelopes, but the rule is the same. “If you'd told me two years ago that I'd enjoy budgeting, I'd have laughed,” says Brianna. “Now I feel like I'm in control.”

title: Forty-Two Kilometres and a Banana
body:
A year ago, I couldn't run for a bus without getting out of breath. Last Sunday, at the age of forty-one, I crossed the finish line of the Dublin Marathon on Merrion Square. It took me four hours, fifty-one minutes and twelve seconds, and I have never been prouder of anything in my life.

It started as a dare. My sister Ciara, who runs half-marathons for fun, bet me I couldn't do a 5K. I joined a beginners' group at the local athletics club in Lucan, and after eight weeks of slowly building up, I ran the whole parkrun without stopping. Then I got a bit carried away and signed up for the marathon.

Training took up most of my free time for six months. I ran four times a week, usually before work, in the dark and the rain. My long runs on Sundays got longer and longer until I reached thirty-two kilometres. I lost two toenails, wore out three pairs of trainers and learned that you should never try a new energy gel on race day.

On the morning itself, I was so nervous I could barely eat. The first half went well. The crowds were incredible: people played music, handed out jelly babies and shouted my name, which was printed on my vest. But at about thirty kilometres, I hit the wall. My legs felt like concrete, and a voice in my head kept telling me to stop. I walked for a few minutes and ate a banana a stranger offered me. I'll never know her name, but she saved my race.

The last two kilometres were the hardest and the best. I could hear the noise from the finish long before I could see it. Ciara was waiting behind the barrier, crying even more than I was.

Will I do another one? Ask me again in a month. My legs are still recovering. But I've already looked at the dates for next year.

title: Tacos on Wheels
body:
When Dani Flores quit her job as a line cook in a downtown Austin hotel, her coworkers thought she was crazy. “You're giving up a steady paycheck for a truck?” one of them asked. A year later, Dani's food truck, Morning Glory, sells around three hundred breakfast tacos a day, and she has two employees of her own.

Getting started was harder than she had expected. She bought a used truck for $45,000, using her savings and a small business loan. Then came the paperwork: a health permit, a fire inspection, a business license and insurance. The truck failed its first inspection because the hand-washing sink was too small. “I cried in the parking lot,” she remembers. “Then I called a plumber.”

Location turned out to be everything. For the first two months, Dani parked near an office building, but sales were disappointing because most people brought lunch from home. A friend suggested a food truck park in East Austin that was popular with students and early-morning cyclists. She moved there in March, and her sales doubled within a month.

The days are long. Dani gets up at four to prepare the fillings, and the truck opens at six thirty. After closing, there is cleaning, shopping and social media, because most of her customers find her on Instagram. In the summer, the temperature inside the truck can reach 110 degrees. She has learned to freeze wet towels overnight and wear them around her neck.

There have been disasters, too. In August the generator broke down on a Saturday morning, her busiest day, and she lost about $1,200 in sales. A hailstorm in April damaged the roof.

Still, Dani has no regrets. Her favorite moment is when regulars order “the usual” and she already knows what they mean. She is now saving for a second truck. “I used to cook other people's recipes,” she says. “Now every taco is mine.”

title: A Letter to Our Readers
body:
Dear readers,

For 112 years, the South Shore Beacon has been printed every Thursday here in Bridgewater, Nova Scotia. It has reported on two world wars, the closing of the fish plant, and every high school hockey final since 1950. This year, I'm sorry to say, we came very close to printing our last edition.

I don't need to explain why. Most of you now read the news on your phones, often for free. At the same time, the money from advertising has dropped by more than half in ten years, because local businesses can reach customers more cheaply online. When I became editor in 2009, we had fourteen staff. Today there are five of us, and I take most of the photos myself.

In the spring, our owners told us that unless something changed, the paper would close by Christmas. So we asked you for help, and you answered.

Over three hundred of you came to a public meeting at the Legion hall in May. You told us what you value: council meetings, school news, obituaries and the court reports that no big national website will ever cover. One retired teacher asked, “If nobody is watching the town council, who will?” I haven't stopped thinking about that.

Since then, several things have changed. We have become a non-profit organization, which means we can now accept donations. We have launched a digital subscription for $6 a month, and 1,400 of you have already signed up. A local credit union has agreed to sponsor our sports pages, and students from the community college are joining us as interns.

We are not safe yet. We still need around 600 more subscribers to break even next year. But for the first time in a long time, I feel hopeful.

Thank you for reading, for arguing with us on the letters page, and for caring about local news. See you next Thursday.

Ian MacDonald
Editor

title: Five Hours Behind
body:
Orla Quinn and Ravi Mehta met at a friend's wedding in Belfast. He was over from Toronto for a week, and they spent most of the reception talking on the steps outside. When he flew home, they both assumed that would be the end of it. It wasn't. That was two and a half years ago.

Since then, their relationship has mostly happened on screens. Toronto is five hours behind Belfast, so when Ravi finishes work at six, it's already eleven at night for Orla. During the week they usually manage a short video call before she goes to bed, and on Sundays they have a longer “date”: they cook the same recipe at the same time and eat together, three thousand miles apart.

They see each other in person about four times a year. Flights aren't cheap, so they both save hard, and they take turns crossing the Atlantic. Orla says the airport goodbyes never get easier. “Every time, I tell myself I won't cry at security,” she says. “Every time, I cry at security.”

There have been difficult moments. Last winter, Ravi's father was ill, and Orla felt useless being so far away. Small misunderstandings can also grow when you can't see someone's face. “If we lived in the same city, a lot of our arguments would be over in five minutes,” Ravi admits. “On a bad video connection, they can last all weekend.”

Friends have often asked them how long they can keep it up. The honest answer is: not for ever. So last month they finally made a decision. Ravi's company has an office in London, and he has asked for a transfer. If it's approved, he will move to the UK next spring, and Orla will look for a job in London too.

Neither of them knows exactly what life in the same time zone will be like. “I'm a bit nervous, to be honest,” Orla laughs. “I've never seen him in the morning before he's had his coffee.”

title: The Only Dad at the Table
body:
I'll be honest: I joined the Parent Council at my daughter's primary school by accident. At the start of the year, a letter came home asking for volunteers. I put it in the recycling. A week later, at the school gate, the chair of the council, a very persuasive woman called Fiona, asked me if I'd ever thought about getting involved. Before I knew it, I had agreed to come to a meeting.

In Scotland, every state school has a Parent Council: a group of parents who work with the head teacher, raise money and give families a voice in school decisions. I'd always imagined it as a club for mums with lots of free time. At my first meeting in the school library in Partick, Glasgow, I discovered I was right about one thing: I was the only dad there. I was wrong about the free time. One member was a nurse who came straight from a night shift; another ran her own bakery.

The first few meetings were confusing. People talked about “the SIP,” “the PEF money” and “the cluster,” and I didn't want to admit I had no idea what any of it meant. Eventually I asked. Fiona made me a list of the abbreviations.

Since then, I've found my place. I work in IT, so I set up an online form that lets parents vote on ideas instead of coming to evening meetings. Within a month, more parents had given their opinion than in the whole of the previous year. We've also organised a sponsored walk that raised £1,800 for new playground equipment, and we persuaded the city council to fix the broken crossing light outside the gate.

Has it been worth it? Yes, although it takes more time than I expected, around four hours a month. My daughter, Freya, is less impressed. “Dad,” she told me last week, “please stop waving at my teacher.”

At the last meeting, two more dads turned up. I'm calling it progress.

title: Twenty Years, Then Day One
body:
I smoked my first cigarette at sixteen, behind the bike sheds at my school in Leeds. I didn't even like it. Twenty years later, I was smoking twenty a day, spending over £300 a month, and coughing every morning like an old man.

I had tried to quit before, many times. Usually I lasted about three days. The problem wasn't just the nicotine; it was the habit. A cigarette went with everything: my morning coffee, the bus stop, a stressful phone call, the end of a meal. Without one, I didn't know what to do with my hands.

What finally changed my mind was my son. He was seven and had started learning about health at school. One evening he asked me, very seriously, “Mum, are you going to die?” I couldn't answer him. The next morning I rang my GP surgery, and they referred me to the local NHS Stop Smoking service.

I'd always thought quitting was about willpower. My adviser, Graham, told me that was only part of it. People who get support are about three times more likely to succeed than people who try on their own. Every week I went to see him, and he measured the carbon monoxide in my breath with a little machine. Watching the number fall was surprisingly motivating. I also used nicotine patches during the day and nicotine gum when the cravings were really bad.

The first two weeks were awful. I was irritable, I couldn't sleep, and I ate an enormous number of biscuits. Graham explained that each craving only lasts a few minutes, so I learned to wait them out: I went for a walk, drank a glass of water, or texted my sister. I also changed my routines. I started drinking tea instead of coffee in the mornings, because coffee made me want to light up.

It's now been eleven months. I can walk up the hill to my house without stopping, food tastes better, and I've saved enough money for a holiday in Spain. I still miss it sometimes, especially at parties. But my son is very proud of me, and so am I.

title: The Honda in the Shed
body:
For as long as I can remember, there was a motorbike under a blue tarp at the back of Dad's shed in Wagga Wagga. It was a 1974 Honda CB350, and he had bought it when he was nineteen with money from his first job at the abattoir. He rode it everywhere until I was born. Then Mum made him promise to stop, and the bike hadn't moved since.

Last summer I was home from uni for three months with no job and no plans. One evening, Dad lifted the tarp and said, “Reckon we could get her going again?” I knew nothing about engines. I said yes anyway.

The bike was in a terrible state. The tyres were flat, the seat had been chewed by mice, and the petrol tank was rusty inside. Dad was patient with me in a way I don't remember from when I was a teenager. He showed me how to take the carburettors apart, clean every tiny piece and put them back together in the right order. I labelled everything in plastic bags and took photos on my phone, because I didn't trust my memory.

Finding parts was the hardest part. Some we ordered from a specialist in Melbourne; others came from a man in Bathurst who had a garage full of old Hondas and very strong opinions. We spent a whole Saturday driving there and back for a single chrome mirror.

We argued, of course. Dad hates reading instructions, and I hate guessing. But somewhere between the oil changes and the burnt fingers, we started talking about things we had never talked about before: his parents, his years at the meatworks, the reasons he gave up riding.

After eleven weeks, the moment came. Dad turned the key and kicked the starter. Nothing. He tried again. On the third kick the engine coughed, then roared into life, and the whole shed filled with smoke. Dad laughed so hard he had to sit down.

He's taken it for a few rides since then, slowly, with Mum's permission. And next summer, he says, he's going to teach me to ride it.

title: Fridays Off at Pine Street Design
body:
When the owner of Pine Street Design, a 22-person web design studio in Portland, Oregon, announced a six-month trial of a four-day workweek, half of her staff thought it was a joke. “I honestly checked the calendar to see if it was April Fools' Day,” says senior designer Marcus Lee.

It wasn't. Starting in January, everyone at the company worked Monday to Thursday, eight hours a day, for the same salary as before. The office was closed on Fridays, and nobody was expected to answer emails. Clients were told in advance, and a small team stayed on call in case of emergencies.

Owner Jenna Kowalczyk says she had been worried about burnout for a long time. “Two of my best designers quit last year because they were exhausted,” she explains. “Hiring and training new people is expensive. I thought, what if we tried something completely different?”

To make the shorter week work, the team had to change how they worked. Meetings were limited to thirty minutes, and Wednesday afternoons became “focus time,” when nobody was allowed to schedule calls. Staff also started using a shared project board, so they spent less time asking each other for updates.

The results surprised even Jenna. According to the company's own figures, projects were delivered on time just as often as before, and client satisfaction went up slightly. Sick days dropped by almost forty percent. In an anonymous survey, nineteen of the twenty-two employees said they felt less stressed.

It hasn't been perfect. Some clients complained that they couldn't reach anyone on a Friday, and the on-call team sometimes felt they were working a five-day week after all. Marcus admits that Thursdays can be intense. “You can't waste time on Thursday afternoon, because there's no Friday to catch up,” he says.

Most employees use the extra day for family, hobbies or errands. Marcus has started volunteering at a community garden.

In July, the trial officially ended. Jenna has decided to make the four-day week permanent. “If the work gets done and people are happier,” she says, “why would I go back?”

title: Counting Chickadees at Dawn
body:
At six o'clock on a freezing Saturday in December, I was standing in a field outside Middlebury, Vermont, with binoculars around my neck and no feeling in my toes. Next to me, Dorothy Martel, who is seventy-eight, was writing in a notebook with a pencil, because, she said, “pens freeze.” We were taking part in the Christmas Bird Count, one of the oldest wildlife surveys in the world.

The count has been running since 1900, when a bird lover suggested that people should count birds at Christmas instead of shooting them, which was a holiday tradition back then. Today, tens of thousands of volunteers across the Americas take part. Each group covers a circle about fifteen miles wide and counts every bird it sees or hears on one day between mid-December and early January. Scientists use the results to track how bird populations are changing.

I signed up because my biology teacher offered extra credit. I expected a boring day. I was wrong.

Dorothy has done the count in this same area for forty-one years, and she can identify a bird from a tiny movement in a tree. Our group of four walked along farm roads, stopped at feeders in people's yards, and stood at the edge of a frozen pond for twenty minutes, waiting for a heron that never appeared. We counted 63 black-capped chickadees, 14 blue jays, a woodpecker and, to everyone's excitement, a snowy owl sitting on a fence post. Dorothy said she hadn't seen one there in six years.

Not all the news was good. Dorothy told me that some species she used to see every year, like the evening grosbeak, have almost disappeared from her lists. Warmer winters are changing where birds can survive. “That's exactly why we count,” she said. “If nobody writes it down, nobody notices.”

At the end of the day, all the groups met at the town library to add up their numbers over hot chili. I was cold, tired and completely hooked. I've already promised Dorothy I'll be back next year, extra credit or not.

title: Swapping Seattle for York
body:
Last August, the Henderson family from Seattle spent two weeks living in a terraced house in York, while the Ahmed family from York lived in the Hendersons' home near Green Lake. Nobody paid any rent, and nobody booked a hotel. They simply swapped houses.

House swapping has become more popular in recent years, especially with families. The idea is simple: you join a website, list your home and look for someone who wants to visit your area while you visit theirs. The two families had never met. They found each other online in January and spent months exchanging emails and video calls before agreeing.

“At first I was nervous about strangers sleeping in our beds,” admits Sana Ahmed, a pharmacist and mother of three. “But after a few calls with Kate Henderson, it felt more like lending our house to a friend.” Both families wrote a guide to their homes: how the washing machine worked, which neighbour had a spare key, where the best playground was, and which bin went out on which day.

For the Hendersons, living in a real neighbourhood was the highlight. Instead of eating in restaurants every night, they shopped at the local market, walked the city walls and learned to love a proper Sunday roast at the pub round the corner. Their two sons were amazed by the age of everything. “Our house in Seattle was built in 1985,” says Kate. “The pub near the Ahmeds' house is older than our country.”

There were a few surprises. The Hendersons couldn't work out the Ahmeds' boiler and had to ask a neighbour for help. Meanwhile, in Seattle, the Ahmeds discovered that American fridges are enormous and that almost nothing is within walking distance.

Both families saved thousands of pounds, or dollars, on accommodation. But they say the best part wasn't the money. “It felt like we lived there for a while, not just visited,” says Sana. The families have stayed in touch, and the Hendersons' boys have already asked if the Ahmed children can visit next summer.

title: Take a Book, Leave a Book
body:
Rhys Morgan has lived on Severn Grove in Cardiff for eight years, but until last spring he knew only two of his neighbours by name. That changed because of a box.

It started when Rhys and his partner cleared out their spare room before their baby was born. They had six bags of books and no idea what to do with them. The charity shops were full. “It felt wrong to throw books away,” he says. So he took an old kitchen cupboard, added a glass door and a little roof, painted it bright yellow and fixed it to a post outside his front garden. On the door he wrote: Take a book, leave a book. Llyfrau am ddim. (That means “free books” in Welsh.)

Then he posted a message in the street's group chat:
Rhys: Hi all, I've put a book box outside number 14. Help yourselves!
Glenys (no. 3): What a lovely idea. I've got loads of crime novels for it.
Sam (no. 22): Is it OK to leave kids' books?
Rhys: Of course!

Within a week, the box was full. People left cookbooks, thrillers, Welsh poetry, travel guides and a surprising number of books about bees. Children started leaving drawings inside for whoever opened the door next. Glenys, who is eighty-one and rarely leaves the house, began reviewing every book she borrowed on little cards and leaving them inside the covers.

There have been problems. Once, someone emptied the whole box and probably sold the books online. Another time, heavy rain got in and ruined a pile of paperbacks. Rhys fixed the roof, and within two days the neighbours had filled the box again. “That was when I realised it wasn't really my box any more,” he says. “It belongs to the street.”

The box has led to other things too. The street now holds a summer party, and a few neighbours have started a monthly book club in the local café. Rhys's daughter, Elin, is now six months old. Her first book, he says proudly, came from the box.

title: Gloria Gets Her Feet Wet
body:
Gloria Washington has lived in Florida for forty years, a short drive from some of the most beautiful beaches in the country. Until this year, she had never swum in the sea. In fact, until she was seventy, she couldn't swim at all.

As a child in rural Georgia in the 1960s, Gloria never had the chance to learn. The public pool in her town was for white residents only, and when it was finally supposed to open to everyone, the town closed it instead. Her parents couldn't swim either, and they warned her to stay away from rivers and lakes. Over the years, that warning turned into fear. “Even in the bath, I didn't like water on my face,” she says.

Things changed last summer at her granddaughter's birthday party. While all the other adults were splashing in a friend's pool in Tampa, Gloria sat on a plastic chair holding everyone's towels. Her granddaughter, Jada, who is nine, asked her why she never came in. “I didn't have a good answer,” Gloria says. “I just felt ashamed.”

The next week, she signed up for an adult beginners' class at her local YMCA. There were six people in the group, all over fifty, and an instructor called Luis, who was endlessly patient. For the first two lessons, Gloria wouldn't let go of the side of the pool. In the third, she put her face in the water and blew bubbles. “That was a big day,” she laughs. “I celebrated with ice cream.”

Progress was slow. She had to learn to float, to breathe, and above all, to trust the water. Several times she nearly gave up. But by Christmas she could swim a full length of the pool, and by March she could swim ten.

In April, the whole family went to Clearwater Beach. Gloria walked into the Gulf of Mexico wearing a new purple swimsuit, took a deep breath and swam out to Jada, who was waiting for her with her arms open.

“People say it's too late to learn things at my age,” Gloria says. “I say it's only too late if you don't start.”
